### Dedication

...religion, which has made God love you and the world honor you. The truth of this religion and the visibility of our Church of England is made manifest in this history over the last four hundred and fifty years. This refutes that common and trivial objection of our common adversary <note>original: "Aduerſarie" (a standard term for the Roman Catholic Church in Protestant polemics of this era)</note> that our religion began with Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546). Catholic critics often argued that if Protestantism was the true faith, it should have been visible throughout history rather than appearing suddenly in 1517. May the Lord in His infinite mercy make you always constant in the profession and defense of the same truth and religion in which you have been born and raised. As your love toward God increases daily, may God’s love toward you increase as well, to your everlasting honor in this life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

# TO THE MOST
# HIGH AND POWERFUL
## LORD, FRANCIS DE BONNE,
->Duke, Peer, and Marshal (now Constable)<-
->of *France*, *Lieutenant General* for his *Ma*-<-

My very good Lord, this history rightly belongs to you, and you may claim it as your due for many reasons. First, because the most populous churches of the Waldensians <note>The Waldensians (or Vaudois) were a pre-Reformation Christian movement that faced centuries of persecution for their beliefs, which the later Protestants saw as a precursor to their own faith.</note> are within the territory and borders of your government. They have had no time to breathe in liberty except when, about forty years ago, you defended them from the outrages of their enemies both within and outside the Kingdom. As God cheered them up by His goodness, they have found sure protection through your love and favor, and a strong bulwark under your name. Furthermore, the proofs of the sufferings of their forefathers in past ages are the holy prizes and spoils that were captured during the taking of Embrun <note>original: "Ambrun," a city in the French Alps that was a stronghold of the Catholic Church during the Wars of Religion.</note>, when you brought that city under the King’s authority. The Archbishops of that place have carefully kept, for more than the last four hundred years, the legal records and proceedings against the said Waldensian churches. These records have brought upon those who persecuted them an everlasting <meta>The catchword "fting" indicates the sentence concludes on the next page, likely as "everlasting infamy."</meta>

<summary>This page introduces a dedication to Francis de Bonne, Duke of Lesdiguières, a French military leader who protected the Waldensian communities in Dauphiné. The author explains that the Duke is the rightful patron of this history because of his military defense of these people and his capture of historical records of their persecution from the Archbishops of Embrun.</summary>
<keywords>Francis de Bonne, Duke of Lesdiguières, Waldensians, Dauphiné, Embrun, religious persecution, French Wars of Religion, church history, legal records</keywords>

...everlasting shame and dishonor. On the contrary, these events have immortalized the piety and judgment of that follower of yours who saved the bag containing the records of those legal proceedings <note>original: "processe," referring here to the inquisitorial records or legal documents used against the Waldensians.</note> from the fire of the Archbishop of that place. The enemy attempted to block his access to the Tower where they were ultimately saved.

It was the Lord of Vulçon <note>Marc Vulson de la Colombière, a counselor in the Parliament of Grenoble and a noted historian.</note>, Counselor to the King in the Parliament at Grenoble, who recovered them and brought them to our hands. In all that conquest, he was satisfied with only that bag of documents—records that indict the devil himself and all his followers—which have been preserved for the good and spiritual growth of the Church of God. When all this is considered, this benefit comes from you, my Lord, and is the fruit of your military victories.

Having therefore decided to publish this history under your name, I have simply returned it to its original source by restoring it to its first benefactor and dedicating this work <note>original: "edifice"</note> to the man who provided its most substantial material. In doing so, I have given the work greater authority, as I have dedicated it to one who has seen and known more about the state of the Waldensians than I could ever write. 

In this, the work of God especially shows itself, seeing how men of the same name and from the same province have had such different intentions. For it is over three hundred years since the noble Arroas de Bonne <note>An ancestor of the Duke who participated in early persecutions of the Waldensians in the 13th century.</note> persecuted the ancestors of those whom our noble and great Francis de Bonne has now restored. Thus the eternal God knows how, when it pleases Him, to make the light of His mercy shine from the very same family line <note>original: "stemme"</note> from which previously sprang nothing but darkness. May you have many long and happy years...

<meta>This page begins the preface to the work, following the author's dedication to the Duke of Lesdiguières. It introduces the historical argument for the continuity of the Protestant faith through the Waldenses and Albigenses.</meta>

# THE PREFACE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring swirling vine and floral motifs.</image-desc> The Church of God in the world is held in higher esteem than the world itself. It is the reward <note>original: "fruition," meaning the result or enjoyment of labor</note> of our Lord Jesus Christ. He was crucified for it, and without it, nothing can be considered good. But just as our Redeemer invites <note>original: "inuiteth"</note> us to enter and to continue within it for our salvation, so Satan endeavors to make men wander from the right way to their damnation. He blinds them so that they might mistake something for the Church which has only the name of it, keeping them in error and seducing them with a worldly, glorious pomp. Thus, he makes them disdain the true Church, primarily because it is subject to persecution in the world. In such a state, those who do not honor the Master cannot cherish the servants. 

Consequently, because they do not acknowledge any other Church than the one that has triumphed for many ages through the blood of those martyrs whom it has killed, they demand with great persistence <note>original: "importunitie"</note>: what was the Catholic <note>original: "Catholicke Church," here used in the sense of the "universal" church</note> Church, and in what parts of the world has it been, if that which has so long and peacefully held the title is not the true one? "Where was it hidden," they ask, "during the last five hundred years <note>original: "fiue ages," referring to the five centuries preceding the Reformation</note>?" They insist that we show them at least one person, in the whole course of so many years, who believed that which has been so highly praised in our times under the name of Reformation.

This history of the Christians called Waldenses and Albigenses will satisfy those who can read it without bias <note>original: "paſſion"</note>. For it reveals that for these last four hundred and fifty years, there have been (especially in Europe) a great number of people in various kingdoms and countries who have made a profession of a religion entirely conforming to the Word of God and the doctrine received in the Reformed Churches. They have mourned under the dark—

<sig>A 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: darkness <note>original: "neffe," completing the word "darkenesse"</note></meta>

<summary>In this preface, the author argues that the Waldenses and Albigenses prove the historical continuity of the Protestant faith, countering the Roman Catholic challenge to show where the "Reformed" church existed before the 16th century.</summary>
<keywords>Church of God, Jesus Christ, Waldenses, Albigenses, Reformation, persecution, Catholic Church, ecclesiastical history, martyrs</keywords>

# THE PREFACE.

*...wickedness of Antichrist, in which they shone like precious stones in a dunghill, and roses among the thorns. To the world, they seemed like nothing but outcasts <note>original: "abiect men"</note>, but God viewed them as his children. He gave them eyes to see, ears to hear, and a heart to understand the truth. Just as he prepared for his judgments by leaving those who had forsaken his word to a spirit of bewilderment <note>original: "amazednesse"</note>, he also prepared for his mercies by withdrawing this remnant of his people from temples polluted with idolatry. He caused the sacred inward ministry of his Spirit to work in them, providing them with temples <note>meaning spiritual temples rather than physical buildings</note> and preserving them from the infection of the external ministry, which was defiled with infinite human inventions.*

*The writings of the aforementioned Waldenses and Albigenses, which have been miraculously preserved until this present time, prove the purity of their religion within this history and justify them against the accusations <note>original: "imputations"</note> of their adversaries. They make it appear to the world that they held the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "Simbole of the Apostles"</note> as the foundation of their faith, while also accepting the Athanasian Creed. For the rule of their obedience, they followed the eternal law of God; for the substance of their prayers, the Lord’s Prayer. Finally, they preserved the Sacraments instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ in the very same purity in which he first ordained them. They also always lived under a good and holy discipline, conducting themselves in their manners and behavior <note>original: "conuersation"</note> according to that same Word, which is the rule of their faith. Nevertheless, we shall show that despite all these things—without which no man can be a true Christian—they were cruelly condemned to death, banished, plundered <note>original: "sacked"</note>, burned, cursed, and persecuted with the violence of arms.*

*It is asked without reason, then, where the Church was in these past ages, since it appears that the almost...*

<summary>The author argues that the Waldenses and Albigenses preserved the true Christian faith through the Middle Ages, despite being persecuted by the established church. He cites their adherence to the Creeds, the Ten Commandments, and the original Sacraments as proof of their orthodoxy.</summary>

<keywords>Waldenses, Albigenses, Antichrist, Apostles' Creed, Athanasian Creed, Sacraments, persecution, church history</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the "hidden" church of the Waldenses and Albigenses. It argues that those persecuted by the Papacy were the true, universal Church because they maintained faith in God and Christ, proving that the truth is as ancient as the lies used to suppress it.</meta>

*...the infinite numbers whom the Popes have put to death for the sake of righteousness were the true Church—no matter how contrary they were to the Church of Rome and the Popes, and in whatever ways they were contrary to that institution, they were consistent with the Church of God.*

*Now, since the first point of the truth which these faithful martyrs maintained concerns God—who is without beginning and without end, and without whose command nothing is true or valid—it must necessarily follow that the inventions of men must yield when God speaks, especially since the truth is as ancient as the lie <note>The author argues that Protestant/Waldensian "truth" is not a new invention, but older than the "lies" of the Roman Church</note>. We must also acknowledge that those who believed in former ages in one only God through Jesus Christ have been the true members of the Church, forming the Catholic <note>original: "Catholike"; here meaning the universal, whole body of believers rather than the Roman Catholic Church</note> Church, in whatever part of the world they were placed. Now, it appears by the doctrine and confession of the faithful (of which much is spoken in this history) that they have always placed their hope in the living God, expecting salvation and life by no other means but by the Son of God. If, then, they were slaughtered for these things, what wrong is done to those who are "guilty" of the same "sins" by the bloody desires of those who wish to banish from the world people whose arguments <note>original: "mouthes"</note> they cannot stop by reason? If these persecutors claim to seek the Church in ages past, let them be directed to those faithful ones whom people like themselves have put to death.*

*Do they not instead have reason to be thankful to God along with us, because the violent assaults of Satan have always been in vain? For the Church has always continued in the person of God’s servants, victorious by faith and triumphant by martyrdom. In this history, we have not measured martyrdom according to the cruelty of the punishment, but by the justice and goodness of the cause. It will add much to the glory of God to follow the trail of this blood <note>original: "follow this bloud by the trace"</note>, gathering together the certain proofs of the faith and constancy of millions of*

<meta>catchword: witnesses,</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the true, universal Church consists of those who have historically suffered for their faith in God and Christ, regardless of their opposition to the Roman Church. The author asserts that the purity of their cause, rather than the severity of their suffering, defines them as true martyrs.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the author's preface. It transitions from a defense of the Waldensian martyrs to an invitation for others to contribute historical accounts of the persecuted "true Church" across Europe. # The Preface.

*...witnesses, who have sealed the truth with the loss of their own lives. Those whose hearts God moves to expand this history by providing a true account of what has happened regarding this subject, in those places where it has pleased the Lord to make them grow and increase—as there is almost no kingdom, state, principality, city, town, or village in Europe where this innocent blood has not been shed—will contribute greatly to the building up <note>original: "edification"</note> of His Church. This happens when many people share what they know of God’s work in past ages, so that we may understand where and how He has preserved the Church.*

*In this holy work, we should expect the venom of wicked tongues and the mockery of atheists and profane people. An upset stomach loves only what is bad for it, and the wicked value nothing except what matches their own corrupt character <note>original: "vitious humour"; in this context, a "humour" refers to a person's temperament or mental state</note>. If the insults <note>original: "quippes"</note> of the wicked had been enough to stop us from the service we owe to God and His Church, we would have given up on this history before writing even three lines of it. Indeed, it has already been attacked <note>original: "snarled at"</note> by various people at the first rumor <note>original: "bruit"</note> of its publication. What, then, will they do when they see truths defended that they never thought we could support so effectively?*

*Undoubtedly, passion will force from malicious minds the usual malicious suggestions. In response to this—and having already informed you, gentle reader, that the first page and title of this history provide its name, structure, purpose, benefits, and goal in just a few lines—I will pray to the eternal God for those who wrong us. I pray that He would be pleased to show them the truth. And for us, whom He has placed and planted in His house, I pray that He would grant us—after the struggles of this life—that inheritance which He has reserved in heaven through His well-beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. To Him be all honor, glory, and power, forever and ever. Amen.*

<summary>The author concludes the preface by calling for further historical accounts of the "true Church" across Europe and dismisses potential critics as malicious or "profane," dedicating the work to God and the memory of the martyrs.</summary>
<keywords>martyrdom, church history, edification, persecution, religious conflict, Waldenses, Albigenses, providence</keywords>

...the Church by faith, and faith by the Scriptures, strengthening them in the midst of their greatest persecutions, and making them know that the cross is profitable, so long as the faithful exchange earth for heaven by that means. The children of God are not lost when, being massacred and cast into the fire by a legal process, we find the seed of the Church in their blood and ashes.

What has been observed in all ages has appeared in a more specific manner among those Christians called *Waldenses*. They were raised up at a time when Satan held men in ignorance, having wrapped the greatest part of those who call themselves Christians in that great sin of the world—I mean idolatry. Kings and princes employed their authority to establish it, sentencing all those to slaughter who would exempt themselves from the punishments <note>original: "wounds"; likely referring to the divine or civil penalties</note> due to idolaters.

This was about the year of our Lord 1160, at which time the punishment of death was inflicted upon all those who did not believe that (once the words of consecration were pronounced by the priest) the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was in the Host under the <term>accidents</term> <note>In Scholastic theology, "accidents" are the physical properties of a thing (like the roundness, whiteness, and taste of bread) that remain even if the underlying substance changes.</note> of the bread—the roundness and whiteness—even the very body, as great and as large as it was upon the cross, with the bread vanishing and being transubstantiated into the flesh of Christ. At that time, it was likewise enjoined <note>original: "enioyned"; commanded or required</note> to adore the Host, to crouch to it, and to bow the knees before it. Indeed, it was called God, and men beat their breasts before it and locked it up in a box to worship it, as they still do even today.

This doctrine was altogether unknown to the Apostles, who never spoke a word of any such mystery, as it was also in the Primitive <note>original: "Primitiue"; the early, original Christian church</note> Church, wherein there was never any...

# Chapter 1. Of the Waldenses.

A certain doctor who taught that this expiatory sacrifice <note>Referring to the Mass, which was taught as a sacrifice to atone for sins.</note> was for both the living and the dead caused many Christians to detest it. They chose instead to suffer a temporary death by resisting such idolatry, rather than consenting to it and suffering in hell.

<margin>
*Guido of Perpignan* in the *Flower of Chronicles*.
</margin>

*Peter Waldo*, a citizen of *Lyons*, showed himself most courageous in opposing this invention. He also criticized various other corruptions that had crept into the Church of *Rome* over time, affirming that she had lost the faith of *Jesus Christ*, and that she was the "whore of *Babylon*" and that "barren fig tree" which our Savior had cursed long ago.

He taught that we were not to obey the Pope, since he was not the head of the Church.

That monasticism <note>original: "Monkerie"</note> was a stinking carcass <note>original: "carrion"</note> and the mark of the Beast.

That Purgatory, the Mass, the dedication of temples, the worship of saints, and the remembrance of the dead were nothing other than the inventions of the devil and the snares of greed <note>original: "Auarice"</note>.

<margin>
See *The Sea of Histories*, folio 203. *Claude de Rubis* in his *History of the City of Lyons*, page 259.
</margin>

*Waldo* was listened to all the more attentively because he was highly esteemed for his learning and piety, as well as for his great generosity toward the poor. He nourished not only their bodies with physical bread, but also their souls with spiritual bread, exhorting them primarily to seek *Jesus Christ*, the true bread of their souls.

<margin>
*Joachim Camerarius* <note>original: "Lois Cam."</note> in his *History of the Orthodox Brethren of Bohemia*, page 7. *Guido of Perpignan* in his *Flower of Chronicles*.
</margin>

Many historians write that he resolved to lead a blameless life, approaching as near as he could to that of the Apostles. This resolution followed a mournful and unlucky accident that occurred unexpectedly. One evening, while he was in the company of some of his friends after supper, passing the time in conversation and refreshment, one of the company fell down dead

upon the ground. All who were present were strangely frightened by this sudden accident, and Waldo, among the rest, was touched to the quick <note>meaning: deeply moved to his core</note>. By this bolt of God’s justice, he was moved to an extraordinary amendment of life, applying himself wholly to the reading of the Scriptures and seeking his salvation in them. Sometimes consulting the writings of the ancients <note>Referring to the Early Church Fathers</note>, he continually instructed those poor people who came to him for alms.

The Archbishop of Lyons, named Jean de Belles-Mains <note>original: "Iohn de Belles Mayons"</note>, being informed that Waldo made a profession of teaching the people—boldly criticizing the vice, luxury, excess, and arrogance of the Pope and his clergy—forbade him from teaching. He argued that, especially as a layman <note>original: "lay person"</note>, Waldo had exceeded the limits of his profession and social standing. Therefore, he ordered that Waldo should not continue his preaching under penalty of excommunication and being prosecuted as a heretic.

Waldo replied that he could not remain silent in a matter of such high importance as the salvation of men, and that he would rather obey God, who had commanded him to speak, than man, who had commanded him to keep silent.

Following this answer, the Archbishop tried to have him arrested <note>original: "apprehended"</note>, but he could not. Because Waldo had many relatives and friends, he was beloved by many and so remained safely in Lyons through the favor and protection of his friends for the space of three years.

Pope Alexander III, having understood that in Lyons there were various people who called into question his sovereign authority over the whole Church, feared that this beginning of rebellion <meta>catchword: might</meta>

<margin>Claude de Rubis in his History, page 269.</margin>
Claude de Rubis says that Waldo and his followers were wholly chased out of Lyons, and Albert de Capitaneis says that they could not be wholly driven out. We could learn nothing else about this first persecution, except that those who escaped from Lyons—who were called Waldenses after Waldo—followed him and afterwards spread themselves into various companies and places.

## CHAPTER II.

*That the dispersion of Waldo and his followers was the*
*means that God used to spread the doctrine of Waldo al-*
*most throughout all Europe.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring ornate foliage and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
Albert de Capitaneis says that Waldo retired himself into Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France</note> at his departure from Lyons, and Claude de Rubis affirms that he lived <note>original: "conversed"</note> in the mountains of that province with certain simple <note>original: "rude," meaning uneducated or rustic</note> persons, who were nevertheless capable of receiving the impressions of his belief. And it is true that the churches of the Waldenses—which have continued for a very long time, and of which there are still a greater number than in any other place in Europe—are those of Dauphiné and their neighboring descendants <note>original: "lineage"</note>, namely those of Piedmont and Provence.
<margin>Vignier in the third part of his Historical Library, page 130.</margin>

This dispersion, rather than destroying the movement, helped establish the Waldensian Church across various regions of Europe.</summary>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>The History Book 1.</header>

<margin>Dubranius in his history of Bohemia, Book 14.</margin>
Shortly after, they suffered great persecutions. For as Dubranius <note>Jan Dubravius (1486–1553), a Czech historian and Bishop of Olomouc</note> says some time later, King Philip Augustus—pressured by church officials—took up arms against the Waldenses of Picardy. He razed and overthrew three hundred houses belonging to gentlemen who followed their cause and destroyed certain walled towns, pursuing them into Flanders, where they had fled, and caused many of them to be burned.

This persecution forced many to flee into Germany, where shortly after they were also severely persecuted <margin>See the *Sea of Histories* <note>original: "Sea of Histories" likely refers to the *Mer des Histoires*, a popular 15th-century world chronicle</note>.</margin>, specifically in the region of Alsace and along the Rhine by the Bishops of Mainz <note>original: "Mayence"</note> and Strasbourg <note>original: "Strasburge"</note>. In the town of Bingen <note>original: "Bnigne"</note>, they burned thirty-five citizens of Mainz in a single fire; in Mainz itself, they burned eighteen others, all of whom suffered death with great steadfastness. In Strasbourg, eighty people were burned at the insistence of the local Bishop. These persecutions multiplied in such a way because of the inspiration <note>original: "edification"</note> received by those who saw them die. Watching them pray to God and hearing them express their certainty of His mercy, people were moved. Consequently, despite the ongoing persecutions, there were as many as eighty thousand people who professed the same faith in the region of Passau and around Bohemia in the year 1315.

They also had established churches in <margin>Matthew Paris in his history of the life of King Henry III, in the year 1223.</margin> Bulgaria, Croatia, Dalmatia, and Hungary, as Matthew Paris <note>A famous 13th-century English chronicler and monk</note> reports. These were instructed and governed by a man named Bartholomew, who was born at Carcassonne. On the other hand, the Albigensians <note>original: "Albegeois," a reformist group in Southern France often associated with the Waldenses</note>, who professed the same faith, filled many countries until, in the end, they were almost completely wiped out <note>original: "extirpated"</note>, as will be explained in their specific history.

Despite mass executions by burning, the movement grew to tens of thousands of followers by the early 14th century.</summary>

## CHAPTER III.

*Concerning the names by which the Waldenses have been called by their adversaries, and the faults and offenses with which they have been charged.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' featuring a stylized floral or leafy pattern framing the letter.</image-desc>
The monks, inquisitors, and mortal enemies of the *Waldenses* were not content with merely handing them over to the secular power <note>The civil government and its judicial system, as opposed to church authorities</note> every day. They also burdened them with many shameful accusations, asserting that they were the authors of every heresy in the world which they were trying to eliminate. They attributed all those monstrous abuses they had invented solely to the *Waldenses*, as if they alone were the vessel for all errors.

<margin>Vaudois. Albigensians.</margin>
First, therefore, they called them *Waldenses*, after Waldo, a citizen of Lyons; and *Albigensians* <note>original: "Albigeois"</note>, after the region of Albi.

Because those who followed the doctrine of Waldo departed from Lyons deprived of all human resources, and most had left their property behind, their enemies called them the "Beggars of Lyons" in derision.

<margin>Chaignards.</margin>
In Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphiney," a province in southeastern France</note>, they were mockingly called *Chaignards*.

<margin>Tramontanes.</margin>
And because some of them crossed the Alps, they were called *Tramontanes* <note>original: "Tramontaines," meaning "those from across the mountains"</note>.

<margin>Josephists.</margin>
And after one of Waldo's disciples named Joseph, who preached in the Diocese of Die <note>original: "Dye"</note> in Dauphiné, they were called *Josephists*.

<margin>Lollards.</margin>
In England, they were called *Lollards*, after the name of a man named Lollard who taught there.

After two priests who taught Waldo's doctrine in Languedoc named Henry and Esperon, they were called— <meta>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "Henri-" indicates the next page continues with "Henricians."</meta>

They were called *Henricians* and *Esperonists*. After one of their pastors named Arnold Hot, who preached in the territory of Albi <note>original: "Albegeois"</note>, they were called *Arnoldists*.

<margin>Siccars.</margin>
In Provence, they were called *Siccars*, a term from "peddler’s French" <note>An early form of slang or cant used by vagabonds and street sellers</note> which means "cutpurse" <note>A pickpocket or thief</note>.

<margin>Fraticelli.</margin>
In Italy, they were called *Fraticelli* <note>original: "Fraticelli," literally "little brothers"</note>, which was interpreted to mean "shifters," because they lived together in true love and harmony.

<margin>Insabathas.</margin>
Because they observed no other day of rest except for the Sabbath <note>referring here to the biblical Seventh-day Sabbath or perhaps their rejection of Church-mandated feast days</note>, they were called *Insabathas*, as if to say they observed no Sabbath at all.

<margin>Patarenians or Paturins.</margin>
Because they were always exposed to constant suffering, they were called *Patarenians*, from the Latin word *pati* <note>original: "Pati," meaning to suffer</note>.

<margin>Passagenes.</margin>
Forasmuch as they wandered from place to place like poor travelers <note>original: "passengers"</note>, they were called *Passagenes*.

<margin>Gazares.</margin>
In Germany, they were called *Gazares*, which meant they were considered cursed and notoriously wicked.

<margin>Turlupins.</margin>
In Flanders, they were called *Turlupins*, meaning "dwellers with wolves," because their persecutions often forced them to live in woods and wildernesses.

<margin>
Toulousains.
Lombards.
Picards.
Lionists.
Bohemians.
</margin>
Sometimes they were called by the names of the countries and regions where they lived, such as *Albigensians* (from Albi), *Toulousains* (from Toulouse), *Lombards* (from Lombardy), *Picards* (from Picardy), *Lionists* (from Lyons), or *Bohemians* (from Bohemia).

<margin>Cathars.</margin>
Sometimes, to make them even more hated, they were associated with ancient heretics, though under ridiculous pretenses. Because they made a profession of purity in their lives and faith, they were called *Cathars* <note>original: "Cathares," from the Greek word *katharos*, meaning "pure"</note>. And because they denied that the bread shown by the priest during the Mass was God, they were called

### Chapter 3: Concerning the Waldenses

<margin>*Arians*.</margin>
They called them *Arians*, as if they denied the divinity of the eternal Son of God. And because they maintained that the authority of Emperors and Kings does not depend upon the authority of the Pope, they called them *Manicheans*, as if they were establishing two separate sovereign powers <note>original: "Princes," referring to the Manichean belief in two competing primary forces of good and evil</note>. And for other reasons which they fabricated, they called them *Gnostics*, *Cataphrygians*, *Adamites*, and *Apostolics*.

<margin>*Ribalds. Buggerers. Sorcerers.*</margin>
Sometimes they spitefully abused them with insults. *Matthew Paris* calls them *Ribalds* <note>meaning coarse, licentious, or irreverent people</note>. The compiler of the *Treasury of Histories* calls them *Buggerers* <note>In this period, the term "bugger" (derived from "Bulgarian") was a common slur for heretics, specifically linking them to the Bogomils</note>. *Rubis* says that when a man speaks of a sorcerer, he calls him a *Vaudois* <note>Waldensian</note>. And what is more, he presumes to prove that they are so. It will be necessary to answer this boldness <note>original: "temeritie"</note> in its proper place, where they shall be cleared of all those false accusations <note>original: "impostures"</note> which their enemies have laid upon them, using the very books from which we have gathered what follows.

<margin>This false accusation is found in the book by *Albertus de Capitaneis*, *Concerning the Origin of the Vaudois*, page 2; in the book by *Rainerius*, *On the Method of Investigating Heretics*, folio 36; likewise in the accusation made by the priests of *Bohemia* to King *Ladislaus* against the *Vaudois*. *Rainerius*, ibid., folio 37.</margin>
First, they impose upon them that ancient slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note> with which the pagans <note>original: "painims"</note> defamed the Christians of the Early Church: that is, that they assembled themselves in the nighttime, in corners and hiding places, and that the pastor commanded the lights should be put out, saying, *He who can take, let him take* <note>original Latin: "Qui potest capere capiat"</note>—that is, "catch who catch can." Whereupon every man tries to grab whomever he can, without any regard for blood or family relation. They claimed that once the lights were extinguished, they committed abominable acts of incest; often the child with his mother, the brother with his sister, and the father with his own daughter. They added, moreover, that they were taught that children conceived from such unions were the most fit to be pastors.

Secondly, they have charged them with maintaining that a man may divorce <note>original: "put away"</note> his wife whenever he wishes, and

*This apology the author, Jean Paul Perrin, set down in two columns: one in French and the other in the language of the Waldenses. For the sake of brevity, we have set it down only in English, referring those who desire to see the original to the French book.*

### Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

...it has never been known that there has been any sexual immorality <note>original: "whoredome"</note> among us that has escaped unpunished, or any such villainy committed. In such a way, our lives and conduct <note>original: "carriages"</note> condemn those who accuse us.

And because the Waldenses speak this of themselves, and to their own praise—and therefore this justification of theirs may seem weak—look a little into what they have written elsewhere against sexual immorality. This should be enough to show that they were very far from this diabolical desire to debase themselves by incest.

<margin>Their book on the remedy against the sin of lust <note>original: "luxury"; in this period, the word "luxury" specifically referred to lechery or the sin of lust</note>, Chapter 21.</margin>

The sin of lust is very pleasing to the devil, displeasing to God, and harmful to our neighbors, because in it a man obeys the basest part of his body rather than God, who has preferred it <note>meaning God set the soul in a position of authority over the body</note>. A foolish woman does not only take from a man his goods, but himself too. He who is given to this vice keeps faith with no man, and therefore David caused his faithful servant to be killed so that he might enjoy his wife. Amnon defiled his sister Tamar. This vice consumes the inheritance of many, as it is said of the prodigal child, that he wasted his goods living luxuriously <note>meaning in excess or lewdness</note>. Balaam chose this sin to provoke the children of Israel to sin, because of which twenty-four thousand people died. This sin was the cause of Samson's blindness; it corrupted Solomon; and many have perished because of the beauty of a woman. Prayer, fasting, and distance of place are the remedies against this sin. For a man may overcome other vices by struggling against them, but in this, a man is never victorious except by fleeing from it and not approaching near to it—of which we have an example in Joseph. It is therefore our duty to pray daily to the Lord that he will keep us far from the sin of lust and give us understanding and chastity.

# The History, Book 1.

<margin>See their *Book of Virtues*, in the chapter on marriage.</margin>
Against the second false accusation <note>original: "imposture"</note>—that they claim a man may divorce <note>original: "put away"</note> his wife whenever he pleases—they argue that marriage is a bond <note>original: "knot"</note> that cannot be untied except by death, unless it is because of sexual immorality <note>original: "fornication"</note>, as our Savior Christ says. And Saint Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7 that the wife is not to depart from her husband, nor the husband from his wife.

<margin>See the book of the Waldenses entitled *Of Virtues*, in the chapter on marriage.</margin>
Regarding the third slander <note>original: "calumny"</note>, concerning the communal ownership of property and wives: they say concerning marriage that it was ordained by God long ago in the Earthly Paradise, and that it is a good remedy against sexual immorality <note>original: "whoredome"</note>. They also note that Saint Paul, speaking of this, says, *Let every man have his own wife, and every woman her own husband.* Furthermore, they believe a husband ought to love his wife as Christ loved his Church, and that the married couple ought to live together in holiness with their children, bringing them up in the fear of God.

<margin>This is shown by the legal records <note>original: "proces"</note> in our possession, which reveal that Louis XII <note>King of France, reigned 1498–1515</note> condemned those who had seized the goods of the Waldenses and ordered them to make restitution. This is also clear from the treatises of Menuobe and other legal cases made by the Waldenses of Provence.</margin>
As for property <note>original: "goods"</note>, every person has owned their own personal wealth <note>original: "proper substance"</note> at all times and in all places. In *Dauphiné* <note>a former province in southeastern France</note>, when the Archbishops of *Embrun*, *John* and *Rostain*, had plundered them of their goods—and when the Lord of *Argentière*, *Montainar*, and *Arreas* of *Bonne* had dispossessed the *Waldenses* who lived in the valley of *Freissinières* and of *Argentière* of their goods and possessions—the return <note>restitution</note> of every man’s inheritance was sought legally by the specific individuals from whom the property had been taken. The *Waldenses* of *Provence* are currently demanding from the Pope the goods and lands that have been annexed to his domain and taken from them by confiscation. Each individual is providing proof for every part and parcel of the goods and lands that had descended to them from their ancestors, the *Waldenses*, from time immemorial, they never having had any such [community...]

### Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

...community among them that might in any way detract from the lawful property which everyone had to his own lands.

The fourth slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note> concerned baptism, which it was said they denied to little infants. However, they cleared <note>original: "quit"</note> themselves of this accusation as follows:

<margin>In the book of the Waldenses entitled the *Spiritual Almanac*, folio 45.</margin>
The time and place for those who are to be baptized is not strictly ordained, but the charity and edification of the Church and congregation must serve as a rule in that matter, etc.

Therefore, those to whom the children were most closely related brought their infants to be baptized—such as their parents, or anyone else whom God had made charitable in that regard.

It is true that, being forced for several hundred years to allow their children to be baptized by the priests of the Church of Rome, they delayed doing so as long as they possibly could. This was because they detested those human inventions which were added to that holy Sacrament, which they held to be mere pollutions of it. And because their pastors (whom they called <term>Barbes</term> <note>From the word for "uncle"; a title of respect for Waldensian spiritual leaders.</note>) were often away serving their churches, they could not have the Sacrament of Baptism administered to their infants by their own ministers. For this reason, they kept them a long time from baptism. When the Catholic priests noticed this, they charged them with this false claim <note>original: "imposture"</note>. Not only did their enemies believe this, but also many others who otherwise highly approved of their life and faith in all other points.

The fifth slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note> was that they worshipped <note>original: "adored"</note> their pastors, bowing down <note>original: "prostrating"</note> before them. To defend <note>original: "justify"</note> the Waldenses against this false accusation <note>original: "imposture"</note>, there needs no more than that

<margin>
It appears by the legal proceedings initiated by the said Albert against the Waldenses of the Alps.
</margin>
The reader will be pleased to take the time to read what they have written regarding the worship <note>original: "adoration"</note> of only one God, in the explanation they made in their book of doctrine concerning the first Commandment of God's Law. There you shall find that they have given much honor even to their pastors, as those who keep the word of Reconciliation. They hosted them charitably, feeling themselves obliged to do so for the sake of conscience; however, the claim that they ever had any intention to give that worship to a created being which is only due to the Creator can never be proven except by way of slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note>. Nevertheless, *Albert de Capitaneis*, their deadly enemy in the Diocese of *Turin*, tried to extort a confession from them that they worshiped their pastors—a confession he could never force them to make.

The sixth slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note> was the claim that they maintained it was not lawful to swear an oath at all.

<margin>
In their book titled the *Spiritual Almanac*, in the explanation of the third commandment.
</margin>
They state and affirm that there are lawful oaths tending to the honor of God and the edification of our neighbors, citing the passage in Hebrews 6:16: *For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation.* They also point out that the people of *Israel* were commanded to swear by the name of the eternal God (Deuteronomy 6:13), and they cite the examples of oaths made between *Abimelech* and *Isaac* (Genesis 26:31) and the oath of *Jacob* (Genesis 31:53).

The seventh slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note> was intended to make them hateful to the people by claiming they preferred peace with the Turks over peace with the Church and the kingdom of Christ. Their enemies claimed they held that the Pope commits a mortal sin when he sends a military expedition—with soldiers wearing the badge of the cross upon their tunics or armor—against the *Saracens* <note>A medieval term for Muslims, specifically those fighting against the Crusaders.</note>.

# Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

<margin>In the book of the causes of their separation from the Church of Rome, p. 235</margin>

To justify themselves in this matter, we must observe that they do not complain about the act of war against the **Turks**. Instead, they complain about the plunder that the Popes make of the Church’s goods and other divine graces under that pretext. They accuse the Popes of deceiving ignorant people with their Bulls and Blessings—people who too willingly believe their lies and inventions, buying them at a high price. They also take issue with the Pope sending out his **Crusades** <note>original: "Croisades"</note>—his "crossed" soldiers, who are strangers—to hunt them down as heretics before they have even been heard or proven to be such.

However, they are not the only ones who condemn this greed, which the vengeful spirits of the Popes have shown through their **Crusades**.

<margin>*Paulus Langius* in his *Chronicle of France*, 1513. See the examination of the Council of Trent, book 1, chapter 5.</margin>

*Paulus Langius*, a German historian <note>original: "Historiographer"</note>, accuses **Leo X** of raising large sums of money under the pretense of a war against the **Turks**, which he shortly after bestowed upon thirty Cardinals whom he had newly created.

*Guicciardini* <note>Francesco Guicciardini, a famous Italian historian</note> notes in his *History* that the same Pope imposed heavy taxes on the people, the profits of which fell into the lap of his sister, **Magdalen**. He notes that this entire collection of money was merely to satisfy the greed of a woman, and that the Bishop of **Aremboldo** was considered by the Pope to be a worthy commissioner <note>original: "commissarie"</note> for such a task, carrying it out with every kind of extortion.

<margin>Apulia <note>original: "Pouille"</note>, a part of Naples whose inhabitants are considered very dangerous.</margin>

**Alexander IV** converted the "vow of Jerusalem" into the "vow of **Apulia**" <note>original: "Pouille"</note>—that is to say, a vow of revenge. For he gave power to his Legates to absolve the King of England, **Henry III**, from his vow to go on a Crusade to **Jerusalem**, on the condition that he should go to **Apulia** to make war against **Manfred** (the son of the Emperor **Frederick** who had died not long before). # The History: Book 1

<margin>*Matthew Paris* <note>A 13th-century English chronicler and monk</note> in his *History of England*. See the first book of the examination of the Council of Trent, chapter 5. In the book of the causes of their separation from the Church of Rome, p. 125.</margin>

This is supported by the historian **Matthew Paris**, who records the complaint made at that time: that the tithes <note>original: "tenths"</note> collected for the relief of the Holy Land were seized and diverted to support the war in **Apulia** <note>original: "Pouille," a region in Southern Italy where the Pope was engaged in territorial conflicts</note> against other Christians.

The eighth slander was that they showed no reverence for holy and consecrated places, holding that a person does not sin more severely by burning a church than by breaking into any other house.

They say that neither the location nor the high office <note>original: "chaire"</note> makes a person holier. They have maintained that people greatly deceive themselves when they take comfort or pride in the dignity of a place. For what place is higher than Paradise? What place is more secure than Heaven? And yet, man was banished from Paradise for sinning there, and the angels were thrown down from Heaven to serve as examples for those who came after. This teaches that it is not the location, nor its greatness or dignity, that makes a person holy, but rather the innocence of their life.

Against the ninth slander—which claims they argue that a magistrate <note>a civil official or judge</note> should not sentence anyone to death—they respond:

<margin>In the book of the Waldenses entitled *The Light of the Treasure of Faith*, folio 214.</margin>

It is written that we must not allow a criminal <note>original: "malefactor"</note> to live, and that without correction and discipline, doctrine serves no purpose; neither would legal judgments be respected nor sins punished. Therefore, righteous anger is the mother of discipline, and patience without reason is the seed of vice, as it allows the wicked to stray from truth and honesty.

The truth is that they found fault with magistrates who sentenced them to death without any other knowledge...

Here you may see what the Waldenses <note>A medieval Christian movement that was a precursor to the Reformation; they were often persecuted as heretics</note> have written against sorcerers based on the Word of God. Without a doubt, he accuses <note>original: "taxeth"</note> the city of Geneva and the states of the Swiss Cantons <note>The member states of the Swiss Confederation</note> that have received the Gospel. He does so without any other show of proof, except that in those places, sorcerers are very commonly condemned to death, following the commandment of God, which allows no sorcerer to live. He could have reached a much better conclusion if he had said that in those places where the Reformation of religion was established in our times, no one speaks with or has any acquaintance with sorcerers; rather, as soon as any such person is found, he is put to death. Therefore, no one can claim Rubis's statement is true, unless he wants to argue that burning sorcerers is a way of supporting them, or that putting them to death by the authority of the Word of God is a kind of heresy.

It was not the will of Christ to commit his Church to such people, who would rather prostitute her by their bad examples and wicked actions than present her as a chaste virgin in the same purity they received from him; therefore, he argues that we are not to obey them. He adds, moreover, that they lived very religiously in all things, their manners well-ordered <note>original: "well seasoned"</note> and their words wise and polished, always speaking by their own will of God and his Saints, persuading others to virtue and to hate sin, to the end (he says) that they might be held in greater esteem by good men.

# The History: Book 1.

Christian as the worst of the said valley of Freissinière <note>original: "Fraissiniere"</note>.

<margin>Joachim Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574) was a German classical scholar and reformer.</note> in his history, page 352.</margin> King Francis I <note>Francis I (r. 1515–1547)</note>, successor to Louis XII, understood that the Parliament of Provence <note>original: "Prouence"</note> had imposed heavy burdens upon the Waldenses living at Merindol, Cabrières <note>original: "Cambriers"</note>, and other nearby places. He desired to be informed of the belief, life, and conduct <note>original: "conuerſation"</note> of these Waldenses. To that end, he commanded William de Bellay <note>Guillaume du Bellay (1491–1543), a French diplomat and general.</note>, Lord of Langey <note>original: "Langeay"</note> and his lieutenant in Piedmont at the time, to make a diligent inquiry into those affairs.

Consequently, the Lord of Langey sent two honest and respected men into Provence, whom he charged with investigating both the lives and religion of the Waldenses, as well as the proceedings of the Court of Parliament against them. These two deputies reported back to the Lord of Langey that the majority of the people in the region of Provence affirmed that the Waldenses were a very hardworking <note>original: "painfull," meaning painstaking or industrious</note> people. They reported that about two hundred years earlier, they had moved from the country of Piedmont to dwell in Provence. Taking up the professions of farmers <note>original: "husbandmen"</note> and shepherds, they had restored many villages that had been destroyed in the wars and made other wild, desert places very fertile through their labor.

The deputies also found through their inquiries in Provence that the aforementioned men of Merindol were a peaceful people, beloved by their neighbors, and men of good and godly conduct. They were careful to keep their promises and to pay their debts without legal disputes. They were very charitable, not allowing any among them to fall into want or beggary, and were generous to strangers and poor travelers to the best of their power. The inhabitants of Provence also affirmed that those of Merindol were distinguished from others in the country because they could never be persuaded to swear or blaspheme.

...Jesus, and in many of their writings and continual preachings, they accused the Pope of being the true Antichrist of whom the Apostle Saint John had prophesied, and therefore insisted that we were to flee from him. <margin>*Vesembecius* <note>Matthias Wesenbeck (1531–1586) was a prominent German jurist who wrote in defense of the Waldensians.</note> in his Oration on the *Waldenses*.</margin>

*Luther* <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German priest who catalyzed the Protestant Reformation.</note> confessed that he hated the *Waldenses* as desperate men until he learned of the piety and truth of their belief through their own confessions and writings. Through these, he perceived that these good and honest men were much wronged, and that the Pope had condemned them as heretics when they were instead worthy of the praise due to saints and martyrs. He also found among the *Waldenses* one thing worthy of admiration, to be observed as a miracle never heard of in the Church of Rome: namely, that the *Waldenses*, having abandoned all human learning, gave themselves wholly—to the utmost of their power—to meditating on the law of God day and night. He noted that they were very expert in the Scriptures and well-practiced in them. On the contrary, those whom we call our "Great Masters" in the Papacy held the Scriptures in such low regard (despite glorying in their titles) that there were some among them who had scarcely even seen the Bible.

Having also read the confession of the *Waldenses*, he said that he thanked God for the great light that it had pleased God to impart to them, taking great comfort...

So, if you persist in his grace, he has greater treasures in store for you, with which he will enrich you and make you perfect, so that you may grow to the full measure of the inheritance of Christ.*

We live in peace in these valleys of Piedmont, and in love and friendship with one another; we have dealings together, never marrying our sons to the daughters of those of the Roman Catholic Church, or our daughters to their sons. Indeed, our manners and customs please them so well that those who are masters and call themselves Catholics desire to choose their male and female servants from among us rather than from their own people. They also come from far away to seek nurses for their children among us, finding more faithfulness in our people than in their own.

<margin>It appears by the *History of the Estate of the Church*, page 337.</margin>
And concerning the doctrine for which the Waldenses have been persecuted, they affirm (he says) that we are to believe the Scriptures only in that which concerns our salvation, not depending on the authority of men in any way. They believe that the Scriptures contain within them everything necessary for salvation, and that we are not to believe anything except what God has commanded us.

That we have only one Mediator <note>A mediator is a go-between; the Waldenses argued that Jesus Christ is the only one who can intercede between God and humanity, rejecting the need for saints as intermediaries.</note>, and therefore we are not to pray to saints.

That there is no Purgatory, but all those who are justified by Christ go to eternal life.

They approve of only two Sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

They affirm that all Masses are damnable <note>original: "damnable"; in this context, meaning spiritually ruinous or worthy of condemnation.</note>, especially those that are said for the dead, and therefore they are to be abolished.

That all human traditions are to be rejected as not being necessary for salvation.

That singing and the frequent repetition of divine services, fasts tied to certain days, superfluous feasts, restrictions on types of food <note>original: "difference of meates"</note>, the many degrees and orders of friars, monks, and nuns, the many blessings and consecrations of objects <note>original: "creatures"</note>, vows, pilgrimages, and the whole confusion

# Chapter 9. Of the Waldenses.

They were succeeded in doctrine by a man named **Henry**; one was a priest and the other a monk. They taught in the Bishoprics of **Arles**, **Embrun** <note>original: "Ambrun"</note>, **Die**, and **Gap**. After being chased away from those areas, they were welcomed at **Toulouse** <note>original: "Tholouse"</note>.

<margin>Same source, page 151.</margin>
There was a certain man (the author says) called **Bartholomew**, born at **Carcassonne**, who organized and governed the churches in **Bulgaria**, **Croatia**, **Dalmatia**, and **Hungary**. He appointed ministers, as the chronicler **Matthew Paris** reports, who calls him their "Pope" or "Bishop." Paris supports this by citing a letter that the Bishop of **Porto** <note>original: "Portuense," the Latin title for the Bishop of Porto near Rome</note>—who was the Pope's Legate in those regions—wrote to the Archbishop of **Rouen** <note>original: "Roan"</note> and his suffragans <note term="suffragan">A bishop who is subordinate to an archbishop or metropolitan bishop.</note>. In the letter, he demanded aid and assistance against them. Consequently, they were at last forced to retreat into the deserts, fulfilling the prophecy in the 12th chapter of **Revelation**. That scripture says the woman great with child, who brought forth a male child (which is the true Church of God), would be so persecuted by the Dragon—who cast a flood of water out of his mouth to carry her away—that she was forced to fly into the wilderness. There, she would be nourished for "a time, and times, and half a time," or for the space of forty-two months, or one thousand two hundred and sixty days.

**Rainerius** <note>original: "Rainerius," referring to Rainier Sacconi, a 13th-century inquisitor and author who wrote about the Waldenses</note> mentions two famous bishops of the Waldenses: one **Belesinanzo** <note>original: "Belazinanza"</note> of **Verona**, and one **John de Lugio**, who taught among them after the leaders named above, around the year 1250.

**Arnold Hot**, a pastor among the Waldenses, maintained a public debate <note>original: "disputation"</note> at **Montréal** <note>original: "Mont Real"</note>, which we shall mention in its proper place.

**Lollard** was also held in great reputation among them,

These two were sent into Bohemia to serve in the churches of the Waldensians gathered together in that realm; but they betrayed the churches and brought much mischief upon them by discovering <term>discovering: revealing or exposing</term> to the enemies of the Waldensians whatever they knew of their groups and meetings. *Louis Paschal* was sent to Rome, where he was condemned and burned alive. Pope Pius the fourth of that name was present along with his Cardinals; Paschal summoned the Pope to appear before the throne of the Lamb <note>A biblical reference to the judgment seat of Christ</note> to give an account of their cruelties.

<margin>This is evident from the bag of legal records <note>original: "bagge of processe"</note> found in the office of the Lord of Avençon <note>original: "Cabinet du Sieur d’ Auençon"</note>, Archbishop of Embrun, during the final capture of Embrun, which contained proceedings against the Waldensians of Freissinières <note>original: "Froissiniere"</note> and L'Argentière.</margin>
Mention is made of various pastors they have had, who were many times imprisoned and put to death by the monks acting as Inquisitors. These Inquisitors had them watched even high in the Alps as they traveled from one community to another. This small number of examples may suffice to help us understand that although their enemies did their best to banish them and root them out from the earth, the eternal God has not ceased to provide laborers for his harvest whenever there was a need. 

Even to this day, in Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphiney"</note> and Provence, there are many thousands who consider it their glory to have descended from the ancient Waldensians. They are inheritors of their ancestors' zeal and piety rather than their earthly wealth, which their persecutors now possess. The Pope is among these, having added to his so-called Apostolic Chamber all the inheritance of the Waldensians who owned property in his territory of Venaissin <note>original: "Venecin"</note>. Under the pretense of heresy, he would take away their lives too if he could. He is far from considering restoring what he has been fruitlessly urged to return—something his officers promised to restore with more vanity and falsehood than honesty or true intent. 

Now, because the reader might not know what kind of men their pastors were and might therefore hold them in low esteem, we will insert what we find in their writings in the following chapter. This will provide proof of their calling <term>vocation: a religious calling or professional office</term>, the exercise of their duties, their zeal, and their piety.

# Chapter 10: Of the Waldensians

<margin>Rainerius, *On the Form of Heretics*, leaf 8. <note>original Latin: "Rain. de forma heret. fol.8." Rainerius Saccho was a 13th-century inquisitor and former Cathar who wrote a famous treatise against heretical groups.</note></margin>
The monk Rainerius reports many things concerning the calling <note>original: "vocation"</note> of the Waldensian pastors that never actually happened. For instance, he claims that they have one presiding Bishop and two followers—whom he calls the "elder son" and the "younger son"—and a deacon. He also claims that this bishop laid his hands upon others with supreme authority and sent them wherever he pleased, like a Pope.

Against these falsehoods, I have set down here what is found in their own writings regarding the calling of their pastors.

<margin>The Book of the Pastors, by George Maurel and Peter Masson, page 8. <note>Maurel and Masson were Waldensian "Barbes" (pastors) who traveled to consult with German and Swiss Reformers in 1530.</note></margin>
> All those (they say) who are to be received as pastors among us, even while they still live with their parents, must entreat us to receive them into the ministry, asking that we would be pleased to pray to God for them, so that they may be made capable of such a great responsibility. The petitioners do this for no other reason than to show their humility.

They are required to learn certain lessons and to memorize all the chapters of Saint Matthew and Saint John, all the Epistles (which they call "canonical" <note>The General Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude.</note>), and a large portion of the writings of Solomon, David, and the Prophets.

Afterward, having provided good evidence of their learning and behavior <note>original: "conversation," referring to their moral conduct</note>, they are received with the laying on of hands into the office or function of preaching.

The most recently ordained <note>original: "received"</note> are to do nothing without the permission and license of the seniors who were ordained before them. Likewise, the seniors must not attempt anything without the approval of their colleagues, so that all things among us may be done in an orderly manner.

We pastors assemble together once every year to decide our affairs in a general council.

Our food and clothing are willingly provided <note>The original text ends here with the catchword "ministred," indicating the sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<sig>H 3</sig>

<summary>This page refutes the claims of the inquisitor Rainerius regarding the Waldensian hierarchy and describes the rigorous biblical training and humble ordination process of their pastors.</summary>

...is administered unto us, and as if by way of alms, very sufficiently by the people whom we teach.

The money that is given to us by the people is carried to the aforementioned general Council and is delivered in the presence of all. There it is received by the elders <note>original: "most ancients"</note>, and part of it is given to those who are travelers or wayfaring men according to their necessities, and part unto the poor.

When any of us who are pastors shall fall into any grave or immoral sin <note>original: "foule or vncleane ſinne"</note>, he is cast out of our company and forbidden from the duty of preaching.

Among other power and authority which God has given to his servants, it belongs to them to choose guides of the people and elders <note>original: "Ancients"</note> in their charges <note>The specific areas or congregations they were assigned to oversee.</note>, according to the diversity of employment in the unity of Christ. This is proved by the saying of the Apostle in his Epistle to Titus, Chapter 1, verse 5:

> *For this cause I left you in Crete, that you should set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I have appointed you.*

Thus you see how the pastors of the Waldensians were chosen and maintained in their office <note>original: "charge"</note>. But so that their zeal may better appear, we will insert in the chapter following a letter which one of the said pastors wrote to one of their churches, by which it may easily appear with what holy and sanctified affection they labored to call the people to repentance and to instruct them in the faith.

<margin>Article 4.</margin>
The books named above teach this: that there is one God Almighty, completely wise and completely good, who has made all things by his goodness. For he created *Adam* according to his own image and likeness; but by the malice of the devil and the disobedience of *Adam*, sin entered into the world, and we are made sinners in *Adam* and through *Adam*.

<margin>Article 5.</margin>
That *Christ* was promised to our forefathers who received the Law, so that by knowing their sin through the Law—and recognizing their unrighteousness and insufficiency—they might desire the coming of *Christ*, so that he might satisfy for their sins and fulfill the Law himself.

<margin>Article 6.</margin>
That *Christ* was born at the time appointed by God his Father—that is to say, at a time when all iniquity abounded, and not for the sake of our good works alone (for all were sinners), but so that he might offer his grace and mercy to us.

<margin>Art. 8.</margin> We also firmly hold that there is no other mediator and advocate with God the Father except Jesus Christ alone. Concerning the Virgin *Mary*, we believe that she is holy, humble, and full of grace; we believe the same of all the other saints: that they await in heaven the resurrection of their bodies on the day of judgment.

<margin>Art. 9.</margin> We also believe that after this life, there are only two places: one for those who will be saved, the other for the damned, which we call Paradise and Hell. We completely deny Purgatory, viewing it as a dream of the Antichrist, invented against the truth.

<margin>Art. 10.</margin> We have also always believed that human inventions are an unspeakable abomination before God—such as the feast days and vigils of saints, holy water, the practice of abstaining from meat <note>original: "flesh"</note> on certain days, and similar things, but especially the Mass <note>original: "Masses"</note>.

<margin>Art. 11.</margin> We abhor all human inventions as coming from the Antichrist; all these things bring troubles with them and are harmful to the liberty of the spirit.

<margin>Art. 12.</margin> We believe that the sacraments are outward signs of holy things, or visible forms of invisible grace. We are of the opinion that it is good for the faithful to sometimes use those signs and visible forms, if it is possible. Nevertheless, we believe and hold that the faithful may be saved without receiving these signs when they lack the opportunity or the ability to use them.

<margin>Art. 13.</margin> We do not acknowledge any other sacrament besides Baptism and the Eucharist.

<margin>Art. 14.</margin> We honor the secular power with all subjection, obedience, readiness, and payment <note>This refers to the payment of taxes and tributes to civil authorities.</note>.

<meta>catchword: CHAP.</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the Waldensian Confession of Faith, detailing their rejection of Purgatory and Catholic traditions while affirming their belief in Christ as the sole mediator, the two-sacrament system, and obedience to civil government.</summary>

<margin>Art. 1.
Taken out of the book of Charles du Moulin, *The Monarchy of the French* <note>original: *Mon. des François*</note>, p. 65.</margin>
WE believe that there is only one God, who is a Spirit, the Creator of all things, the Father of all, who is above all, and in us all, who is to be adored in spirit and truth, upon whom alone we wait, and to whom we give all glory for our life, our nourishment, clothing, health, sickness, prosperity, and adversity: we love him as the author of all goodness, and we fear him as the one who knows our hearts.

<margin>Art. 2.</margin>
We believe that Jesus Christ is the Son and image of his Father; that in him dwells the fullness of the divinity; by whom we know the Father, who is our mediator and advocate, and there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we can be saved; in whose name alone we call upon the Father, and use no other prayers but those that are contained in the Holy Scriptures, or those agreeing with them in substance.

<margin>Art. 3.</margin>
We believe that the Holy Spirit <note>original: "holy Ghost"</note> is our Comforter, proceeding from the Father and the Son, by whose inspiration we make our prayers, being renewed by him, who does all good works in us, and by him we have knowledge of all truth.

<margin>Art. 4.</margin>
We believe that there is one holy Church, which is the congregation of all the elect and faithful, who have been from the beginning of the world, and shall be until the end, of which our Lord Jesus Christ is the head. <margin>Art. 5.</margin>

<margin>Art. 8.</margin>
We hold the holy sacrament of the Table or Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ to be a holy remembrance and thanksgiving for the benefits which we have received by his death and passion, which is to be received in faith...

### Chapter 14.

->*The Creed <note>original: "Symbole"</note> of Athanasius in the Waldensian language.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'W' (originally 'Q' for "Qualquequal") featuring foliate and floral ornamentation within a square frame.</image-desc>
Whoever <note>original: "Qualquequal"</note> wishes to be saved, before all things it is necessary to hold the Catholic <note>The term "Catholic" here is used in its original sense to mean "universal" or the whole of the Christian faith shared across time and place.</note> faith, which if anyone does not keep entirely, without doubt they shall perish eternally. But this is the Catholic faith: That we worship one God in Trinity, and the Trinity in Unity, neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance. For there is one person of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit. The Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated, and the Holy Spirit is uncreated. The Father is immeasurable <note>original: "mesuriuol"; traditionally translated as "incomprehensible" in English versions of this creed, meaning "not limited by space or measure."</note>, the Son is immeasurable, and the Holy Spirit is immeasurable. The Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, and the Holy Spirit is eternal. Therefore <note>original: "emperço"</note>, they are not three eternals, but one eternal; likewise <note>original: "enaimi"</note> there are not three immeasurables, nor three uncreated. Similarly, the Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Holy Spirit is almighty; therefore, they are not three almighties, but one almighty. Likewise, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; therefore, there are not three Gods, but one God. Likewise, the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; therefore, there are not three Lords, but one Lord. For just as we are compelled to confess by Christian truth that each person is God or Lord, so we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to say there are three Gods or three Lords. The Son is from the Father alone, not made, nor created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and from the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding. Therefore, there is one Father, not three Fathers; one Son, not three Sons; and one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits. In this Trinity, nothing is first or last, and nothing is greater or lesser, but all three persons are together co-eternal and equal. Likewise, in all things, as has been said above, the Trinity in Unity is to be honored, and the Uni-

<header>Chapter 13. Concerning the Waldenses.</header>

> <note>The following text is translated from the original Occitan, the Romance language used by the Waldenses in the Alpine regions.</note> ...Unity in Trinity. Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved must think thus of the Trinity. But for eternal salvation, it is necessary to faithfully believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, the right faith is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, is God and man. And he is God, begotten before the ages from the substance of the Father, and he is man, born in the world <note>original: "segle"</note> from the substance of his Mother, being perfect God and perfect man: of a rational soul and human flesh, equal to the Father according to his Divinity, and less than the Father according to his humanity. Who, although he is God and man, yet he is one Christ and not two; but one, not by the conversion of the Divinity into flesh, but properly by the taking of humanity into God <note>original: "de la Humanita en Dio"</note>; one totally, not by the confusion of the Divinity into flesh, but properly by the taking of humanity into God: one totally, not by the confusion of substance, but by the unity of persons. For as the rational soul and the flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ, who suffered for our salvation, descended into hell, rose again from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead. At whose coming all people must rise again with their bodies and shall give an account of their own deeds. And those who have done good shall go into eternal life, and those who have done evil shall go into eternal fire.

The belief of the Waldenses is sufficiently known by what is contained in the pure and holy doctrines of their confessions mentioned above. And yet, nevertheless, it is for this very faith that they have been persecuted for the space of four hundred and fifty years, and still would be if they lived near those places where human inventions are preferred over the Word of God. #### CHAPTER 1

->*By whom the Waldenses have been persecuted, for what reasons, by*<-
->*what means, and during what times.*<-

<margin>Rainierius's account of the Waldenses.</margin>
<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'T' depicting a scholar or monk seated at a writing desk with an open book, surrounded by ornate foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>
The Waldenses have had no greater enemies than the Popes. This is because, as the monk Rainierius <note>Rainierius Saccho (c. 1200–1259) was a Dominican inquisitor and former Cathar who wrote an influential treatise against heretical groups.</note> says, among all those who have raised themselves against the Church of Rome, the Waldenses have always been the most dangerous and harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note>. This is because they have resisted the Church for a long time, and also because this sect (as he calls them) is more widespread; indeed, there is almost no country...

<summary>This page introduces the second book of the history, focusing on the long-standing persecution of the Waldenses by the Papacy and citing the inquisitor Rainierius Saccho on why they were considered so dangerous.</summary>

<header>The History Book 2.</header>

...country in which it has not taken root. And thirdly, because all others, through their blasphemies against God, strike a horror into men's hearts; but this group, on the contrary, has a great appearance of piety. For they conduct themselves uprightly before men and believe correctly concerning God in all things, holding all the articles contained in the Creed <note>original: "Simbole"; referring here to the Apostles' Creed or a basic statement of Christian faith</note>, while hating and reviling the Church of *Rome*. In this (he says), they are easily believed by the people.

<margin>Rainier, chapter on the effort to pervert others and the method of teaching, folio 98. <note>original: "Rainer. cap. de studio pervertendi alios & modo docendi. fol. 98."</note></margin>
And in another place, the same *Rainier* says that the first lesson the *Waldenses* give to those whom they win over to their sect is this: they teach them what the disciples of Christ ought to be, using the words of the Gospel and the Apostles. They affirm that they alone are the successors of the Apostles because they imitate their way of life. From this, he says, they infer that the Pope, the bishops, and the clergy—who possess and enjoy the riches of this world and seek after them—do not follow the examples of the Apostles. Therefore, they are not the true guides of the Church. They argue it was never the purpose of *Jesus Christ* to commit his chaste and beloved spouse <note>The "Spouse of Christ" is a traditional theological metaphor for the Christian Church.</note> to those who would rather debase <note>original: "prostitute"</note> her by their bad examples and wicked actions than preserve her in that purity in which they received her at the beginning: a chaste virgin without spot.

Out of hatred for the various discourses which the *Waldenses* have written against the luxury, greed, pride, and errors brought in by the Pope, the authorities have always persecuted them to the death.

The means they have used to utterly exterminate them have been, in the first place, their "thunderbolts" <note>A figurative term for papal bulls, excommunications, or formal condemnations.</note>, curses, canons, constitutions, decrees, and whatever else might make them hateful to kings and princes...
