<header>Chapter 1: Of the Waldenses.</header>

...princes, and people of the earth, giving them over, as much as lies in their power, unto Satan. They forbid <note>original: "interdicting"</note> them all communion and society with those who obey their laws, judging them unworthy and incapable of any positions <note>original: "charges"</note>, honors, or profits. They are barred from inheriting, making wills, or being buried in common churchyards. The authorities confiscated their goods and disinherited their heirs; and whenever they could capture them, they condemned them to be delivered to the secular power <note>The "secular power" refers to civil authorities who carried out executions, as the Church itself technically did not shed blood.</note>, their houses to be razed, and their lands and possessions <note>original: "moueables"</note> confiscated or given to the first person to seize them.

<margin>
These sentences are to be seen in the manual of the Inquisitors, along with the letters of Pope Alexander XIII <note>The text says "thirteenth," though this is likely a historical error in the original document or transcription for Pope Alexander III (reigned 1159–1181), who was the first to officially move against the Waldenses.</note> and of various other Popes who succeeded him.
</margin>

And we still have the records <note>original: "scedule"</note> of all these sentences today, issued by the Popes, along with the legal documents they used for such executions. We also have the commands they gave to kings, princes, magistrates, consuls, and the common people to perform a thorough investigation <note>original: "exact inquiſition"</note>, to shut the city gates, to demand the assistance and help of the people, to ring the alarm bell <note>original: "Tol-bell"; a bell rung to summon the community in an emergency or for a manhunt.</note>, and to arm themselves. If the accused could not be captured by other means, they were ordered to kill them and use every kind of violence deemed necessary in such a case. They gave the accusers a third part, or some other portion, of whatever was confiscated; meanwhile, all advisors and supporters of the accused were condemned to the same punishment.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, because no prince, magistrate, or any other official had the power to conduct a trial <note>original: "frame a proces"</note> regarding the matter of alleged heresy, a command was given to the bishops. Each was ordered within his own jurisdiction to investigate his flock and take note of how every individual person felt about the ordinances of the Popes and the Church of *Rome*. <header>The History: Book 2.</header>

<margin>
This Council was held at the Lateran <note>The Third Council of the Lateran, held in 1179–1180, which officially condemned the Waldenses.</note> in 1180. See the 27th Chapter.
</margin>

...out against the corruptions of the said Church of Rome. Alexander III, who was then Pope, commanded the Archbishop of Lyon to take action <note>original: "proceed"</note> against him. Because the Archbishop did not banish him as quickly or as thoroughly as the Pope desired, the Pope quickly assembled a Council. There, he excommunicated <term>Waldo</term> <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205), the leader of the Waldensian movement.</note> and all those who followed his doctrine, even if they went by other names.

However, this method was considered too mild for such a pressing situation as the Waldensian movement. Despite these "thunderbolts" <note>This refers to papal bulls or decrees of excommunication.</note> of the Church, they did not stop preaching that the Pope was the Antichrist, the Mass was an abomination, the Host <note>The bread used in the Eucharist, which Catholics believe becomes the literal body of Christ.</note> was an idol, and Purgatory was a myth <note>original: "fable"</note>. These points of doctrine, if accepted, were enough to overthrow the entire authority of the Pope and to dry up the rivers of wealth and indulgence <note>original: "gaine and grease"</note> that sustained the clergy.

Therefore, Innocent III—who succeeded Pope Celestine III around the year 1198—took a different approach than the ordinary bishops to manage the legal proceedings against the Waldenses and others whom he labeled "heretics." He authorized certain monks who held the full power of the Inquisition in their hands. They managed the legal cases and delivered the accused to the secular <note>civil</note> power by their full and absolute authority. This was a much faster but much more cruel method, delivering people by the thousands into the hands of magistrates, and the magistrates to the executioners. 

In just a few years, all of Christendom was deeply moved by these pitiful and mournful sights: seeing all those people burned or hanged who trusted only in one Lord Jesus Christ for their salvation and rejected the vain hopes invented by men for their own profit. This was the primary result of the aforementioned Inquisition, which we shall discuss in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Of the Inquisition: by whom it was first put into practice: and by what subtleties and cruelties the Waldenses have been troubled by it.*<-

<margin>
The Treasure of History in the year 1206.
</margin>
<margin>
Book of the Inquisition, chapter on "not killing," folio 100. Thus was killed Saint Peter of the Order of Preaching Friars <note>original: *Lib. Inquisit. cap. de non occidendo. fol. 100. Sic fuit occisus Sanctus Petrus de Ordine fratrum Praedicatorum.* This refers to Peter of Verona, an inquisitor murdered in 1252.</note>.
</margin>

At the start of the Popes' efforts to completely exterminate the Waldenses, they were satisfied with the methods mentioned in the previous chapter. However, the work progressed slowly, and despite those methods, the number of believers increased in such a way that those tactics were found to be weak. Consequently, Pope Innocent III resolved to try <note>original: "assay"</note> whether he could achieve through preaching what he could never accomplish through violence.

He therefore sent certain bishops and monks who preached in the Waldensian areas suspected of practicing their religion. But as the author of the *Treasure of Histories* says, these preachers converted no one except a few poor people; for the most part, he says, the people continued to persist in the profession of their faith. 

In Narbonnese Gaul <note>original: *Gallia Narbonensi*; a region in southern France.</note>, two monks were employed: Pierre de Chateauneuf <note>Peter of Castelnau (d. 1208), a Cistercian monk and papal legate whose later assassination was used as a pretext for the Albigensian Crusade.</note> and Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221), the founder of the Dominican Order.</note>, who was born at Calahorra in Spain. They were joined by a certain Abbot of Cîteaux <note>original: *Cisteaux*; the headquarters of the Cistercian Order.</note>, and many other priests and monks arrived in a large group, including a certain Bishop of Cestre <note>Likely the Bishop of Chester, or a reference to a French bishopric like Sisteron.</note>. The monk Pierre de Chateauneuf was killed during this mission and was canonized as a saint for it. Dominic...

...out against the corruptions of the said Church of Rome. Alexander III, who was then Pope, ordered the Archbishop of Lyon to take action against him; and because that prelate did not banish him as quickly as the Pope desired, he speedily convened a council where he excommunicated Waldo and all those who followed his doctrine, even if they went by other names.

But this method was considered too lenient for such an urgent situation as that of the Waldenses, who did not stop preaching despite these threats <note>original: "thunderbolts"</note>. They continued to teach that the Pope was the Antichrist, the Mass was an abomination, the consecrated bread <note>original: "Hoste"</note> was an idol, and Purgatory was a myth <note>original: "fable"</note>. These were points that, if accepted, were enough to overthrow the entire authority of the Pope and dry up the vast sources of income and wealth <note>original: "rivers of gaine and grease"</note> of the clergy. 

Therefore, Innocent III—who succeeded Pope Celestine III around the year 1198—took a different approach than the local bishops to build the legal cases against the Waldenses and others whom he called heretics. He authorized certain monks who held the full power of the Inquisition in their hands. They managed the trials <note>original: "framed the Proces"</note> and delivered people to the secular <note>civil or non-religious</note> power with absolute authority. This was a much faster but far more cruel method, delivering people by the thousands into the hands of the magistrates, and the magistrates to the executioners. Consequently, within a few years, all of Christendom was deeply moved by these pitiful and tragic spectacles: seeing all those who trusted only in one Lord Jesus Christ for their salvation, and who renounced the empty hopes invented by men for their own profit, being burned or hanged. This was the entire result <note>original: "fruit"</note> of the aforementioned Inquisition, which we shall speak of in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the Inquisition: by whom it was first put into practice, and by what deceptions and cruelties the Waldenses have been tormented by it.*<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
In the beginning of the Popes' prosecution, seeking to utterly exterminate the Waldenses, they were content with the means mentioned above in the preceding chapter. However, either because the business moved too slowly, or because—despite those means—the number of believers increased in such a way that these methods were found to be weak, Pope Innocent III resolved to test whether he could achieve through preaching what he could never do through violence. He therefore sent certain bishops and monks who preached in those places suspected of professing the Waldensian religion; but as the author of the *Treasure of Histories* <note>original: *Le Tresor des Histoires*, a medieval chronicle</note> writes, these preachers converted no one but a few poor people. For the most part, he says, they still persisted in the profession of their faith.

<margin>The Treasure of Histories in the year 1206.</margin>
In Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, two monks were employed: Pierre de Chateauneuf and Dominic (born at Calahorra in Spain), to whom they joined a certain Abbot of Cîteaux. In a group, as if together, many other priests and monks came, and among the rest, a certain Bishop of Castres <note>original: "Cestre"</note>.

<margin>Mendicant monks <note>original: *Moynes qui mandient*</note>.</margin>
Dominic continued his persecution of the Waldenses in both word and deed. This monk, seeing himself in a position of authority, established an order of mendicant <term>begging monks who lived on alms</term> monks, who were called "Dominicans" after his name. This monk was later canonized <note>declared a saint by the Catholic Church</note>, and his order was confirmed by Pope Honorius. The Pope claimed he was encouraged to do this by a dream, for it seemed to him that the Church of Rome was falling, and that Dominic upheld it with his shoulders. In return for this, the Pope commanded that the Dominican Order should hold the primary place among the mendicants.

<margin>Mendicants.</margin>
<margin>The Martyrology regarding the life of Dominic <note>original: *Martirologe*, a directory of saints</note>.</margin>
It is said of this monk that when his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed she had a dog in her womb that spat flames of fire from its throat. His followers interpret this to his advantage, as if we were meant to understand that he would be the "dog" who would vomit out the fire that would consume the heretics. But on the contrary, those whom he delivered to death every day might well say that he was the dog who had set all of Christendom on fire, and that the flames coming out of his throat represent those fiery and hellish sentences which he pronounced against the Christians. 

In any case, he managed these affairs so well that before he died, he built many fine houses in Languedoc, Provence, Dauphiné <note>original: "Dolphine," a historical province in southeastern France</note>, Spain, and elsewhere. Through these, he obtained great revenues, either from the generosity of those who favored his order or from the confiscations of the Waldenses' property. From these spoils, Count Simon de Montfort gave him great privileges and charity—effectively being generous with other men's property <note>original: "cutting large thongs of another mans leather," an old proverb for being charitable with what one has stolen or taken from others</note>.

He worked in the Inquisition as the chief official, with

<page-num>7</page-num>
### Chapter 2: Concerning the Waldenses

...such contentment to the Popes, that from that time forward, the monks of his Order have been always employed in the Inquisition.

The power given to these monk-inquisitors was without limits. They could assemble the people whenever they pleased by the sound of a bell, proceed against even the bishops themselves, and issue legal processes if needed—imprisoning people and opening prisons without any oversight. All types of accusations were considered valid: a sorcerer or a harlot were deemed sufficient witnesses, without any grounds for challenge <note>original: "reproach"</note>, in cases of alleged heresy. It did not matter who the accuser was, nor whether the accusation was made verbally or through notes <note>original: "tickets"</note> thrown before the inquisitor. Without any personal appearance or confrontation between the parties, legal proceedings were framed without a defense, without witnesses, and without any law other than the will of the inquisitor. 

To be wealthy was a crime nearly equal to heresy; anyone who had property to lose was on the path to being ruined, either as a heretic or, at the very least, as a supporter <note>original: "favourer"</note> of heretics. A mere suspicion was enough to silence fathers, mothers, and relatives, so that they dared not intervene against the punishments to come. Anyone who pleaded for so much as a cup of cold water or a bit of straw to lie on in some stinking dungeon was condemned as a supporter of heretics and subjected to the same or even worse treatment. No lawyer dared to undertake the defense of even his closest relative or friend, nor did any notary dare to record any legal document in their favor. Furthermore, once a man was entangled in the snares of the Inquisition, he could never live with any sense of security, for he was always forced to start the process all over again:

<meta>This page continues the description of the terrifying power of the monk-inquisitors, focusing on the legal and social consequences for those accused of heresy, even after death.</meta>

<page-num>8</page-num>
<header>The History Book 2.</header>

...brought back again. For if any man were set at liberty, it was only for a time until they might better consider the matter. Death itself did not end the punishment, for they have left to us certain copies of their sentences against the bones of the dead, ordering them to be exhumed <note>original: "dis-interre"</note> and burned, even thirty years after the death of the accused party. 

Those who were heirs had no certainty of their future; for upon any accusation of their fathers or relatives, they dared not undertake the defense of their own rights, nor possess their own inheritance, without facing the crime or suspicion of heresy. It seemed they inherited the "bad faith" and opinions of their ancestors rather than their goods. 

The people—even the most powerful and richest among them—were forced, in a manner, to adore these monks, the Inquisitors, and to bestow upon them great presents for the building of their convents and the endowment of their houses. This was done for fear of being accused of heresy or for fear of not being seen as sufficiently zealous for the faith of those "holy fathers." 

To better maintain an atmosphere of fear <note>original: "entertaine men with an apprehension"</note> regarding these things, the Inquisitors sometimes made spectacles and displays of their prisoners, leading them in triumph during their processions. Some were ordered to whip themselves; others were forced to go covered in the manner of "St. Benedicts"—that is to say, wearing certain red coats <note>original: "Cassockes"</note> with yellow crosses <note>The author is referring to the *sanbenito*, a penitential garment used by the Inquisition</note> to signify that they were people who had been convicted of some error. This also signaled that if they committed a second offense, they were already condemned as heretics. Others appeared in their shirts, barefoot and bareheaded, with a rope <note>original: "with," referring to a withe or a noose made of flexible twigs</note> about their necks and a torch in their hands. Being thus prepared and displayed, they might strike terror into the beholders to see such persons of all social classes <note>original: "estates"</note> and genders...

<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>Chapter 2: Of the Waldenses</header>

...brought to such a miserable condition, being all forbidden from entering the church. Instead, they were forced to stay in the porch or merely catch a glimpse of the Host <note>The consecrated bread used in the Eucharist, which was "shown" or elevated by the priest</note> when it was displayed by the priest, until the Inquisitor fathers decided otherwise.

To fully satisfy these "fathers," those they accused were exiled as a penance to the Holy Land or enrolled in some other expedition against the Turks or other non-believers <note>original: "Infidels"</note>. These expeditions were organized by the command of the Pope to serve the Church for a certain amount of time at the individuals' own expense. In the meantime, these "holy fathers" took possession of the property of the poor pilgrims. Worst of all, upon their return, the men were forbidden from asking whether the monks had been intimately involved <note>original: "priuate familiarity"</note> with their wives during their absence, for fear that they might be condemned as backsliders, impenitent, and completely unworthy of any mercy.

These violent acts were carried out from the year 1206—which was around the time that Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (c. 1170–1221), founder of the Dominican Order, which ran much of the Inquisition</note> established his Inquisition—until the year 1228. During this time, such great havoc was wreaked upon poor Christians that the Archbishops of Aix, Arles, and Narbonne met at Avignon in the year 1228. They gathered at the request of the inquisitor monks to consult with them about various difficulties in carrying out their duties. However, they felt compassion for the misery of the great number of people who were accused and kept in prison by the inquisitor monks, saying:

<header>The History: Book 2</header>

<margin>You would have had. <note>original: "Veus tuissies" (Middle French "Vous eussiez"). This refers to the bishops' statement that the Inquisitors would have needed an impossible amount of stone and mortar to house all their prisoners.</note></margin>
...nourishment, but to provide lime and stone to build prisons for them. "We therefore counsel you," they said, "that you delay such imprisonments for a little while, until the Pope may be informed <note>original: "aduertised"</note> of the great numbers that have been arrested, and so that he may advise what he wishes to be done. If not, there is no reason you should take offense regarding those who are stubborn <note>original: "impenitent"</note> and beyond correction <note>original: "incorigible"</note>, or that you should doubt they might relapse, or escape, or infect others if they had their liberty, because you may condemn such persons without delay."

There needs to be no other proof than this testimony of the aforementioned Prelates to make it clear that the number of those whom the Inquisition had delivered unto death was very great. For regarding the question raised by the said Inquisitors—whether those who have associated with the Waldenses and have received the Lord's Supper with them are to be excused because they say they offended out of ignorance, not knowing that they were Waldenses—the answer of the said Prelates was that they were not to be excused. "Because," they said, "who is such a stranger as not to know that the Waldenses have been punished and condemned for these many years past? And who does not know that for a long time they have been pursued and persecuted at the expense and labor <note>original: "charge and trauell"</note> of Catholics? This pursuit is confirmed <note>original: "sealed"</note> by so many persons condemned to death that it cannot be doubted."

# Chapter 2: Concerning the Waldenses

<sig>Bb 2</sig>

<margin>George Morel in his memorials, page 54.</margin>
...was so successful that, despite the bloody persecutions after the time of Waldo in the year 1160, there were, according to the report of Morel, more than eight hundred thousand people who professed the faith of the said Waldenses.

Regarding the deceptive tactics <note>original: "subtleties"</note> of the said Inquisitors, we would have no knowledge of them except from those who escaped the Spanish Inquisition, if it were not God’s will that their cunning tricks should not be so closely hidden. Instead, we have examples of these tactics even from the Inquisitors themselves.

Here, then, are the crafty tactics of the Inquisitors, which served as their rules in building legal cases <note>original: "proces"</note> against the Waldenses:

*   It is not advisable to debate matters of faith in front of common people <note>original: "lay-people"</note>.
*   No person shall be considered truly repentant <note>original: "penitent"</note> if he does not accuse those he knows to be like himself.
*   Anyone who does not accuse those like himself shall be cut off from the Church as a rotten limb, for fear that the healthy <note>original: "found"; likely a transcription of "sound"</note> members should be corrupted by him.
*   After someone has been handed over to the secular authorities <note>original: "secular power"</note>, great care must be taken that he is not allowed to defend himself or demonstrate his innocence before the public. This is because if he is put to death, it causes a scandal among the common people; and if he escapes, his loyalty is dangerous.
*   Care must be taken not to promise life to a person condemned to death in front of the public, considering that a heretic will never allow himself to be burned if he can escape through such promises.

And if he promises to repent before the people, yet is not granted his life, a scandal will arise among them; it will be thought that he is being put to death wrongfully.

Note (they say) that the Inquisitor ought always to assume the facts of the case <note>original: "presuppose the fact"</note> without any conditions. He is only to inquire about the specific circumstances of the act, such as: "How often have you confessed yourself to heretics?" or "In what room of the house did they stay?" and similar things.

The Inquisitor may look into any book as if he found the life story of the accused—and everyone else he is questioning—written there. <note>This was a deceptive tactic used to make the accused believe the Inquisitor already possessed a written record of their secret lives.</note>

It is necessary to threaten the accused with death if he does not confess, and to tell him that the facts are too obvious. Tell him it is proper for him to think of his soul and renounce his heresy because he must die anyway, and therefore it would be good for him to patiently accept whatever happens to him. And if he should answer, "Since I must die, I would rather die in the faith I profess than in that of the Roman Church," then you may conclude for certain that his previous display of repentance was merely a show; therefore, let him suffer justice <note>original: "iuſtice"; in this context, execution.</note>.

We must not think we can defeat heretics through learning or by using the Scriptures, because even learned men are often confounded by them. As a result, the heretics strengthen their own resolve when they see they are able to deceive <note>original: "delude"</note> even the most educated scholars.

Again, great care must be taken because heretics never answer directly. When they are pressured by frequent questioning, they have a habit of claiming that they are merely simple and foolish people,

They also issued a prohibition <note>original: "inhibition"</note> to the victims' neighbors, forbidding them from assisting them in any way whatsoever. They were not to welcome them, visit them, defend them, or provide them with any relief or food <note>original: "sustenance"</note>. Anyone who did so faced the penalty of being charged and convicted as a supporter of heretics. Such supporters were declared unworthy of all public offices, positions of responsibility, and councils. 

Everyone was forbidden from using the service of any of these people as witnesses <note>original: "in matter of testimony"</note>, and the condemned themselves were judged legally incapable of making a will or of receiving any inheritance. Furthermore, if any of those condemned were judges, their rulings were to have no legal force, and no legal cases were to be brought before them. If any were advocates <note>lawyers</note>, their defenses and pleas were not to be accepted. If they were notaries, their legal documents <note>original: "instruments"</note> were to be of no effect, but were instead to be canceled and destroyed. 

If they were priests, they were to be stripped of all offices and benefices <note>A "benefice" was a church office that provided a living or income.</note>. Regarding the **Waldenses** of the valley of **Pragela**, they were attacked <note>original: "assayled"</note> by their enemies from the direction of **Susa**, a town in **Piedmont**, around the year 1400. ### Chapter 3: Of the Waldenses

Most of the infants' mothers died after them, and various others were taking their last breath.

Having retreated into the houses of these poor people during the night, the enemies ransacked and looted whatever they could carry to **Susa**. To complete their cruelty, they hanged a poor **Waldensian** woman named **Margaret Athode** from a tree, whom they had met on the mountain of **Meane**.

The inhabitants of that valley consider this persecution to be the most violent that their fathers ever told them about—the worst they or their grandfathers had ever suffered. They still speak of it today as if it were a recent event, fresh in their memory. The story of this unexpected surprise, which caused so much misery among them, has been passed down so often from father to son.

Meanwhile, the **Waldenses** of the valley of **Frassiniere** <note>modern: Freissinières</note> who remained and had escaped the previously mentioned persecution were again violently mistreated by their neighbor, the Archbishop of **Ambrun** <note>modern: Embrun</note>, in the <margin>1460.</margin> year 1460. ## The Letters of King Louis 
->the Eleventh<-

Louis, by the grace of God, King of France, Dauphin of Viennois <note>original: "Dauphin de Vienois"</note>, Count of Valentinois <note>original: "Conte de Valentinois"</note>, and Diois <note>original: "Dioys"</note>; to our well-beloved and faithful Governor of our province of Dauphiné, greetings and affection <note>original: "health and dilection," a formal greeting expressing goodwill</note>:

The History Book 2.

In Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphine"</note>, a certain counselor named Ponce was appointed to ensure that this mixed judgment might be without appeal. The sentence was pronounced in the great church at Embrun <note>original: "Ambrun"</note> and afterward fastened upon the door of the church on a large tablet. In the lower part of this tablet, there were thirty-two articles regarding the beliefs of the Waldensians <note>original: "Waldenses"</note>. These articles were against the Mass, Purgatory, the invocation of saints, pilgrimages, the observation of feast days, the distinction of foods <note>original: "Viandes"</note> on certain days, and other matters affirmed by the Waldensians.

But this Inquisitor added to the articles of their belief the claim that they held that, for the increase of humankind, a man might have sexual relations with his own sister, niece, or any other relative regardless of the degree of proximity, because God has said, "Increase and multiply."

Furthermore, he claimed they believed that every man who burns with lust may carnally know any woman whatsoever without sinning, because the Apostle says that it is better to marry than to burn, and because it is said in the Gospel, "He who is able to receive it, let him receive it" <note>original: "qui potest capere capiat"</note>, which they interpreted as "let him take what he can."

However, the records <note>original: "informations"</note> upon which they grounded their sentence have come into our hands, and this imposture has been discovered to their own condemnation. There is not a single witness—or at least among the vast majority of those who were heard—who was not a priest or monk. When these witnesses were asked by the monk whether they knew if the beliefs contained in these articles were true, they answered that they never knew any such things to be either taught or practiced among the Waldensians.

# Chapter 3: *Of the Waldensians*

In the same collection of legal proceedings <note>original: "bundle or bag of proces"</note> against the Waldensians, there is one case framed against two pastors who were captured near the hill on the side of the plain <margin>On the pass of Côte Plaine, 1492 <note>original: "Sur le col de coste Plane"</note></margin> named Francis Gerondin and Peter James, in the year 1492. When asked why the "sect" of the Waldensians grew and increased so quickly, spreading into so many places over such a long time, the monk recorded the answer of Pastor Gerondin as follows:

That the dissolute lives of the priests was the cause, and because the Cardinals were covetous, proud, and lived in luxury <note>In this context, "luxury" refers to lewdness or sexual immorality</note>. It was a thing known to all that there was neither Pope, Cardinal, nor Bishop who did not keep mistresses, and few or none who did not use young men for sodomy. Therefore, it was an easy matter for the Waldensian pastors to persuade the people that the religion of such scandalous persons was not good, since their "fruits" (their actions) were so bad. 

Immediately afterward, the said pastor was asked what they taught regarding luxury <note>lust</note>. They recorded his answer as: "that luxury is no sin, except when it is between a mother and her child." 

The author notes the absurdity of this: it would have been impossible for the pastors to draw people away from the Church of Rome by condemning the luxury of the priests if they themselves taught that luxury was no sin. 

Again, being asked why incest between a child and a mother was a sin, they recorded his answer: "because God has forbidden it." When asked where He had forbidden it, they made him say that Jesus Christ said to John before He ascended into heaven: "Take care where I have failed once, and do not return there again" <note>original: "Garde to doue ser ay failli una volta non tornar piu"</note>. ### Chapter 3. Of the Waldenses.

The Waldenses in Dauphiné, also called Chagnards <note>A local nickname for the Waldenses in the Dauphiné region</note>. Fabri the Inquisitor, and one Gobandi, a notary of Embrun <note>original: Ambrun</note> and secretary to the said inquisitors, carried to Embrun a certain indictment framed against Peironette of Beauregard in Valentinois, the widow of one Peter Berand. We do not mention her for her steadfastness <note>original: constancie</note>, but because she delivered in her answers many things that may add to this history.

Being therefore asked whether she had seen or heard of <note>original: understood of</note> any of the pastors of the Waldenses, she answered at first that she had not, being resolved to answer all interrogatories negatively. The inquisitors ordained that because she had not satisfied their demands, she should be conveyed to the prison of the Bishop of Valence. After being threatened with further interrogation <note>original: urged touching the question</note>, she confessed that about twenty-five years ago, there were two men clothed in gray who came to her husband’s house. After supper, one of them asked her, "Have you never heard speak of a handful of people who are in the world, without whom the world must have an end?" <note>original Provençal: N’aues vous iamais auai parlar d’un plen pung de mond, que ſi non era tot lo monde ſeria afin.</note> 

Having answered that she never heard any speech of it, except from one Monsieur André <note>original: Monsen Andre</note>, the parson of Beauregard, who often told her that there was a small number of people in the world without whom the world must perish, he then likewise told her that he was now come there to confer with her about that "little flock." He gave her to understand that they were the men who had learned by the commandments of God how to serve Him, and that they traveled about the world to instruct men,

...how they ought to adore and honor him, and to reform the abuses of the Church of Rome. He said that church officials <note>original: "Ecclesiastical persons"</note> were too rich, which was why they supported their mistresses <note>original: "strumpets"</note> and lived scandalously. Regarding the Pope, he said in his own language: "The Pope is as bad, or even worse than any other man, and therefore he has no power" <note>original Provençal: "Autant crois & autant maluais es, lo Papa coma nengun autre, & per co non ages de poiſſanfa"</note>. He also taught that it was better to give to the poor than to make offerings to priests, and that it was a pointless thing to bow the knee before images of saints.

She was sent back to prison and called again the next morning. Persisting in her previous statement, she added that the pastors had told her that priests who received money for the Masses they sing were like Judas, who sold his Master for silver; and those who gave money for their Masses were like the Jews who bought Christ with money.

### Chapter 3: Of the Waldenses

These Inquisitors released this **Peironette** until they were further advised, having first extracted from her everything she knew regarding the assemblies of the **Waldenses**: the people who attended them, and the locations and times they were held. This information afterwards brought great trouble to the Waldensian Churches, but profit and prey to the Inquisitors.

<margin>1597</margin>
In the year of our Lord 1497, the Archbishop of Embrun <note>original: "Ambrun"</note>, named **Rostain**, wanted to know upon his arrival how matters had proceeded up to that point against the Waldenses of his diocese. He found that those who lived in the valley of Freissinières <note>original: "Fraissiniere"</note> had been excommunicated by the Inquisitors, who had then framed their indictments and delivered them to the secular power <note>The "secular power" refers to the civil government, which was responsible for carrying out the physical punishments, such as executions, decreed by the church courts.</note>. Nothing had hindered the execution of the sentences pronounced against them except for their flight. 

Despite being earnestly requested by a man named **Fazion Gay**, an inhabitant of the valley, the Archbishop refused to enter the area. He argued that because they had been condemned by the authority of the Roman Pontiff <note>original Latin: "authoritate Pontificis Romani"</note>, he could not begin a mission to them without consulting the Pope <note>original Latin: "inconsulto Pontifice"</note>. He said, "But when our holy father loosens my hands <note>original Latin: "laxabit mihi manus"; meaning when the Pope grants him the legal authority or permission to act</note> and their absolution is made plain and apparent to me, I will go to visit them." 

**Fazion Gay**, speaking on behalf of the inhabitants (who claimed they intended to live as good Catholics), answered that the King had already granted relief from such punishments, provided that they lived as good Catholics from that time forward.

The Archbishop replied that he would do nothing until he had sent word to the Pope. For that purpose, he appointed a Master of Theology called Friar **John Columbi**, and he intended to write to the Pope

### Chapter 3: Of the Waldensians

The *Waldensians* <note>original: "Waldenses"</note>, on the other hand, were very insistent that the Archbishop specifically be ordered to return their property. This was because many portions of the said goods had been added to the Archbishop's own estate. Whenever they demanded them, he would refer the matter to the Pope, which hindered the orders that the late deceased King had established.

The Great Council, having taken notice of this business, decreed that no changes should be made <note>original: "nothing should be innovated"</note> regarding the *Waldensians* of *Freissinières* <note>original: "Frassiniere"</note>. The King had written to the Pope requesting that Apostolic Commissioners <note>Papal representatives appointed to handle specific legal or religious tasks</note> be joined with the Archbishop, acting as the Ordinary <term>Ordinary: a church official, such as a bishop, with immediate jurisdiction over a specific territory</term>, to finally settle this business.

To carry out this decree, a certain confessor to the King and the Official <term>Official: a judicial officer representing a bishop in legal matters</term> of *Orléans* were named as Apostolic Commissioners. They arrived in *Embrun* <note>original: "Ambrun"</note> on July 4, 1501.

### Louis, by the grace of God, King of France, etc.

> *Because it has come to our knowledge that the inhabitants of Freissinières <note>original: "Frassiniere"</note> have endured great troubles, harassment, punishments, and hardships <note>original: "trauels"; meaning labors or sufferings</note>, we, desiring to relieve them and ensure they are restored to their goods—both movable and immovable—do by these presents command all those who withhold the said goods to immediately and without delay cease their claims, surrender the said goods, and restore them to the said petitioners <note>original: "Suppliants"</note> or their attorneys acting for them, each to his own place and rank. <header>The History: Book 2</header>

<margin>1560</margin>
In the year 1560, the *Waldenses* of *Freissinières* <note>original: "Frassiniere"</note> and *Pragela* had their churches furnished with pastors, who kept them in the practice of their religion during that time when they persecuted to death all those who made profession of the Reformation. The President *Truchon* made a speech <note>original: "Oration"</note> to the Estates of *Provence* assembled that same year, on the sixth of November, for the purpose of exterminating the said *Waldenses* of *Freissinières* and *Pragela*. He said that it was necessary to purge the "old and ancient leaven" <note>original: "Leuen"; a biblical metaphor (from 1 Corinthians 5:6) referring to a small influence that can spread and affect an entire group.</note>, which was likely to sour the whole province of *Dauphiné* <note>original: "Dauphine"</note> if some course were not taken to prevent it. By these Estates, it was resolved to extirpate <note>To root out or destroy completely.</note> them by open force and by arms; for this purpose, commissions were given out to levy troops of men and to march into the said valleys. But as soon as the drum was struck up and the men were in arms throughout *Provence*, the unexpected death of King *Francis II* <note>King Francis II of France died at age 16 in December 1560, leading to a period of political shift under the regency of Catherine de' Medici.</note> changed the plan. Afterward, the said *Waldensian* churches in *Dauphiné* continued, as they still do by the unique favor of God.

### CHAPTER 4.

*Concerning the Waldensian Churches in Piedmont and the persecutions they endured which have come to our knowledge.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' set within a square woodcut border featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

The Waldenses have had famous churches in the valleys of Piedmont, Angrogna <note>original: "Angrongne"</note>, Perosa <note>original: "la Perouse"</note>, the Valley of Saint Martin, Luserna <note>original: "Lucerna"</note>, and other bordering places from time immemorial <note>original: "for time out of minde"</note>. It is held for certain among them that they are a branch of the Waldenses from Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphine"</note>, Pragela, Freissinières <note>original: "Frassinieres"</note>, and other neighboring places. As they grew in number over time, the land could no longer support them, and they were forced to disperse far and wide to find places where they could best settle. They have been as dear as brothers to one another. Despite being constantly oppressed with troubles, they have always supported <note>original: "succoured"</note> each other with a most sincere love and charity, sparing neither their lives nor their goods for their mutual preservation.

The first troubles the Waldenses of Piedmont endured resulted from reports made by certain priests sent there by the Archbishop of Turin. These priests reported that the people committed to their charge did not live according to the customs and beliefs of the Church of Rome. They did not make offerings for the dead, nor did they care for Masses or absolutions, nor for rescuing any of their family members from the pains of Purgatory by any of the usual...

...usual means. The Archbishops of *Turin* have persecuted them as much as lay in their power, making them hateful <note>original: "odious"</note> to their Princes. However, those Princes heard the good reports that their neighbors gave regarding their mild and honest conduct <note>original: "conversation," meaning their way of life</note>. They loved integrity and plain dealing, and were always ready to serve their Princes, very willingly yielding to them all dutiful obedience with cheerfulness <note>original: "alacrity"</note>. 

The Waldenses were in such grace and favor with their neighbors that the people of *Piedmont* sought to bring the Waldensian youth into their service and specifically looked for nurses among them to bring up their young infants. Because of this, the Princes continued for a long time in their purpose not to harass <note>original: "molest"</note> them. 

However, the priests and monks who lived among them gained nothing from the Waldenses' religious beliefs. They charged them with an infinite number of slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note>. Whenever any Waldenses went into *Piedmont* on business, the clergy always caught one or another and delivered him to the Inquisitors, and the Inquisitors delivered him to the executioner. In this manner, there was hardly any town or city in *Piedmont* in which one or another of them was not put to death. 

For instance: 
* ***Jordan Tertian*** was burned at *Susa* <note>original: "Suſe"</note>.

* ***Anthony Hiun*** was also hanged.

### Chapter 4. Of the Waldenses.

...fifty years, and others above a hundred and fifty. But among all the rest, the steadfastness <note>original: "constancy"</note> of one Catelin Girard is worthy of remembrance. While he was standing upon the block where he was to be burned at Revel in the Marquisate of Saluzzo <note>original: "Saluces"</note>, he requested that his executioners give him a couple of stones. They initially refused to do so, fearing he intended to throw them at someone. But after he protested that he would not, they finally delivered them to him. <margin>Vignaux in his *Memorials*, folio 7.</margin> Holding them in his hands, he said to them: "When I have eaten these stones, then you shall see an end to that religion for which you put me to death," and with that, he cast the stones upon the ground.

<margin>1488.</margin> The fires of execution were kindled until the year 1488, at which time the authorities resolved to attack the Waldenses by open force. They realized that the steadfastness of those whom they publicly put to death drew a great number of others to the knowledge of God; they likewise found that by the previous means, they would never achieve their intended design. Therefore, they recruited <note>original: "levied"</note> men to join with Albert de Capitaneis, an official commissioned by Pope Sixtus IV and Pope Innocent VIII. Eighteen thousand soldiers were mustered, besides a great number of the inhabitants of Piedmont who ran from all parts to join in the plunder <note>original: "pillage"</note>. They marched all at once toward Angrogna, Luserna, La Perosa, San Martino, Prauiglerm, and Biolet (which is in the Marquisate of Saluzzo). They also raised troops in Vaucluse in Dauphiné, overrunning the Valley of Pragelato <note>original: "Pragela"</note>. They did this so that, being bound to their own defense, these communities would not be able to help their neighbors, the Waldensian churches.

### The History Book 2.

In Piedmont, all of this was guided by the singular providence of God, in that the enemies divided their troops into small bands, more out of pride than for better speed <note>original: "expedition"</note>. Even though they were all employed in their own defense and could not help one another, the enemy’s division so diminished their forces that they were beaten everywhere, but especially in the Valley of **Angrogna**, where they made their most violent assault. Because such a recruitment <note>original: "levy"</note> of men could not be raised without some warning <note>original: "advertisement"</note> that it was intended against them, they prepared themselves to receive the attack. They held the narrow passages where few men were able to make an assault, being armed with certain long shields <term>targets: large, often rectangular shields used for infantry protection</term> of wood that covered them completely, and in which the arrows of their enemies struck without causing them any harm. The front line being thus armed and covered, the rest did good service—with great advantage—using their bows and crossbows under the cover of the said shields. 

As the enemy tried to approach the passages, the women and children (who were spectators) fell upon their knees and cried out in their own language: "O God help us" <note>original: "O Dio aiutaci, &c."</note>. The enemies made fun of them, and among others, one **Captain Saquet**, mocking the said women, was killed and cast headlong from the mountain into a deep pit <note>original: "bottome"</note> which to this day is called the **Gulf of Saquet**. At the same time, a certain Captain named **Le Noir de Montdeni** cried out to the women who prayed to God: "Mine, mine will make the passage" <note>original: "i miei, i miei faranno la passada"</note>—meaning that his soldiers would break through to put them to death—but he was killed by an arrow shot in the throat.

### Chapter 4. Of the Waldenses

Seeing this—and seeing that the rocks, the stones, and the arrows overwhelmed them—the soldiers all took to their heels, and the majority of them threw themselves down from the cliffs. These people witnessed another act of God’s providence: as the enemies approached the strongest natural fortification, which is the Valley of *Angrogna*, called *le Pré de la Tour*, where they might have fortified themselves and made themselves masters of the valley, God sent such a thick cloud and so dark a fog that the enemies could hardly see one another. Consequently, they had neither the time nor the means to recognize the strategic value <note>original: "goodness"</note> of the location or to remain there. 

At this, the *Waldenses* took courage and pursued them in such a way that the enemies, being completely scattered and unable to see where they were going, mostly fell headlong down the mountains and fled. They abandoned their weapons and the loot they had seized upon entering the valley, where they had poured out the people's wine and grain and loaded their servants with their most precious belongings <note>original: "moveables"</note>.

It pleased God to touch the heart of their Prince with some compassion for these poor people. This was *Philip* the seventh of that name, *Duke of Savoy* and *Prince of Piedmont*, who said that he did not want those people—who had always been true, most faithful, and obedient to him—to be harshly handled by way of *arms*. He was satisfied to have a dozen of the leaders <note>original: "principal amongst them"</note> come to *Pinerolo* <note>original: "Pignerol"</note>, where he was staying, to ask pardon for all the rest for having taken up arms in their own defense. He threw himself into the said valleys with his troops of men, which he performed so quickly that before the people were aware of it, he had entered their valleys with five hundred men—some on foot and some on horseback—ransacking, pillaging, and wasting whatsoever was before them. The people, leaving their plows and tilled fields, positioned themselves in the mountain passes. With their slings, they charged their enemies with such a multitude of stones, and with such violence, that the soldiers were forced to flee and abandon their prey, with many of them left dead upon the ground. 

This news came immediately to his Highness. He was also told that experience had taught them before that force of arms was not the way to reclaim and subdue these people, as the locations of their dwellings were so favorable to them. The Waldenses knew the straits <note>narrow mountain passes</note> and paths of the country better than the assailants did; therefore, there was nothing to be gained when the skin of one of the *Waldenses* had to be bought with the loss of the lives of a dozen of his other subjects. 

He decided, therefore, that it was not good to molest them any more with the military. Instead, he ordered that they should be taken "by retail" <note>Meaning captured individually or in small numbers rather than through mass military action.</note>, one by one, as they came into *Piedmont*. He intended for exemplary justice to be executed upon them if they did not change their belief, so that little by little they might be destroyed to the astonishment of all others who dwell in the said valleys. In this way, their ruin might be brought about imperceptibly <note>original: "insensibly"</note> and without endangering any of the Prince's other subjects.

All this did not stop the people; they still persisted in their resolution. To ensure that all things might be done in order among them, they assembled together from all their valleys at *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrongne"</note>...

Angrogne, in the year one thousand five hundred thirty-five, on the twelfth of September; that is to say, all the heads of every family with their pastors met. At this meeting, it was certified by them that their brethren, the Waldenses of Provence and Dauphiné, had sent their pastors, George Morell and Peter Masson, into Germany to confer with Oecolampadius, Bucer, and other servants of God who preached the Gospel there. They were to discuss the beliefs which the Waldenses have held from father to son since time out of mind. 

They found that God had been very merciful and gracious toward us, in that he has preserved us undefiled in the midst of so many idolatries and superstitions which have infected all of Christendom in past ages under the tyranny of the Antichrist of Rome <note>A common term used by Reformers to refer to the Papacy.</note>. They have encouraged us with holy advice <note>original: "advertisements"</note> and reasons, and exhorted us not to bury those talents which God has granted to us. They found it an evil thing that we have so long delayed making a public profession of adhering to the Gospel and causing it to be preached to the ears and knowledge of everyone. They urged us to leave the results to God—whatever he pleases should happen to us while we procure his glory and the advancement of the Kingdom of his Son. 

Afterward, having read the letters of the said Oecolampadius and Bucer, which were sent to them as brethren of the Waldenses of Provence and Dauphiné, the following propositions or articles were ordered, read, and approved. They were signed and sworn to by all those present with one mind and consent: to preserve, observe, believe, and retain these articles among them inviolably, without any contradiction, as being conformable to the doctrine...

doctrine, which has been taught to them from father to son for these many hundred years, and taken out of the word of God.

**ARTICLE I.** That Divine Service <note>original: "Diuine Seruice"; referring to public worship or liturgy.</note> cannot be performed except in spirit and in truth; for God is a spirit, and whoever will pray to him must pray in spirit.

**II.** All who have been or shall be saved have been chosen by God before the world began <note>original: "before all worlds"</note>.

**III.** Those who are saved cannot help but be saved <note>This expresses the doctrine of the "perseverance of the saints," meaning those chosen by God will certainly reach salvation.</note>.

**IV.** Whoever maintains the doctrine of free will completely denies the predestination and the grace of God.

**V.** No work is called "good" except that which is commanded by God; and no work is "evil" except that which is forbidden by God.

**VI.** A Christian may swear by the name of God without in any way contradicting what is written in the fifth chapter of *Saint Matthew*, provided that he who swears does not take the name of the Lord in vain. Now, a man does not swear in vain when his oath contributes to the glory of God and the good of his neighbor. Also, a man may swear in a court of judgment, because he who holds the office of a magistrate—whether he is a Christian or an infidel <note>A non-believer or someone outside the faith.</note>—holds the power of God.

**VII.** Auricular confession <note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest.</note> is not commanded by God. It is concluded according to the Holy Scriptures that the true confession of a Christian consists in confessing himself to the only God, to whom belongs honor and glory. There is another kind of confession, which occurs when a man reconciles himself with his neighbor, as mentioned in the fifth chapter of *Saint Matthew*. The third man—

These Articles, once they were resolved upon, astonished the priests who were among them to gather the revenues of their cures <term>A "cure" refers to the spiritual charge or office of a parish priest, as well as the income derived from it</term>. Perceiving that the door was now shut against their financial gain, they withdrew without saying a word. Upon their retreat, the Mass vanished by itself in the valleys of the said *Waldenses*. And because they had only the New Testament and some books of the Old Testament translated into the *Waldensian* tongue <note>The Waldensian language was a variety of Occitan, the medieval language of southern France</note>, they resolved quickly to send the whole Bible to the press, as their books were currently only manuscripts, and very few in number.

# Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

Having framed various indictments against specific individuals in these Valleys and having collected whatever evidence he could imagine might harm the people, the President also attempted to win them over through the preaching of the monks whom he had brought with him into the Valley of *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrongne"</note>.

The monk gave a long exhortation for them to return to the Church of *Rome*, making many claims about it which the people did not believe. After the monk had said as much as he wished and fell silent, the majority of the people requested that the pastors who were present—or one of them speaking for everyone—be permitted to answer the preacher’s discourse in a loving and mild manner.

However, the President would not allow this by any means. Consequently, a certain rumor or muttering arose among the people, which struck the President and his monks with such astonishment that they would have been quite content to be anywhere else. But hiding <note>original: "dissembling"</note> their fear, the President retreated to *Turin* without saying another word. Once he arrived there, he reported what he had done to the Parliament. ## The History, Book 2.

Because the places where they lived were so favorable to them, it was feared that it would take a great deal of labor and much blood would be shed before they could either be brought into the Church of *Rome* or removed from the world <note>i.e., killed</note>. It was argued that rooting them out was a task for a King, specifically the King of *France* <note>original: "Franc"</note>. Therefore, it was necessary to send the reports and leave the outcome of such a difficult undertaking to his own will and pleasure. 

This advice was followed; the indictments and reports were sent to the King. However, as the business of the Court is never finished quickly, a whole year passed before any other course of action was discussed or taken against them, other than that of the Inquisitors, who were always handing someone over to the secular power <note>The "secular power" refers to the civil government, which carried out the physical punishments and executions decreed by the church's Inquisitors</note>. 

But once the year had passed, express commands came from the Court from the King to force them to do by power what they would not be brought to do through words or friendly treatment. The Parliament sent the President of *Saint Julian* back. As soon as he arrived at *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrongne"</note>, he commanded them in the name of the King to go to Mass, upon pain of the confiscation of their lives and their goods. 

They demanded a copy of both his commission and his speech, promising to answer him in such a way that he would have reason to be satisfied. But nothing could satisfy the President, who continued to press them to change their religion, but in vain. For they answered him that they were not bound by such commands when they went against the commandment of God. He then commanded that twelve of the principal men among them, along with all the ministers and schoolmasters, should <note>The text continues onto the next page with the word "should"</note>

# The History Book 2

...enemies, once they have gained this advantage over us, and when we have no one left to comfort, counsel, reprove, or exhort us, will undoubtedly do everything in their power to forever shut the gates against the return of our good pastors. It is through their ministry that we have been so well instructed and fortified against a world of temptations. Therefore, so that we may not be accused as rebels for calling them back home later, it would be better for us not to deprive ourselves of the fruit of their ministry at all. From now on, let us be known as those who serve God by protecting those whom he has sent to preach his word to us. He is just as powerful to protect us now as he has been in the past. We would be ungrateful wretches to doubt his assistance, or to think that we—such a miserable flock—would not be devoured by wolves once the dogs <note>The author uses "dogs" here as a metaphor for the pastors who guard the "flock" of believers from spiritual danger.</note> have been chased away.

These and many similar speeches and arguments <note>original: "motions"</note> were made by those who were the most clear-sighted and more zealous than the rest. However, this could not stop others from entreating their pastors to withdraw for a few days to *Pragela* <note>modern: Pragelato</note>, a valley near theirs inhabited by their brethren, the *Waldenses* of *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France</note>. Here, one could perceive the heavy judgment <note>original: "justice"</note> of God upon them and the beginning of their misery. Everyone dissolved into tears, and the rocks resounded with cries and lamentations as even women and infants escorted their pastors to the high mountains to cross over to the other side. ### Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

For upon arriving at *Turin*, the deputies were immediately locked up in high-security prisons. Indictments were framed against them as heretics, and the roads were guarded to prevent anyone from reporting the treatment and "entertainment" <note>original: "entertainment," used here ironically to mean their reception or handling</note> received by those who had been sent on this mission. 

Meanwhile, the Count de *la Trinité* told the people that he knew His Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy</note> had agreed to all their demands. He claimed the Duke had written to him saying the deputies were only being detained to ensure they kept their promises for the future. For this same purpose, he also began building a fort near *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrongne"</note>. 

This made the people worry deeply about their situation, especially since they could hear no news of their poor prisoners, and *la Trinité* would certainly not allow them to send anyone there to check on them. In the end, after consulting among themselves for a long time about what to do—seeing a fort being built that might control and "bridle" them forever if allowed to be finished, yet fearing that if they acted against the workers, it would cost the lives of the deputies sent to *Turin*—they were in extreme distress. They did not know which path to take, for they realized they had been mocked by that deceiver <note>original: "Prater," meaning a trifler or one who talks idly and deceitfully</note> *la Trinité*. Therefore, they decided they must leave the outcome to the providence of God and reconcile themselves to him through prayer and fasting. Once they had done this, they called home

# The History, Book 2

Missing their pastors, the people asked for help from their neighbors in *Pragela* <note>A valley in the Cottian Alps, then under French control, home to fellow Protestants</note>, who came to their aid with arms. They entered the churches <note>original: "Temples"</note> where *La Trinité* had ordered altars to be built and images placed; they overthrew the altars and leveled them to the ground, even razing the foundations. They broke down the images, besieged the fort and took it, killed all those who resisted, and defeated the reinforcements <note>original: "succours"</note> that were sent to the fort, putting them to flight and killing a great number of them.

The Prince *Emanuel Philibert* <note>The Duke of Savoy</note> was greatly offended by this and wanted to take revenge on the prisoners he held. However, Madame *Margaret* <note>Margaret of France, Duchess of Savoy, who frequently advocated for the Waldenses</note> intervened for them and pacified the Prince. She showed him that it was necessary to consider how the people reacted to the treatment and "entertainment" <note>original: "usage and entertainment," referring to their reception and handling</note> His Highness had given to their deputies. She argued that seeing themselves on the road to total destruction, they had taken this desperate path <note>original: "oblique means"</note> to relieve and help themselves.

His Highness, therefore—at the advice and urging of the Pope’s Nuncio <note>A diplomatic representative of the Pope</note>—had forced the deputies to attend Mass and there ask pardon from God, the Pope, and their "holy mother," the Church of Rome, with a promise to live according to its laws. Afterward, he sent them to prison while waiting for the completion <note>original: "perfection"</note> of his fort. 

But seeing his expectations frustrated, he followed the course proposed by Madame *Margaret*, under which they have lived until the present. We do not insert that agreement here because it is set down elsewhere in their history. It is true that they afterwards suffered various persecutions at various times, which they bore patiently and with much zeal.

## Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

<margin>1570</margin>
Among the other periods of hardship, the year 1570 was particularly extreme. For their Prince <note>Emanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy</note>, having entered into an offensive league against the Protestants along with many other European princes, began to trouble and harass his subjects in the Waldensian valleys. 

First, he forbade them from having any trade or contact <note>original: "commerce"</note> with the Waldenses of *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France</note>, under penalty of death. Secondly, he prohibited them from assembling in any synod <note>A council of church leaders</note> or meeting except in the presence of the Governor of *Castrocaro*. To ensure this was carried out, the Governor made sure to attend the very first synod they called at *Bobio* <note>modern: Bobbio Pellice</note>. 

The pastors and elders <note>original: "Ancients"</note> who were present informed the Governor that his presence at their synods did not displease them in any way. They explained that the matters to be handled were such that if the whole world were a witness to them, their piety toward God and their loyalty toward their Prince would only be more apparent. They stated they intended to deliberate on nothing except what might lead to the glory of God and their obedience to their superiors. 

They further argued that since His Highness had reason to distrust them, it must be due to the false information provided by some of their enemies. Therefore, being certain in their own consciences that they had never deserved such treatment, they could only view this new requirement <note>original: "novelty"</note> as a manifest breach of the treaty and agreement he had made with them, and a form of persecution that threatened the free exercise of their religion. 

They therefore pleaded with the Governor of *Castrocaro* to withdraw and not to harass them with such innovations that deviated <note>original: "swarming," likely a variant of "swerving"</note> from the former treaties—at least until they had the opportunity to justify themselves before His Highness and he provided a different order. However, the Governor remained determined to stay. The pastors and—

# Chapter 4: Of the Waldenses

We will include this story here because by his steadfastness <note>original: "constancy"</note> he greatly encouraged <note>original: "edifie"</note> the people. It also serves to show the world that the Popes do not cease to demonstrate how hateful the doctrine of the Gospel is to them. If it were in their power to rule the hearts of the kings and princes of Europe as they pleased, the execution fires would still be burning today in all those places where they have any power or authority.

<margin>1601</margin>
It was in the year 1601 that *Bartholomew Copin*, a *Waldensian* of the Valley of *Luserna* <note>original: "Lucerna"; one of the Waldensian valleys in the Cottian Alps</note>, was at *Asti* in *Piedmont* with his merchandise at a fair that was to be held the next morning. While at the table for supper that evening with several other merchants, one of them began a discussion about the diversity of religions. He said many things intended to dishonor the *Waldenses* of the Valleys of *Angrogna* <note>original: "Angrongne"</note> and their neighboring areas. *Copin*, hearing him speak of his brethren with less modesty than was appropriate for those who called themselves merchants, and hearing his religion spoken of to the dishonor of God, thought it would be a fault in himself if he did not reply to the blasphemies he heard.

He therefore answered the man who held this discussion in defense of his religion. "And what," said the man who had been corrected by *Copin*, "are you a *Waldensian*?" He answered, "Yes." "And do you not believe that God is in the Host?" <note>the bread used in the Catholic Mass, which the Church teaches becomes the literal body of Christ</note>. "No," said *Copin*. "Shame on you!" <note>original: "Fie vpon you"</note> replied the other, "what a false religion is yours!" *Copin* said, "My religion is as true as it is true that God is God, and as sure as I am that I shall die."

The next morning, *Copin* was summoned before the Bishop of *Asti*, who told him that he had been informed <note>original: "aduertised"</note> of certain scandalous discussions and opinions which he had held only the day before.

### Chapter 4. Of the Waldenses.

...many would gain heart and courage to speak out loudly against the Roman Church <note>original: "Romish Religion"</note>. On the other hand, there was a clause in the treaty made between His Highness <note>referring to the Duke of Savoy</note> and the Waldenses which cleared him of all offense, in these words: *“And if any question shall be moved to them regarding their faith, while they are in Piedmont with other subjects of His Highness, it shall be lawful for them to answer without incurring any punishment, whether financial or physical <note>original: "real or personal"; in legal terms, "real" refers to property or land, and "personal" refers to the individual's body or liberty.</note>.”* 

Now, he had been asked the question, and therefore he should have been free from blame. But the Bishop did not want it to be said that he had imprisoned him unjustly. To that end, so that his death might not be blamed on him and it might not be thought that he had sent him away acquitted <note>original: "absolved"</note>, the Bishop sent his indictment to Pope Clement VIII to understand what course of action he should take in this matter. 

It was never discovered what answer the Bishop received, but shortly afterward the prisoner was found dead in prison. There were signs that he had been strangled, for fear that if he were publicly executed, he might inspire <note>original: "edifie"</note> and strengthen the people by his testimony <note>original: "confession"</note> and steadfastness. After his death, he was condemned to be burned; his body was brought out of prison, his sentence was read in that same place, and he was cast into the fire. This was the last of the Waldenses known to us who has been persecuted to death for his belief.

...not only prohibited, but by a new edict, everyone within the said Marquisate <note>A territory ruled by a marquess; here, Saluzzo.</note> who made profession of any religion other than that of the Church of Rome was banished. # The History Book 2.

Villages that have been peopled by the *Waldenses* since time immemorial <note>original: "time out of minde"</note> were located in the best part of those lands, among which was *Jausiers* <note>original: "Iosiers"; a village in the Ubaye Valley.</note>. These settlements continued for a long time, as the Princes of *Piedmont* did not mind the presence of these people within their provinces. However, the priests made them hated by the world because they were unprofitable to the clergy; they did not live like other people who paid the priests for rites for both the living and the dead. Consequently, when his Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note> persecuted those in his state who had left the laws of the *Roman* <note>original: "Romish"</note> Church, these people were not overlooked, especially when the governors of that valley turned against them.

<margin>1576.</margin> They were, therefore, among those summoned in the year 1576 to either attend Mass or leave his Highness’s country. They found no better way to help themselves than to join with others who, being threatened with the same banishment, appealed to the Protestant Princes. They begged these leaders to intercede for them with their Prince, requesting that he would be pleased not to trouble them for their faith, which they had professed from father to son for many hundreds of years. During that time, their Princes had no subjects who yielded more faithful obedience than they did, being second to none in their duties, submissions, and taxes <note>original: "contributions"</note>, which they had always most willingly paid to their Princes. They were still ready to continue this, yielding obedience to his commands, asking only that they might not be troubled in their consciences.

# Chapter 6. Of the Waldenses.

The Prince *Palatine* of the *Rhine* sent a counselor of state and several other honorable officials as delegates to the Prince of *Piedmont*. Upon arriving at *Turin*, they greeted His Highness in the name of the Prince *Palatine* and delivered their letters of credence <note>diplomatic documents identifying them as official representatives</note>. He requested that His Highness would be pleased to allow them to live peaceably while practicing their religion, without doing any violence to their consciences. He stated that the Prince Palatine would view this favor as if it were done to himself, and that it would place all the Protestant princes of *Germany*—who made the same request through these representatives—under obligation to him. 

He further argued that His Highness would find God to be more favorable and his subjects more faithful if he did not show himself to be inexorable <note>original: "inexorable"; unyielding or impossible to persuade</note>. He suggested that the chaos occurring in the states of all those kings and princes who had attempted to rule over and reclaim the souls of their subjects by force of arms and violence should serve as a warning to all other princes who had not yet reached such extremes. Because those who had avoided such rigorous methods had won the hearts of their people and made them more faithful, and since this same path was within his power, they humbly begged him to imitate the most gracious and gentle princes in this matter.

Among other actions, the Governor of the "New-lands" <note>likely referring to the *Terres Neuves*, areas near Nice and the Alps newly governed by the House of Savoy</note> announced at the end of the following November by the sound of a trumpet that anyone who did not attend Mass within a month's time must leave his Highness's lands and territories. Those who remained faced the penalty of losing both their lives <note>original: "confiscation of body"</note> and their property. 

These poor people of the New-lands could not escape to any safe place without risking their lives. In *Provence*, they were burning those whom the Parliament of *Aix* labeled *Lutherans* <note>In this period, "Lutheran" was often used as a generic label for any Protestant or religious dissenter</note>. In the territories of *Honorat*, Earl of *Tende*, they were handed over to executioners. *Gonzaga* <note>original: "Gonfague"</note>, Duke of *Nevers*, commanding on behalf of the King of France in the Marquisate of *Saluzzo* <note>original: "Saluces"</note>, put them to death. In *Dauphiné*, the Archbishop of *Embrun* <note>original: "Ambrun"</note> threw everyone he could capture into dungeons to rot or left them to perish from cold and hunger in the *Tour Brune* <note>original: "Tower Brun"; the "Brown Tower" in Embrun was used as a prison</note>. Meanwhile, they were being banished from *Piedmont*. No help remained for them except to attempt a journey in the dead of winter, traveling by night over high mountains that were almost...

[...They fled through places] inaccessible, covered with ice and snow, into the Valley of *Freissinières* <note>original: "Fraſſiniere"; now known as Freissinières, a valley in the French Alps</note>, if they possibly could. However, before they could reach the summit, most of the women and children were numbed by the cold. Night overtook them while they were at the top of the hill, and they were forced to lie upon the ice; consequently, a great number of them were found dead the next morning. Those who escaped the danger retreated into the Valley of *Freissinières*. 

After the houses of these poor people had remained empty of inhabitants for some time, no one was willing to seize or take possession of their lands—much less till and farm them. Therefore, their governors permitted the *Waldenses* to continue there and tolerated them professing their faith. The only condition was that they had to leave the borders of the Prince's state to practice their religious exercises. Since then, they have repopulated the valley. 

Thus, you have heard as much as has come to our knowledge regarding their sufferings and how they have been persecuted from time to time, from father to son, just like the rest of the *Waldenses* in *Dauphiné* <note>original: "Dauphine"; an old province in southeastern France</note> and *Piedmont*. However, their specific legal records <note>original: "indictments"</note> have not come into our hands.
