#### *Of the Waldenses dwelling in Calabria, and the persecutions which they have suffered.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' with elaborate floral and foliate scrolling patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>1370</margin>
About the year of our Lord 1370, the Waldenses <note>original: "Waldenſes"; a medieval Christian movement that sought to return to apostolic poverty and simplicity</note> of the Valleys of Pragela <note>now known as Val Pragelas in the Piedmont region of Italy</note> and Dauphiné <note>original: "Dauphine"; a former province in southeastern France</note> grew to such a great number in so small a country that they were forced to send away a certain number of their younger people to seek some other country to inhabit. In their travels, they found in Calabria <note>a region in the "toe" of the Italian peninsula</note> certain waste and uncultivated land that was sparsely populated, but yet very fertile, as they could well judge by the neighboring parts. Therefore, finding the country fit to produce grain <note>original: "corne"; in this period, "corn" referred generally to any cereal crop such as wheat or barley</note>, wine, olive oil, and chestnuts, and that there were hills fit for the breeding and nourishing of cattle, and to furnish them with fuel and timber fit for building, they came to the Lords of those places to negotiate with them regarding their stay in those countries. The said Lords received them lovingly and agreed to their laws and orders to the great advantage of these new inhabitants. They came to an agreement with them concerning their rents, tithes <note>original: "Tenthes"; a tax of one-tenth of annual produce or earnings, typically for the support of the church</note>, tolls, and penalties in case any differences or offenses should occur among them. So, having been assigned certain quarters or parts of the country, most of them returned to inform <note>original: "aduertiſe"</note> their parents of the good fortune that had happened to them in a rich country, likely to abound in all earthly blessings <note>original: "temporall benedictions"</note>. ### Chapter 7: Of the Waldenses.

[The fear that if the priests complained] were a kind of people who disregarded the laws of the **Roman** <note>original: "Romish"</note> Church, they might happen to lose them, deterred their priests from complaining about these people. In every other way, they showed themselves to be honest men who had enriched the entire country—and even the priests themselves. Indeed, the tithes <note>a tax of one-tenth of annual produce paid to the church</note> which the priests received from that great abundance of fruits arising from those lands (out of which, in former times, they received no profit at all) were reason enough for the priests to tolerate other matters. 

They argued that these people had come to inhabit those places from far-off countries where perhaps the people were not so devoted to the ceremonies of the Church of **Rome**. Yet, since they were fundamentally faithful and honest, charitable toward the poor, and God-fearing, the authorities were very willing to ensure they were not harassed by any further investigation into their consciences. 

These reasons were very effective even with those who bore them ill will. The Lords of those places silenced their complaining neighbors, who could by no means draw the Waldenses into any alliance with them. These neighbors saw that the Waldenses' goods, their cattle, and all that they possessed were blessed in a more remarkable manner than other men's. They were a temperate and wise people, not lewd or immoral, not given to dancing, and not frequenters of taverns. No blasphemy ever came out of their mouths. To be brief, living in a country where the inhabitants were prone to all kinds of wickedness, they were like precious stones in a common sewer <note>original: "sinke"; a drain or cesspool</note>. Therefore, they were both envied and admired, but always protected by their Lords, who compared these subjects and vassals with others...

## The History Book 2.

Displeased with what had happened, and being retired to Cosenza <note>original: "Cossence"</note>, where the Syndic <note>A "syndic" was a local magistrate or government official.</note> of San Sisto <note>original: "Saint Xist"</note> appeared before them, they urged him to quickly withdraw himself for fear that the Viceroy should know of his being there and so apprehend him. Among others, he tormented one Stephen Charlin with such violence that his bowels burst from his belly, all to extort from him a confession to this false accusation <note>original: "imposture"</note>: namely, that they sometimes gathered by night to commit acts of lust and damnable incest after the candles were extinguished <note>Accusations of nocturnal orgies and "extinguishing candles" were common tropes used by authorities throughout history to dehumanize and justify the persecution of religious minorities.</note>. But notwithstanding his extreme torture, they could never get from him a confession of such great wickedness.

There was another man named Verminel, who, due to the extreme pain he endured upon the rack, promised to go to Mass. The Inquisitor thought that since the torture of the rack had forced him to abandon his religion, doubling the violence of it might draw a confession of the previously mentioned false accusations from this weak and exhausted person. And so he caused him to be tormented in such a manner that many times he left him eight hours together upon the rack; yet he still could never get from his mouth so horrible a slander <note>original: "calumnie"</note>.

# Chapter 7: The History of the Waldenses.

Another man named Marcon, after being stripped stark naked, was beaten with iron rods, then dragged through the streets and burned with torches <note>original: "fire-brands"</note>. One of his sons was killed with knives; the other was taken to a high tower, where he was offered a crucifix with the promise that if he kissed it, his life would be saved. He answered that he would rather die than commit idolatry. Though he was threatened with being thrown headlong from that tower, he said he would rather have his body broken to pieces here on earth than have his soul cast into hell for denying Christ and His truth. The Inquisitor, enraged by this answer, commanded him to be thrown from the tower, saying, "Let us see whether his God will protect him."

Bernard Conte was condemned to be burned alive. As he was led to the fire, he threw a certain crucifix to the ground which the executioner had fastened to his hands. Because of this, the Inquisitor commanded him to be sent back to prison so that his suffering might be increased <note>original: "aggravated"</note>. He then sent him to Cosenza <note>original: "Cossence"</note>, where he ordered him to be covered in pitch and burned. 

Additionally, this Inquisitor Panza slit the throats of eighty people, just as a butcher does his sheep <note>original: "muttons"</note>. Afterward, he ordered them to be divided into four quarters and commanded that stakes be set up along the highways from Montalto to Castrovillari <note>original: "Chasteau Vilar"</note> for a distance of thirty miles, with a body part fastened to every stake. In a place called Morano <note>original: "Moran"</note>, he had four of the leading men of Guardia Piemontese <note>original: "la Garde"</note> hanged and strangled: namely, James Ferner, Anthony Palomb, Peter Iacio, and John Morglia, who all died with great steadfastness <note>original: "constantly"</note>.

He defended himself for a long time against those who would have arrested him, but in the end, being wounded, he was taken and led to a high tower. There, he was told to confess his sins to a priest who was present before he was cast from the tower. He refused to do so, saying that he had already confessed himself to God. The Viceroy gave him a kick to the head with his foot, saying, "Is this dog still alive? Cast him out to the hogs."

Sixty women of San Sisto <note>original: "Saint Xist"</note> were brought to the rack <term>a torture device that stretches the limbs</term> and treated with such violence that the cords cut deep into their arms and legs. Because of this, a great quantity of worms <note>Likely maggots resulting from infected wounds.</note> were generated in their wounds, which fed upon them while they were still alive. They did not know how to remedy this until someone, having compassion for them, secretly gave them lime <note>Quicklime or calcium oxide, used here as a harsh means to kill the parasites.</note>, which caused the worms to fall from them. Almost all of them died miserably in prison. Nine of the leading and most beautiful <note>original: "hansomest"</note> women among them were lost, and it was never known what became of them after they were delivered to the Fathers of the Inquisition.

This Inquisitor retired to Sant'Agata <note>original: "Saint Agathe"</note>, where he delivered a great number of people to the secular power <term>the civil authorities, who carried out the death sentences issued by the Church</term>. If any man offered to speak on their behalf, the Inquisitor had him put to the rack as a supporter of heretics; as a result, in the end, there was no one who dared to open his mouth in their defense.

But the Pope might have wished himself elsewhere, or that **Paschal** had been silent, or the people deaf. For Paschal spoke many things against the Pope based on the Word of God, which caused the Pope a great deal of distress. Thus this good man died, calling upon God with such fervent zeal that he deeply moved the bystanders and caused the Pope and his Cardinals to gnash their teeth in anger. Thus you have seen the end of the **Waldenses** of **Calabria**, who were completely exterminated. For if any of the fugitives have returned, it is only on the condition that they live according to the laws of the Church of **Rome**.

## CHAP. VIII.

### *Of the Waldensians inhabiting Provence, and the persecutions which they have suffered.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring swirling vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>

The **Waldensians** <note>original: "Waldenses"</note> living in **Provence**, specifically in the areas of **Cabrières**, **Mérindol**, **Lacoste**, and other nearby places, have been considered the original descendants of the Waldensians living in **Dauphiné** and **Piedmont**. This is very apparent from families sharing the same names, as well as those among them who can prove their ancestry. It was for this reason that those from **Calabria** settled in **Provence**—to relieve their home valleys of the great multitudes of people who lived there. Although the country was a wilderness when they first arrived in **Provence**, within a few years they made it fertile and fit (by the blessing of God) to yield grain <note>original: "Corne"; in this period, "corn" referred to any cereal crop like wheat or barley</note>, wine, olive oil, chestnuts, and other fruits in great abundance.

For instance, there was the commission of the Archdeacon of **Cremona**, **Albert de Capitaneis**, and of the Franciscan friar <note>original: "Monke frier Minor"</note> **Francis Borelli**. # The Letter of Oecolampadius, written to the Waldensians of Provence, who thought they could serve God while prostituting their bodies before Popish Idols. Written in the year 1530.

## *Oecolampadius wishes the grace of God the Father, through His Son Jesus Christ and His Holy Spirit, to his well-beloved brothers in Christ, who are called Waldensians.*

A Hebrew term used in the Bible to describe the personification of worthlessness or wickedness, often identified with Satan.</note>. And if you communicate

I know that your weakness is great, but it is necessary that those who have learned that they are bought by the blood of Christ should be more courageous and always fear Him who can cast both body and soul into hell. And will it be enough for us to care for this life only? Shall this life be more precious to us than the life of Christ? Are we content to have tasted the delights of this world only? Crowns of glory are prepared for us; shall we turn back again? 

Who will believe that our faith has been true if it fails and faints in the heat of persecution? Let us therefore pray to God to increase our faith. For certainly, it would be better for us to die than to be overcome by temptations. And therefore, brothers, we exhort you to examine the depths of this matter <note>original: "dive into the bottom of this business"</note>.

The inhabitants of *Merindol* were summoned, in the persons of five or six of their leaders, at the urgent request of the King’s Attorney in the Parliament of *Aix*, and through the solicitation of the Archbishop of *Arles*, the Bishop of *Aix*, and other ecclesiastical officials. A sentence was issued against them—the most excessive, cruel, and inhumane sentence that was ever given in any Parliament. In every respect, it was like the edict of King Ahasuerus <note>original: "Assuerus"</note>, granted at the request of Haman <note>original: "Aman"</note> against the people of God, as it is written in the Book of Esther.

For in addition to the fact that the men and women who were summoned for contempt of court <term>original: "contumacy"; the stubborn refusal to obey a legal summons</term> were condemned by the said sentence to be burned alive and their children and families outlawed, it was also decreed that the town of *Merindol* should be made completely uninhabitable. The decree ordered the woods to be cut down for two hundred paces all around the town, and all of this was decided without any hearing or permission granted for anyone to speak a single word in their defense.

When the King was informed of the severity <note>original: "rigour"</note> of this edict, he sent Lord *du Langeai* to *Provence* to inform him of the customs and beliefs of these *Waldensians*. Understanding that many accusations had been made against these people of which they were not guilty, King *Francis I* sent letters of grace and favor, not only on behalf of those who had been charged with contempt of court, but for all the rest of the region of *Provence*. He specifically commanded the Parliament from that time forward not to proceed as harshly in this case as they had done in the past. These letters were suppressed <note>Local authorities often withheld royal pardons to continue their own agendas.</note>. Those who were personally summoned requested that it might be lawful for them to respond through a legal representative <term>original: "Proctor"</term>.

*Francis Chai* and *William Armand* appeared on behalf of everyone else, requesting in their names that it might be shown to them where they had erred, and that this be done through the Word of God. They stated they were ready to renounce <term>original: "abjure"; to formally reject a belief or claim</term> all heresy if they were once shown they had fallen into any. For this reason, they delivered a written confession of their faith to the authorities, so that if anything was found worthy of criticism <term>original: "reprehension"</term> according to the Holy Scriptures, they might be instructed on what they needed to recant. Alternatively, if nothing was found to criticize, they asked that they might no longer be harassed by such numerous and severe <note>original: "grievous"</note> persecutions. They feared that while the authorities thought they were only making war against men, it might turn out that they were fighting against God, His truth, and those who upheld it.

All their petitions served no purpose other than to provoke the authorities even further. Because the judges were convinced they were heretics, they refused to take the trouble to learn and examine the truth; instead, they issued all their rulings in favor of the priests who accused them. Consequently, when the Cardinal of *Tournon* had obtained letters from the King—at a high cost—authorizing the execution of the previously mentioned decree, it was carried out, despite the pardon and revocation that had been obtained earlier.

King **Francis** <note>King Francis I of France</note>, being informed of the cruelties executed in pursuit of the said arrest <note>meaning the legal decree or warrant for the suppression of the Waldenses</note>, was much displeased by it. To such an extent that, at the point of death and feeling the remorse of conscience—principally because it had all happened under his name and authority—he was sorry that he could not punish those who had shed so much innocent blood before his own death. He charged his son **Henry** <note>the future King Henry II of France</note> to take revenge on them. As for the rest who escaped this massacre, some withdrew to **Geneva**, others to **Switzerland**, and others to **Germany**. Some remained nearby, tilling their land in secret. Little by little, they returned home to their old dwellings, which they rebuilt and repaired whenever they could by the benefit of the aforementioned Edicts. These survivors were afterwards the seed of many fine churches which are today gathered together, flourishing in all piety and zeal, like other churches in the Kingdom of **France**.

### CHAPTER IX.

#### Concerning the Waldenses who fled into Bohemia, and those persecutions which they suffered, that have come to our knowledge.

<margin>Albertus de Capitaneis, *Book on the Origin of the Waldenses*.</margin>
<margin>Thuanus, *History of His Own Time*, page 457.</margin>
<margin>Peter Waldo, their leader <note>original Latin: *antesignanus*; literally "standard-bearer"</note>, having left his native country, came into Belgium and into what they today call Picardy. Having gained many followers there, he traveled into Germany and stayed for a long time among the Vandalic <note>original Latin: *Vandalicas*; likely referring to the Hanseatic or Baltic coastal cities of northern Germany</note> cities, and finally settled in Bohemia.</margin>

Many have written that Waldo, upon his departure from Lyon <note>original: "Lion"</note>, came into Dauphiné. From there—having established and organized several churches and laid their foundations, which have been miraculously preserved until this present time—he went into Languedoc. There he left excellent pastors who organized and instructed those churches, which later cost the Pope and his clergy so much effort to destroy. From there he went into Picardy; being driven out <note>original: "chased"</note> from that region, he traveled into Germany, and from Germany he retired to Bohemia, where (according to the opinion of some) he ended his days.

The Waldenses living in Dauphiné, Piedmont, and Provence have maintained communion and communication <note>original: "intelligence"</note> with their brothers who retired to Bohemia. As proof of this, we have the account of Daniel de Valence and Jean de Molin, pastors in Bohemia. These men caused much harm to the churches of that country by revealing to their adversaries those flocks or congregations which were previously hidden and unknown because of the great and grievous persecutions occurring at that time.

# Chapter 9: Of the Waldenses

<margin>Pious followers and seekers of the restored Gospel, being misled by false signs and the accusations of adversaries, take us for Waldenses. <note>original Latin: *evangelicæ instauratæ cultores & sectatores pÿ seducti & indicationibus falsis & criminationib. aduersariorum, pro Valdensib. nos habeant.*</note></margin>

They desired to be distinguished from the Waldenses so that if it were observed that the **Waldenses** had done much to establish the truth in their own times, it might likewise be known that the **Hussites** <note>Followers of the reformer John Hus</note> have done no less in theirs.

After conferring with him, Hus made a profession of their doctrine, and they themselves do not deny it. For they say that **Wycliffe** <note>original: "Wicklif"</note> was helped to shake off the yoke of the Pope by the example of the **Waldenses**, and that **Wycliffe** was the instrument which God used for the instruction of **John Hus**, who taught in **Bohemia**. Therefore, they have thought themselves deeply indebted to the Churches of the **Waldenses**, because they say that whatever good existed in those churches was passed down to their own; thus, the Waldenses were, in a sense, their beginning.

# Chapter 10.
## Concerning the Waldenses living in Austria, and the persecutions which they suffered.

<margin>See the Chronicle of Hirsauge <note>Hirsauge was a famous Benedictine abbey in Germany known for its historical records</note>.</margin>
The number of Waldenses who lived in Austria was very great. They were severely persecuted there, as is evident from the Chronicle of Hirsauge, which notes that around the year 1400, a great number of them were burned in the city of Krems <note>original: "Creme"</note>, which is in the Duchy of Austria. But even more than that, what deeply troubled the persecutors was the testimony of one man who was executed in Vienna, the capital city of Austria. At his execution, he stated that there were more than eighty thousand <note>original: "fourescore thousand"</note> people in that country who shared the same faith he professed.

And that was, that they yielded too much to their weaknesses <note>original: "infirmities"</note>; since having once known the truth, they nevertheless frequented Catholic <note>original: "Papisticall"</note> churches, being present at those idolatrous ceremonies which they condemned, basely profaning and polluting themselves. A certain inquisitor named *Conrad of Marburg* was appointed by the Pope as the Superintendent of the Inquisition. He carried out this duty with extreme cruelty against all kinds of people, showing no respect even for the priests themselves, whose bodies and goods he confiscated. He tested men with a hot iron, saying that those who could hold a red-hot iron in their hands without being burned were good Christians; but on the contrary, if they felt the fire, he handed them over to the secular power <note>The "secular power" refers to the civil authorities who carried out the death penalty, usually by burning, as the church itself officially did not shed blood.</note>. During these times, the *Waldenses* had many schools in the Diocese of *Trier* <note>original: "Treves"</note>, where they had their children instructed in their beliefs. Despite all the inquisitions and persecutions carried out against their followers <note>original: "flockes"</note>, they still ventured to preach, calling their assemblies together by the ringing of a bell. They maintained "in a public position" <note>original: "in publica statione"</note> (according to the historian) and publicly declared that the Pope was a heretic; his prelates were practitioners of simony <note>original: "Simonaicall"; simony is the buying or selling of church offices or privileges.</note> and deceivers of the people. They claimed that the truth was not preached anywhere except among them. They further stated that if they had not come to teach, God—before He would have allowed their faith to perish—would have raised up others, even the stones themselves, to enlighten His Church through the preaching of the Word. "Until these times," they said, "our preachers have buried the truth and preached lies. We, on the contrary, preach the truth and bury falsehood and lies. Finally, we do not offer a fake <note>original: "feined"</note> remission of sins invented by the Pope, but one offered by God alone, according to our calling."

About the year 1330, they were strangely tormented in many parts of Germany by a certain Jacobin monk <note>Jacobin was a common term for monks of the Dominican Order.</note> and Inquisitor named Echard. After many cruelties were executed upon them, and as he pressured the Waldenses to reveal the reasons why they had separated from the Church of Rome, he was overcome by his own conscience. Acknowledging that the defects and corruptions they alleged to be in the Church of Rome were true, and being unable to disprove the points of their belief by the Word of God, he gave glory to God. Confessing that the truth had overcome him, he became a member of that Church which he had for a long time persecuted to the death. When the other Inquisitors were informed of this change, they were much displeased; they immediately sent so many people after him that he was eventually captured and brought to Heidelberg. There he was burned, maintaining to the end that it was an injustice and a wrong to condemn so many good men to death for the righteousness of Christ against the inventions of the Antichrist.

It is true that the bones of **Wycliffe** <note>original: "wicklif"</note> were dug up more than thirty years after his death and condemned to be burned, along with whatever books his adversaries could find. However, he had already enlightened such a large number of people that it was beyond his enemies' power to completely deprive the Church of them. For the more they tried to prevent the reading and knowledge of these books through horrible threats and even death itself, the more the passions of many were sharpened to read them with even greater intensity.

But having afterwards forsaken them, he became a monk and a very violent persecutor, in such a way that he caused many to be burned in *Flanders*. Now, his own friends, having realized that he greatly abused the power and authority of his office—laying to their charge many things of which they were innocent, and executing his authority against many who were altogether ignorant of the belief of the *Waldensians*—he was not only deprived of the office of an Inquisitor but cast into prison. Being convicted of various crimes, he was condemned to perpetual prison.

## CHAPTER 19.

->The Conclusion of the History of the<-
->*Waldensians*<-

Based on what is contained in this first and second book, it appears that the Christians called *Waldensians* have opposed the abuses of the Church of *Rome*. For over four hundred and fifty years, they have been persecuted—not by the "sword of the Word of God" <note>Meaning they were not defeated by scriptural argument</note>, but by all kinds of violence and cruelty, in addition to many slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> and false accusations. Nevertheless, the Lord has preserved their remnant in such a way that, despite the rage of Satan, they have remained invincible against the Antichrist. They have engaged him in spiritual combat, destroying him by the "breath of the Spirit of God" <note>A reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:8</note>. 

They cried with a loud voice, not only throughout all of *Europe* but in many other parts of the earth, that it was time to "depart out of Babylon" <note>A common Reformation-era metaphor for leaving the Roman Catholic Church, referencing Revelation 18:4</note>, lest we share in her plagues. And what is most remarkable in this great work is that the doctrine they believed and preached has also been miraculously preserved among them in the midst of all the grievous and continual persecutions they suffered for the sake of righteousness. It is also worthy of admiration that their enemies <note>original: "adversaries"</note> have kept a record <note>original: "register"</note> of the evils they unjustly forced them to suffer. Their enemies gloried in shedding that blood which cries out for vengeance; they exiled the Church into the wilderness for a limited time and made it known through their own histories that the "Dragon" <note>A symbolic reference to Satan or a persecuting power, from Revelation 12</note> has done only what was permitted to him—that is, to make war against the Saints. But having been delivered from their great tribulation, and their robes washed white in the blood of the Lamb <note>A reference to Revelation 7:14</note>, they have been led to living fountains of water, and God has wiped all tears from their eyes.

<header>The History Book 1.</header>
<sig>A 2</sig>

The doctrines that they maintained against the Church of Rome were these:

1. That the Roman Church is not the holy Church and Spouse of Christ, but a Church nourished with the doctrine of devils. It is that "Babylon" which Saint John described in the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalypse"</note>, the mother of fornications and abominations, covered with the blood of Saints.
2. That the Mass was not instituted by Christ, nor by his Apostles, but that it is the invention of men.
3. That the prayers of the living do not benefit the dead.
4. That Purgatory, maintained by the Church of Rome, was a human invention created to satisfy the greed <note>original: "covetousness"</note> of the priests.
5. That Saints are not to be prayed to.
6. That Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine used in the Mass become the actual body and blood of Christ.</term> is the invention of men and an erroneous doctrine, and that the adoration of the Bread is manifest idolatry.

Because of this, they believed they had to forsake the Church of Rome, where the opposite was affirmed and taught. They held that a person must not be present at Masses where idolatry is practiced, nor can they attain salvation by any other means than through Jesus Christ. Furthermore, one must not transfer the honor due to the Creator to created things, nor say of the Bread that it is God and adore it as being God without incurring eternal damnation—for idolaters shall not inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.

For all these beliefs, they have been hated and persecuted even unto death.

### Chapter 2: Concerning the Albigenses

...religion some weakness if there were not any pastor who would take it upon himself to defend it. Therefore, the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingenses"</note> concluded to inform the bishops that their pastors—or any one of them representing the rest—were ready to maintain their beliefs by the word of God, provided that the conference was well-ordered and moderated. Specifically, they required that there be moderators—men of authority from both sides—who had the power to prevent any rioting or civil disorder. It was also required that the debate be held in a place with free access, and that the location be secured for all persons who might assist or be present at the said conference. Furthermore, it was required that a specific topic or subject be chosen by mutual agreement and not be abandoned until it was decided; and that anyone who could not defend their position by the word of God would be considered and held to be defeated.

<margin>This debate <note>original: "disputation"</note> was the most famous ever held between the Albigenses and the bishops and priests.</margin>
The bishops and monks all agreed to these conditions. The location was **Montreal**, near **Carcassonne**, in the year 1206. The arbitrators agreed upon by both parties were B. de Villeneuve and B. Auxerre for the bishops, and for the Albigenses, R. de Bot and Anthony Riviere.

<margin>Chaffagnon mentions this in his first book of the *History of the Albigenses*, page 72.</margin>
<margin>Also Jacques de Riberia in his collection on the city of Toulouse.</margin>
**Arnold Hot** was the pastor representing the Albigenses, accompanied by those who were considered fit for such an event. He was the first to arrive at the appointed place and time. Afterward came Bishop Eusus and the monk **Dominic** <note>original: "Dominique"—this refers to Saint Dominic, the founder of the Dominican Order</note>, a Spaniard, with two of the Pope’s legates: **Peter Chateauneuf** <note>original: "Peter Chastel"—referring to Peter of Castelnau</note> and **Raoul de Just**, Abbot of Candets, and P. Bertrand, Prior of Hauterive, as well as the Prior of Palats and various other priests and monks.

# The History: Book 1

<margin>This debate <note>original: "disputation"</note> was sent to me from the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingéses"</note> by Mr. Rafin, Pastor of the Church of Realmont, from old manuscripts.</margin>

The theses—or general questions—proposed by **Arnold** were as follows:

1. That the Mass, along with the doctrine of Transubstantiation <note>the belief that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ</note>, was the invention of men and not the ordinance of Christ or his Apostles.

2. That the Roman Church is not the Spouse of Christ, but rather the "church of tumult and trouble," made drunk with the blood of Martyrs.

3. That the administration <note>original: "policie"</note> of the Church of Rome is neither good nor holy, nor was it established by Jesus Christ.

**Arnold** sent these propositions to the Bishop, who requested a fifteen-day delay <note>original: "respit"</note> to respond, which was granted to him. On the appointed day, the Bishop did not fail to appear, bringing a long and extensive written response. **Arnold Hot** asked to be heard in person, saying that he would respond to everything contained in that writing. He asked his audience not to find it troublesome if he took a long time to answer such a long discourse. It was granted that he should be heard with attention and patience, and without interruption.

He spoke at various times over the course of four days, with such impressive skill <note>original: "admiration"</note> and readiness that all the bishops, abbots, monks, and priests had reason to wish they had been somewhere else. For he organized his answer according to the points set down in the Bishop's writing with such order and clarity that he made everyone present understand that although the Bishop had written much, he had nevertheless concluded nothing that might truly benefit the Church of Rome or counter Arnold’s propositions.

Afterward, **Arnold** made a request that, since the bishops and he had agreed at the beginning of their conference that they were bound to prove whatever they affirmed—

### Chapter 2: Of the Albigenses

...affirmed by the word of God alone, it might be required of the Bishops and Priests to prove that their Mass, exactly as they sing it part by part, was instituted by the Son of God and sung in the same manner by his Apostles—beginning from the entrance unto the "Go, it is the dismissal" <note>original: *Ite Missa est*, the formal conclusion of the Roman Rite Mass</note>, as they call it. But the Bishops were not able to prove that the Mass, or any part of it, was ordained in such a ceremony by either Jesus Christ or his Apostles. Because of this, the Bishops were much discontented and ashamed. 

For **Arnold** had brought them to the only Canon <note>the fixed portion of the Mass containing the prayer of consecration</note> which they claimed to be the best part of their Mass; regarding this point, he proved that the Holy Supper of our Lord was not the Mass. For if the Mass were the Holy Supper instituted by our Savior, all that was in the Supper of the Lord would remain after the Consecration—that is to say, Bread. But in the Mass there is no bread, for by Transubstantiation <note>the belief that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the actual body and blood of Christ</note> the bread has vanished away. Therefore, the Mass (he said), being without bread, is not the Holy Supper of the Lord, for in that Supper there is bread.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Jesus Christ broke bread, | The Priest breaks the body, |
| St. Paul broke the bread, | not the bread. |

Therefore, the Priest does not do what Christ Jesus and St. Paul did.

Upon these oppositions <note>original: "Antitheses"</note> which **Arnold** made regarding the Supper of the Lord and the Mass—to prove that the Mass did not come from Christ nor his Apostles—the monks, bishops, legates, and priests withdrew <note>original: "retired them-selues"</note>. They were unwilling to hear any more, fearing that he might leave such an impression on those present that it would shake their belief concerning the Mass.

# The History Book 1

<margin>The Monk of the Valley *Cernay* <note>original: *Seruay*; Pierre de Vaux-de-Cernay, a Catholic chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade</note>, in his *History of the Albigenses*, chapter 5.</margin>

The Monk of the Valley *Cernay* <note>original: *Seruay*</note> attempts to cast doubt on this event. He claims that when the heretical judges realized they were outnumbered and saw the weakness of their cause and the poor quality of their arguments, they refused (he says) to pass any judgment. He also claims they would not hand over their written arguments to their opponents for fear that these writings would be exposed and used against the heretics. 

But how could two of the Pope’s legates <note>representatives of the Pope with his full authority</note>, the bishops, abbots, monks, and priests, put themselves in a position where they could be so overwhelmed by numbers? This same monk says in the same passage that the primary leaders of the "heretics" came to the Catholics at the Castle of **Montreal** to debate with them. Since the Catholics held the castle at that time, there was no reason for them to doubt their safety or fear any such violence. 

Furthermore, why would the bishops ask the moderators to judge the debate when they believe no other judgment is needed except the Pope’s, who (according to them) cannot err? Again, how could the monk know that the **Albigenses** <note>original: *Albingenses*; a dualist Christian sect in Southern France</note> were defeated if no judgment or sentence was ever declared against them? 

Around the same time, many other debates took place, such as at *Sérignan* and *Pamiers* <note>original: *Pannies*</note>, but these were only intended to stall the **Albigenses** and keep them from making further progress. For while the Bishop of **Toulouse** and the Bishop of **Ozon** <note>original: *Onezimonde*</note> debated at **Pamiers**, and the Pope’s two legates debated with **Arnold** at **Montreal**, **B. of Villeneuve**—the arbitrator and moderator for the bishops—announced that nothing could be decided or agreed upon. This was because of the arrival of the armies that were coming to fight under the sign of the Cross <note>the Crusaders of the Albigensian Crusade</note>. This was the clever strategy of the

### CHAPTER III.

*The end of the religious debates, which the Pope and his legates did not continue for long. The Pope’s role in announcing the expedition against the Albigenses <note>original: Albingenfes</note>. Earl Raymond humbles himself before the Pope’s legate; he is whipped by the legate and deprived of his Earldom of Venaissin <note>original: Venessin</note> by the Pope. <margin>So called because everyone who undertakes the journey wears the badge of the Cross on his cassock or surcoat <note>original: Coate-armour</note>.</margin>
Now when Pope Innocent had prepared his Armies of the Cross and had dispersed them here and there throughout the countries of the Albigenses, there were no longer any debates, except those conducted with fire and wood <note>original: "Fire and Faggots"; a reference to execution by burning at the stake</note>. The chief debaters were now the executioners and the Inquisitor monks—the Harpies <note>mythological ravenous birds; here referring to the predatory nature of the Inquisitors</note> or birds of prey whom the Pope used for the total destruction of the Albigenses.

> "We ordain," he said, "that all Archbishops and Bishops are to denounce Earl Raymond throughout all their dioceses as accursed and excommunicated, for being the murderer of a good servant of God. This is to be done with the ringing of the bell and the extinguishing of candles every Sunday and on festival days. We promise, moreover, to all those who shall take up arms to avenge the said murder the forgiveness of their sins, seeing that these pestilent 'Long Slops' <note>original: "Long Slops"; a derogatory reference to the loose-fitting garments worn by the Albigenses</note> seek nothing else but to take away our lives. And since, according to the law of the holy canons, faith is not to be kept with him who does not keep his faith with God, we would have all understand that every man who is bound to the said Earl by oath of fidelity, society, alliance, or otherwise, is absolved from any such bonds by the Apostolic authority. It shall be lawful for every Catholic man not only to pursue the person of the said Earl, but also to hold and possess his land, etc."

### Chapter 3: Of the Albigenses

...to abolish the heretical depravity and these sectarians, and to do so more severely than against the Saracens <note>original: "Sarafines"; a medieval term for Muslims</note>, attacking them with a strong hand and a stretched-out arm as being worse than they, etc. Driving them out of the field of the Lord, taking from them their lands and livelihoods, in which (once the heretics are banished) let Catholic inhabitants be substituted in their place.

The Pope wrote to all Christian princes to prepare themselves to obtain the same pardon for fighting against the Albigenses <note>original: Albingenses</note> as they would have received if they had traveled across the seas against the Turks. Specifically, the author of the *Treasure of Histories* says that the Pope entreated King Philip and various barons to undertake this enterprise with him against the heretics to gain their pardons. The King answered that he was to be excused because of his wars with Emperor Otto <note>original: Otho</note> and King John of England. Of the barons (he says), there were many who yielded to the enterprise for the sake of the pardon.

Earl Raymond <note>original: Remond</note>, being informed of what was plotted against him in Europe at the urging of the Pope, sent word to him, humbly beseeching him not to condemn him before he had heard him speak. He assured the Pope that he was in no way guilty of the death of Friar Peter of Castelnau <note>original: Peter de Castrauneuf</note>, and that it was clearly proven that the murderer had fled to Beaucaire. He complained of the malice of his enemies, who had provided false information against him concerning the murder. But all was in vain, for before his excuses reached Rome, the troops of the Crusaders <note>original: Croises</note>—that is, those who bear the badge of the cross upon their armor—had come to pour down their vengeance upon him and his lands; these were led by the Duke of Burgundy.

...the Earl of Nevers <note>original: "Enneuers"</note>, the Earl of Saint-Pol, the Earl of Auxerre, the Earl of Geneva, the Earl of Poitiers, the Earl of Forez <note>original: "Forests"</note>, and the Earl Simon de Montfort. Also the Lord of Bar, Guichard of Beaujeu <note>original: "Ginchard of Beauieu"</note>, and Gauthier of Joigny <note>original: "Ganchier of Ioigui"</note>. There were also ecclesiastical persons who had levied in their dioceses a number of pilgrims <term>pilgrims: here referring to Crusaders who took a vow to fight for the church</term> and wandering people; these were the Archbishop of Sens, the Archbishop of Rouen <note>original: "Rouan"</note>, the Bishop of Clermont <note>original: "Clermond"</note>, the Bishop of Nevers, the Bishop of Lisieux, the Bishop of Bayeux, and the Bishop of Chartres, along with various others. Every bishop traveled with the pilgrims of his jurisdiction, to whom the Pope promised paradise in Heaven, but gave them not one penny upon earth; he only let them know that in such a war there were more blows than pardons.

This levy of pilgrims or wandering persons was in the year 1209. There was now a necessity either to oppose violence with violence, or to come to submissions. The latter was thought the easier path, yet it was still dangerous. For to yield himself to the discretion of his enemies was to bring himself into the danger of his own ruin. Count Raymond <note>original: "Remond"</note> therefore came to Valence before the Pope's Legate, named Milo.

Having entered the snare <note>original: "toile"; literally a hunting net or trap</note>, he began to excuse himself, saying: That it seemed strange to him that so great a number of men should come in arms against him, when he used no other arms to defend himself than his own innocence; that he was much wronged by those who persuaded the people that he was guilty of the death of the monk, Friar Peter of Castelnau <note>original: "Casteauneuf"</note>; and that before they had thus moved heaven and earth, as it were, they should have inquired into the truth of the facts and not condemned anyone before he was heard.

# Chapter 3. Of the Albigenses.

He stated that he had many witnesses to the death of the monk who was killed at Saint-Gilles by a certain gentleman whom the monk had been pursuing; this man then immediately retreated to his friends at Beaucaire. He claimed that this murder was very displeasing to him, and therefore he had done everything in his power to apprehend and punish the killer, but the man had escaped his hands. He argued that even if it were true—as they charged—that he had stained <note>original: "embrewed"</note> his hands with that blood, legal proceedings should have been taken against him personally, rather than venting <note>original: "wrecked"</note> their anger upon his subjects, who were innocent in this matter. 

And therefore, he said to the Legate, since he had come to surrender himself into their hands out of trust and confidence, armed only with the testimony of a clear conscience, what need was there to employ these "pilgrims" or wandering people <term>pilgrims: here referring to the Crusader army who took a vow to fight</term> against a man who was already in their power? He noted that it had been promised to him that once his honesty was known, those who were armed to fight against him would instead defend him. Therefore, he humbly requested the Legate to send a countermand <term>countermand: an order revoking a previous one</term> to his soldiers before they advanced any further into his lands and territories, promising to justify himself against all charges in a way that would satisfy both the Pope and the Church. He offered his own person as a sufficient pledge for the fulfillment of these promises.

The Legate replied that Count <note>original: "Earle"</note> Raymond had done well to present himself and declare his innocence, of which the Legate would inform His Holiness and act as a mediator <note>original: "Interceſſor"</note> for him; however, the matter was of such great importance that...

He <note>Referring to the Legate, Milo</note> dared not rely only upon his own knowledge, much less send back his Soldiers of the Cross <term>Soldiers of the Cross: the Crusader army, whose members wore a cross on their clothing</term> that had cost so much labor to gather together, unless the Count would give such assurances of his words as might take away from the Pope and the Church any appearance or shadow of a doubt that he might hereafter deal falsely with those who put their trust in him. Count Raymond knew well the error he had committed by putting himself in such a vulnerable position <note>original: "under the hatches"</note>, but it was too late to change his mind because the advice the Legate gave him was effectively a command. He knew himself to be a prisoner and that he must now receive the law from the man into whose power he had unwisely cast himself; therefore, he made a show of great willingness to obey whatever was prescribed by the Legate, acknowledging that both his person and his possessions were at the service of his Holy Father. He only begged the Legate that his subjects might receive no more damage from the soldiers. The Legate promised all the favor that he desired in this regard and immediately sent Master Theodisius, Canon of Genoa <note>original: "Gennes"</note>, to the Comtat Venaissin to place a garrison in the castles and places of importance in the said county, and to give orders to all the consuls <term>consuls: city officials or magistrates</term> of the cities there to report immediately to the Legate. ### Chapter 3: Of the Albigenses

[...desired from the] Pope, as proof of his fidelity to the Church, of which they were to be informed. This was so that from that time forward, they should acknowledge themselves to be the lawful subjects of His Holiness, in case the aforementioned Count Raymond <note>original: "Earle Remond"; Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse</note> should do anything against the oath of obedience which he had made to the Pope and to the Church of Rome. In such a case—as they were already at that time discharged of all oaths of loyalty given in times past to the Count—his lands were confiscated to the Pope. 

The Consuls <term>Consuls: elected municipal magistrates who governed cities in Southern France</term>, being much astonished to see their Lord thus stripped of all his lands and possessions, could not refuse in his own presence to do whatever the Legate required of them. But what afflicted them most was that they saw Count Raymond conducted to Saint-Gilles <note>original: "St. Giles"; a town and abbey in the Gard department of France</note>, where he was reconciled to the Pope and to the Church with the following ceremonies:

First, the Legate commanded the said Count Raymond to strip himself stark naked outside the Church of Saint-Gilles, having only a tight-fitting pair of linen breeches to cover his nakedness; the rest was all bare: head, feet, and shoulders. Then he put a stole <term>stole: a liturgical vestment consisting of a band of colored cloth worn around the neck</term> (which Priests wear about their necks) upon the Count's neck, and leading him by the stole, he made him go nine times around the grave of the deceased Friar Peter of Castelnau <note>original: "Peter de Chateauneuf"; a papal legate whose assassination in 1208 was the immediate catalyst for the Albigensian Crusade</note>, who had been buried in the said church, scourging him with rods which the Legate had in his hand as long as he went around the said sepulcher.

Since the murder was committed within his territories and he had made no pursuit of the murderer, this crime was deservedly blamed on him. The Legate made him swear upon the *Body of the Lord* <note>original Latin: *Corpus Domini*; the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> (as they call it) and certain other relics which were brought there for that purpose, that he would be obedient in all things to the Pope and the Church of Rome for the rest of his life. He also swore that he would wage perpetual, deadly, and irreconcilable war against the Albigenses until they were either utterly exterminated or brought under the obedience of the Church of Rome. 

After he had taken this solemn oath by force, the Legate—partly to honor him and partly to bind him to his word—appointed him Captain and Leader of the "Soldiers of the Cross" <note>the Crusaders</note> for the siege of Béziers. The Legate did this so that the Albigenses would lose all hope of ever being protected by the Count, who, having renounced their religion, now had both the authority and the duty to persecute them.

### CHAPTER 4

*The perplexity Count Raymond was in after his reconciliation: The siege of Béziers: The intercession of the Count of Béziers for his city: The intercession of the Bishop avails nothing: The taking of Béziers, how it happened, and with what cruelty.*

Count *Raymond* was very troubled by the command given to him to lead the army of the "Soldiers of the Cross" <note>original: "Souldiers of the Crosse"; referring to the Crusaders</note> to *Béziers*. For to behave as an enemy against the *Albigenses* was to go against his conscience and to fight against those whose side he had taken until then as a principal protector and leader. This was to bind himself into the perpetual servitude of the Pope and his Legates. On the other hand, if he were to flee and desert the army, this would provide them with new reasons to persecute him. In such a case, they might justly pursue him as a treacherous, relapsed, and perjured <term>perjured: someone who has broken a holy oath</term> person; if he were captured, he would be in danger of losing his life, property, and friends all at once. 

And yet, by doing what the command the Legate laid upon him required, he would have to be an instrument in the fall of *Béziers* and the total destruction of the subjects of his nephew, the Count of *Béziers*, and even the destruction of his nephew himself. In this extremity and anguish of spirit, he chose to stay with the army for a few days, and afterward took his leave of the Legate and went to *Rome* to humble himself before the Pope—a request which could not be denied him. # The History: Book 1

...righteousness, or with the danger of an eternal death, profess a religion which does annihilate the merit of Christ and buries his righteousness; and that therefore they would make a covenant for themselves as best they could, and promise nothing contrary to the duty of true Christians.

This being understood, the Roman Catholics sent their Bishop to the Legate, humbly to entreat him that he would not include in this punishment of the *Albigenses* those who were always obedient to the Church of *Rome*. The Bishop testified that he had certain knowledge of their loyalty, and was likewise assured that the rest were not altogether past hope of repentance, but that they might be won by gentle means—the approach best befitting the Church, which took no pleasure in the shedding <note>original: "effusion"</note> of blood.

The Legate at this fell into an extreme rage <note>original: "choller"</note> and passion, swearing and protesting with horrible threats that if everyone in the city did not acknowledge their fault and submit themselves to the Church of *Rome*, they should all drink from the same cup <note>original: "taste of one cup"; a metaphor for sharing the same fate</note>. Without respect for Catholic status, sex, or age, they would all be exposed to fire and sword. Immediately, he commanded that the city should be summoned to surrender itself to his discretion; when they refused to do so, he caused all his engines of war to fire and commanded an assault and a general scaling of the walls <term>escalado</term> <note>a military tactic of attacking a fortified place by using ladders to scale the walls</note> to be made.

<margin>The *Treasure of Histories* regarding the taking of Béziers. Paul Æmilius, page 317.</margin>
Now it was impossible for those within to resist such great violence; thus assaulted by over a hundred thousand Crusaders <note>original: "Pelerins" (pilgrims); the soldiers of the Albigensian Crusade were granted the same indulgences as those going to the Holy Land and were often referred to as pilgrims</note>, in the end (says the compiler of the *Treasure of Histories*), those within were defeated. The enemy, having entered, slaughtered a great multitude, and afterwards...

### Chapter 4: Of the Albigenses

...set fire to the city and burned it to dust.

Once the city was taken, the priests, monks, and clerks came out of the great church of *Béziers*, called *St. Nazaire*, carrying the banner, the crosses, and their holy water. They were bareheaded and dressed in church vestments <note>original: "ornaments"</note>, singing "We praise you, O God" <note>original: "Te Deum laudamus"</note> as a sign of joy that the town was captured and purged of the *Albigenses*. The soldiers, who had received a command from the Legate to kill everyone, rushed in upon them. They broke the order of their procession and made the heads and arms of the priests fly about, each soldier striving to do his "best," until they were all cut to pieces. 

To excuse this cruelty—which was condemned by some who witnessed it—certain reports were inserted into the history. Specifically, they claim that the Pilgrims <note>original: "Pelerins"; here referring to the Crusaders</note> were incensed against the inhabitants of *Béziers* because the citizens had thrown a book of the Gospels over the city walls, crying out to them, "See there the law of your God!" Because of this, the soldiers resolved to kill everyone they found within the boundaries of *Béziers*, ensuring they did not spare those who had committed such blasphemy. 

But how could the *Albigenses* do anything so impious against the Gospel of our blessed Savior? After all, one of the primary reasons they had left the Church of *Rome* was because the Gospel of Jesus Christ was essentially buried among them, and the people were forbidden to read it. Furthermore, one of the great crimes charged against *Earl Raymond* <note>Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse</note> was that he always carried the *New Testament* with him. To this, the historians added a "miracle": that *Béziers* was captured on the feast day of *Mary Magdalene* because (as they say)

Now that the city had been burned, razed, and ransacked, the Pilgrims <note>This term was commonly used for the Crusaders</note>—who believed they earned Paradise through this sack <note>original: "sacceige"</note> and shedding of blood—were quickly led to *Carcassonne*. This took place before the forty days of fighting which they had promised to the Church of Rome had expired; once that time was up, every man was permitted to return to his own home.

...time, because he knew very well that having taken **Béziers**, the Legate would not allow the city of **Carcassonne** to remain in peace. Because Carcassonne was strong by nature, the Legate knew there was no better storehouse for the war, nor a better place of rest for the soldiers than that city. The Earl was advised to retreat there and quickly ensure it was supplied with everything necessary to endure a long siege. Therefore, he entered **Carcassonne**, accompanied by his most faithful followers.

He was followed, almost step by step, by the Legate's army. This force was joined by new **Crusaders** <note>original: "Croises" or "soldiers of the Cross"</note>: specifically, the Bishop of **Agen**, the Bishop of **Limoges**, the Bishop of **Bazas**, the Bishop of **Cahors**, and the Archbishop of **Bordeaux**, each arriving with the "pilgrims" of their own diocese. There also arrived the Earl of **Turenne**, **Bertrand de Cardaillac**, and the Lord of **Castelnau** and of **Montratier**, who led the troops of **Quercy**. The chief leader of all these troops was the Earl of **Dunois**.

<margin>Jean Chassagnon in his *History of the Albigenses*, book 1, page 112.</margin>

There also came a great number of **Provençals**, **Lombards**, and **Germans**—so many, in fact, that the army of the Legate **Milo** <note>original: "Milon"</note> grew to three hundred thousand fighting men <note>Medieval chronicles often cited extremely high, likely exaggerated, numbers to emphasize the scale of the campaign</note> by the time he arrived before **Carcassonne**.

The layout of **Carcassonne** is as follows: there is a "City" <note>The fortified upper town, known today as the Cité</note> and a **suburb** <note>original: "Bourrough" or town</note>. The City is situated upon a small hill, encircled by a double wall. The suburb is on the plain, about two miles <note>In reality, the medieval suburbs were much closer to the walls; this distance may be an error in the original text or refer to the extent of the surrounding territory</note> from the City. At that time, the City was considered a place of great strength, and it was home to a large number of **Albigenses**. ...great violence upon the first rampart <note>original: "Rampier"</note>, and filled the ditch with bundles of sticks <note>original: "fagots"; bundles of wood or branches used to fill moats or provide cover</note>; but they were beaten back with such courage and resolution that the ground was covered with the dead bodies of "pilgrims" <note>The Crusaders were often referred to as "pilgrims" because they had taken a religious vow to fight</note> all around the city.

The young Earl of *Béziers*, Lord of *Carcassonne*, won great honor in this first day's encounter, encouraging his subjects and telling them that they must remember how the people of *Béziers* had been treated. He told them that they were dealing with the same enemies, who had changed the location of the siege but not their temperament, nor their will to exterminate them if they could. He argued that it was far better for them to die fighting than to fall into the hands of such cruel and merciless enemies. 

He declared that for his own part, he was a follower of the *Roman Catholic religion*, but he saw very well that this war was not for religion. Instead, it was a planned robbery agreed upon to invade the goods and lands of Earl *Raymond* <note>original: "Remond"</note> and all his people. He told the citizens they had greater cause to defend themselves than he did: while he could lose nothing more than his goods and his life without being forced to change his religion, they might lose both their lives and the practice of their religion as well. He swore he would never abandon them in so honorable an action, which was to defend themselves against the invasions of their common enemies—men masked with an outward appearance of piety, but who were in reality nothing but thieves.

The *Albigenses*, being greatly inspired by the speech of this young Lord, swore to him that they would sacrifice their goods and their lives for the preservation of the city of *Carcassonne* and for everything that concerned the Earl. The next morning, the Legate commanded an assault and a general scaling of the walls <term>escalado: an attack on a fortified place using ladders to climb the walls</term>.

The Legate listened to hear and understand what the King of Aragon would relate to him. The King told him that he found the Earl of Béziers, his kinsman, much discontented with the former proceedings against his subjects of Béziers and the town of Carcassonne. This gave him reason to believe that, since they had spared neither the Roman Catholics nor the priests, it was not a war undertaken for the cause of religion; rather, it was a kind of thievery <note>original: "thee-uery"</note> under the color of religion. 

The King stated that his hope was that God would give him the grace to make his innocence known, as well as the just cause he had to defend himself. He said they should no longer hope that he and his people would surrender to their mercy <note>original: "discretion"</note>, because they saw that their "mercy" was nothing else but to kill as many as should yield themselves to it. Therefore, if it would please the Legate to grant the Earl of Béziers and his subjects some tolerable settlement <note>original: "composition"; a mutual agreement or terms of surrender</note>, gentleness and mercy would sooner join the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingenfes"</note> to the Church of Rome than extreme cruelty. Above all, they should remember that the Earl of Béziers was young and a Roman Catholic, who might do good service in reclaiming <note>original: "reducing"</note> those who placed any trust in him.

The Legate answered the King of Aragon that if he would withdraw for a little while, they would consult together about what would be most fit to be done.

When the King was called back, the Legate informed him that for his sake, and in consideration of his intercession, he would receive the Earl of Béziers into mercy. ### Chapter 5. Of the *Albigenses*

...their term of forty days <note>original: "tearme of fortie daies"; this was the standard period of military service required for a Crusader to receive a plenary indulgence, or "Paradise"</note>, during which they had gained Paradise, and they refused to fight any longer after such a successful acquisition, for fear they might trade their previous happiness for bruises and wounds.

The Legate was very troubled to see his company reduced to such a small number. He had no hope of capturing that place—which was so important for housing the person who would lead the Church's army in the future—so he thought of a strategy, which he carried out as follows: He sent for a certain well-spoken gentleman in the army and told him that it was in his power to do a notable piece of service for the Church. For this, in addition to the reward he would receive in Heaven, he would be compensated in this life according to his merit. 

The Legate told him to approach as near as he could to the ramparts <term>rampiers: defensive walls or embankments</term> of the city of Carcassonne and make a sign to the besieged that he desired to have a parley <note>original: "parley"; a discussion or conference between enemies under a truce</note> with them. He was to say he wanted to speak with the **Earl of Béziers** as his kinsman and servant, to whom he had something to say that would result in great honor and benefit for the Earl and everyone within Carcassonne. The Legate told him to use all his ingenuity and do his best to fill the Earl with fear, persuading him to seek mercy. He was to influence him through persuasions, promises, and oaths—even using solemn religious vows (which the Legate, as the Pope’s representative, always had the power to excuse and release him from later)—to convince the Earl to allow the gentleman to lead him to the Legate, with the assurance that he would be brought back safely to Carcassonne.

He was committed to the guard and custody of the **Duke of Burgundy** <note>original: "Burgongue"</note>.

### Chapter 5: Of the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingenses"</note>.

<page-num>33</page-num>

All means of escape (to outward appearance) were taken away, for they were shut up on all sides, and the trenches were full of men. But one person among the rest told them that he remembered hearing some elders of the city say that there was in **Carcassonne** a certain vault or tunnel under the ground, large and spacious, so much so that men might walk in it upright and many together. He said it stretched to the Castle of **Cabaret** <note>original: "Cameret, in Cabiaret"</note>, about nine miles <term>league: an old unit of distance, usually about three miles</term> from Carcassonne, and that if the entrance to it could be found, God had provided a miraculous deliverance for them. 

Upon this, all the citizens were employed in the search for this vault, except for the guards who were on the ramparts <term>ramparts: defensive walls of a castle or city</term>. At last, the mouth or entrance was found, and they all began their journey through it at the beginning of the night with their wives and children, carrying with them only some food <term>victuals: food or provisions</term> for a few days.

<margin>Chass. book 2, chapter 14, page 121.</margin>
This departure—accompanied by outcries, groans, and the sorrow of leaving their houses and belongings <term>movables: personal property that can be moved</term>, which were furnished with all manner of goods—to set out on an uncertain course to save themselves by flight, leading their infants and the elderly and infirm with them, amidst the pitiful screeching and outcries of the women, was a most heavy and sorrowful sight. Finding his weakness, they took advantage of it; as proof, after the last departure of the Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"; participants in the Albigensian Crusade were referred to as pilgrims because they took a vow and received indulgences similar to those traveling to the Holy Land.</note>, he had lost over forty towns and castles to which the people had previously brought him the keys, and who were now all revolted from him and the Church. After this expedition, Earl **Simon** besieged the Castle of **Termes** in the same territory of **Narbonne**, a place that seemed impregnable by any human force. The Lady of the city was **Giraude** <note>original: "Gerande"</note>, the sister of **Aimeri**, Lord of **Montréal**. The Legate had taken all of the Lord of **Montréal's** estates, which was why he had gone into the city of **Lavaur** to defend his sister. There were many honorable men within this place. Crusaders came from all parts to join the Legate: from **Normandy**, the troops were led by their bishops, especially the Bishop of **Lisieux**; and six thousand Germans <note>original: "Alemans"</note> also came to him. The Earl of **Foix**, having been informed of the route they were taking, went and lay in ambush for them. He defeated them all, with no one escaping except for a certain Earl who fled at the first encounter to carry the news to Earl **Simon**. Simon pursued the Earl of **Foix** with fourteen thousand men, but in vain, for the Earl had already retreated to **Montgiscard**.

<margin>Chassanion, Book 3, page 150.</margin>
After a six-month siege, the city of **Lavaur** was taken by storm, and everyone there was put to the sword except for eighty gentlemen whom Earl **Simon** ordered to be hanged and strangled. **Aimeri** was hanged on a gallows <note>original: "gibbet"</note> higher than all the rest, and the Lady of **Lavaur** was thrown alive into a pit <note>original: "ditch"</note> and covered with stones. We read of only one act of humanity performed by Earl **Simon's** troops: a gentleman, learning that there were several sick women and children in a house, begged for **them** <meta>catchword: them</meta>

In the year of our Lord 1211, Theodisius <note>original: "Theodize"</note> gave Earl Raymond to understand that he would receive justice and fairness regarding his affairs, and with kind words persuaded him to come to Saint-Gilles <note>original: "St. Giles"</note>. Roger, the son of the Earl of Foix, was much afflicted by the submission of his father, seeing it as an action too base for the greatness of their house. The King of Aragon likewise disliked it. For although he was allied to Earl Simon, he did not fear to let him understand that he could not approve of his usurpations under the pretense of religion.

The King of Aragon wrote to the Earl of Foix that, because the Legate <note>A high-ranking representative of the Pope.</note> and Earl Simon had deceived him by not restoring those lands and places they had promised to return, he should no longer put any trust in them, since Earl Simon’s intentions were now too well known. 

The King explained that Simon endeavored to make himself great and rich with the property of others under a pretense of religion. He warned that if Simon's ambition and greed <note>original: "auarice"</note> were not stopped by the collective arms and cooperation <note>original: "intelligence"</note> of those he had already robbed—and by all others who realize that, having started with their neighbors, he will continue this course without end—his covetous desires would be limitless. 

The King stated he knew very well that Simon did not seek an alliance out of a desire for honor, but only to prevent the King from helping those whom Simon wished to strip of everything they owned. He also wrote letters to Roger, the son of the Earl of Foix, urging him to fortify himself against the unjust seizures <note>original: "vsurpations"</note> of Montfort; otherwise, everyone would laugh at him. He claimed that Earl Simon <note>OCR: "Somon"</note> was actually weak and accompanied by only a few "Pilgrims" <note>Crusaders who took a vow to fight for a limited term, often forty days, in exchange for an indulgence.</note> who were ready to leave due to their own dissatisfaction. Therefore, Roger should take to the battlefield, and he would quickly find allies to assist him.

Earl Raymond <note>original: "Remond"</note>, being very distressed by the King of Aragon's distancing himself—caused by the marriage of the King's son to the daughter of Simon de Montfort—thought it necessary to do his best to win the King back through another marriage alliance. He therefore offered his only son and heir in marriage to the King's daughter. The King of Aragon gave his consent to this proposal.

### CHAPTER 10.

*The siege of Castelnaudary <note>original: "Castlenau d'Arri"</note>; the retreat of Earl Simon; the Earl of Foix offers him battle; the King of Aragon intercedes for the Earls of Toulouse, Foix, and Comminges; he writes for them to the Council of Lavaur <note>original: "de la Vaur"</note> and obtains nothing. The first exploit of this war undertaken by the Confederates <note>The allied lords of the Languedoc region</note> was the siege of Castelnaudary, toward which they marched in this order: The vanguard was led by the Earl of Foix and his son, Prince Roger. The main body of the army was led by Raymond <note>original: "Remond"</note>, Earl of Toulouse. The rear guard was led by the Prince and Lord of Béarn. This army was composed of fifty thousand infantry and ten thousand cavalry; besides that, the city of Toulouse was furnished with a good, strong garrison and all the munitions and instruments of war. Earl Simon moved into Castelnaudary. The situation of this place was good and the castle was one of the best; there were many soldiers and great captains in the city, and a large store of supplies for a long siege. Earl Roger was wounded there by a stone thrown from the city by one of their engines. The Earl of Toulouse encamped himself upon a little hill right across from the castle, entrenching and surrounding himself with rails and barriers. The Prince of Béarn lay on the other side of the city. The army of the Albigenses increased daily upon reports that Earl Simon <note>Simon de Montfort</note> was shut up there, so great was everyone's desire to see his ruin. Because there were too many Albigensian soldiers at this siege, it was thought best that Earl Raymond should take part of the army to surprise certain small strongholds and castles that were somewhat disadvantageous to the army's position. He took Puylaurens, Albi, Rabastens <note>original: "Rabasteins"</note>, Gaillac, Montaigu <note>original: "Montagut"</note>, and Saverdun.

Earl Simon began to see his oversight in allowing himself to be enclosed within Castelnaudary <note>original: "Castlenau d’ Arri"</note>. He realized that as the General, it was necessary for him to be at liberty to provide for all other places under his authority. He left Guy de Lévis—called the Marshal of the Faith—within the town. In order to slip out more easily, he ordered a sally to be made against the besiegers, engaging certain troops as a distraction while he made his escape in the meantime.

When Earl Raymond was informed of Earl Simon’s departure, he was much offended by it,

In the end, they resolved to end the siege because of the approaching winter and a large levy of Pilgrims <note>In the Albigensian Crusade, "Pilgrims" refers to the Crusaders who took up the cross to fight against the Albigenses</note> marching toward them. Earl Simon did not greatly value the lives of these men because he held the Pope's Bull <term>An official edict or decree issued by the Pope</term> stating that whoever lost his life in that war would go immediately to Paradise, as clean of all sin as a hen-roost is of droppings <note>The author uses this earthy comparison to mock the Catholic Church's promise of absolute absolution for Crusaders</note>. Earl Simon was strangely puffed up with pride, making light of those great preparations for war which were ultimately unhelpful to the Albigenses, especially since they had allowed him to escape when they outnumbered him twelve to one. Upon this retreat, the people in Castelnaudary <note>original: "Castlenau"</note> felt compelled to follow the army, but it cost them dearly; for Roger made a furious counter-attack upon them, killing many and beating them back even to the gates of the city.

The Monk of the Valley Sernay <note>original: "Sernay" refers to Peter of les Vaux-de-Cernay, a chronicler who wrote a pro-Crusade history of these events</note> tells this fable: that although there were a hundred thousand fighting men in the Albigensian army, the people of Castelnaudary still went out to their grape harvest and gathered their grapes as if there were no enemy before the city; and that their servants went to water their horses half a league from the city, without the Albigenses daring to attack them. # The History: Book 1

Be our leader, serving as our example, our watchtower, and our guide. In this way, we will commit our wills and our lives to show ourselves as your most humble servants in time of need and as brave soldiers when the opportunity arises. And though I am now worn with age, I never had greater courage or a better resolution.

Earl *Raymond* <note>Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse</note>, for his part, pleaded with the King of *Aragon* not to abandon their cause, offering him both his possessions and his life to fight under his authority.

### CHAPTER XI.

*The exploits of Earl Simon before the King of Aragon had prepared his army; the King of Aragon would come to no agreement <note>original: "composition" — a formal settlement or peace terms</note> with Earl Simon, who was in a weak position; the city of Muret taken by the King of Aragon; the battle fought; the King of Aragon is slain, and his army dispersed.*

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and leaf-like scrollwork in a square frame.</image-desc>In the year of our Lord, one thousand two hundred and thirteen, on the thirteenth of September, the King of *Aragon*—along with Earl *Raymond* of *Toulouse*, *Raymond* Earl of *Foix*, the Earl of *Comminges*, and the Prince of *Béarn*—appeared in the field with their army. This force was composed of seven thousand cavalry <note>original: "horses"</note> and thirty thousand infantry <note>original: "foot"</note>. They took *Muret*, a small city on the borders of the Earldom of *Foix*, situated upon the *Garonne* River, but they did not take the castle. Earl *Simon* was of the opinion that this was the place where the army of his enemies would wear itself out <note>original: "waste and spend it selfe"</note>, because the castle was good and strong. He believed that if he offered resistance for some time, the enemy force would eventually be scattered and overthrown. He therefore placed himself inside that castle with a small number of his most expert and valorous soldiers. He furnished it with supplies <note>original: "munition"</note> and gave such confidence to the besieged by his presence that they thought themselves invincible. Such is the power of the good opinion that soldiers have of their captain to strengthen those who are most weak.
