The Monk has noted some of these; for instance, he says that Earl *Simon* wrote certain letters to the King without any salutation. These letters contained terms stating that if the King continued in his obstinate defiance, he returned the challenge back upon him. He declared that from that point forward, he did not consider himself bound to do the King any service, and he did not doubt that, with God's help, he would defend himself against the King and his confederates.

The King of *Aragon*, having these insolent speeches engraved in his memory, thought the Earl unworthy of any grace or favor in this moment of weakness. He especially imagined that this submission might only be a way to avoid this dangerous clash and wait for his Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims" — a term commonly used for Crusaders, who were legally considered pilgrims with military duties</note> to arrive, so that he might afterwards be more insolent than before. He recalled that at other times, when Earl *Simon* was at his greatest height and followed by a hundred thousand men, it was his constant habit to mock the submissions of Earl *Raymond* of *Toulouse* and the Earl of *Foix*. Therefore, the King felt it would be a great weakness not to return like for like. The King of *Aragon* performed maneuvers <note>original: "made his turnes and returnes"</note> at the head of his army. This was considered a great oversight, because the General of an army must not conduct himself like a Captain of arquebusiers <note>original: "Arquebuziers" — soldiers armed with an early form of long gun</note>, nor perform curvets <note>original: "Curuets" — a high-spirited leap performed by a horse</note> just to be seen. ...that they saw in this an extraordinary proof of the judgment of God, because the King of **Aragon** at that time attributed more to his own power and providence than to the help and succor of the eternal God. <margin>Judges 20.</margin> So four hundred thousand men of **Israel** were beaten by twenty-six thousand of the children of **Benjamin**, who maintained a bad cause and slew forty-two thousand men in two battles. *Judges 20.*

<margin>1 Samuel 4.</margin> So the **Philistines**, being uncircumcised idolaters, got the better in two battles against the **Israelites**; they killed thirty-four thousand of them and captured the Ark of God. So **Jonathan** was slain by the **Philistines**.

<margin>2 Kings 23.</margin> So **Josiah**, who was zealous for the service of God, received his deadly blow fighting against the King of **Egypt** at **Megiddo**. So King **John** [II of France], having an army of sixty thousand men, was defeated <note>original: "discomfited"</note> and taken prisoner by the **Prince of Wales** [Edward the Black Prince], who had no more than eight thousand men, even though the cause of the King of **France** was very just, as he was defending himself against his enemy who assaulted him in his own country. <note>This refers to the Battle of Poitiers in 1356, used here as a historical parallel.</note>

The war of the **Albigenses** intensified; for Earl **Simon** [de Montfort] thought it necessary that he should pursue his enemies while they were half-dead and overthrown. The **Albigenses**, for their part, knew that they must of necessity defend themselves or be defeated and brought into slavery <note>original: "thralldom"</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial 'T' featuring a bird perched amidst scrolls of flowers and foliage.</image-desc>Earl **Simon**, being puffed up with this victory, sent a messenger to summon the Earls of **Toulouse**, **Foix**, and **Comminges**, and the Prince of **Béarn**, to deliver to him the keys of those cities and castles they possessed. ### Chap. 12. Of the *Albigenses*.

...who accompanied him. Seeing so many crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"; participants in the Albigensian Crusade took religious vows and were often referred to as pilgrims</note>, the Legate began to fear that Prince **Louis** might take control of various places held by the **Albigenses**, to the detriment of the Pope's authority, in whose name all these conquests were made. To avoid this, he sent the Church's absolution and protection to all the places held by the said **Albigenses**. Consequently, whenever the Prince intended to attack one of them, the inhabitants produced their letters of absolution and showed that they were under the protection of the Church. 

This Legate became so audacious that he told Prince **Louis** that, since the Prince had become a soldier of the Cross, he was subject to the Legate's commands. This was because the Legate represented the person of the Pope, whose pardons the Prince had come to obtain by obeying the Church, rather than by giving orders as the son of a king. He further reproached him, stating that the King, his father, had made no effort to contribute to the destruction <note>original: "extirpation"</note> of the **Albigenses** when the time was right and opportunity was greatest. Yet now, after these victories had been miraculously won, he had come to glean the rewards <note>original: "glean the ears"; a metaphor for gathering the final bits of grain after a harvest</note> of that glory which belonged only to those who had sacrificed their lives for the Church. 

The Prince hid his reaction to this audacious boldness. **Narbonne** was dismantled with the Prince’s agreement—an enterprise that neither the Legate nor Earl **Simon** would have dared to undertake without his presence. The Bishop of **Narbonne** did everything he could to prevent the city's dismantling, arguing that it was vital for a place on the frontiers of **Spain** to be preserved with its walls and ramparts. However, Earl **Simon** and the Legate were very insistent to the contrary, and they ultimately got their way.

The Pope was willing enough to participate in his overthrow, but because the Earl came to him with submissions, the Pope feared it might discourage others from ever placing confidence in the Papacy. He was generous with his Crosses, his Bulls <note>original: "Bulls"; formal proclamations or edicts issued by a Pope</note>, and his words, but in reality, he commanded his Legate not to restore those places to the Earl until he had given strong proof of his obedience and justification.

The Earl of Toulouse and the King of Aragon resolved to levy their subjects and immediately build a fort at Montgranier, a place naturally very strong. In a few days, they turned it into a defensive stronghold through the labor of their poor subjects. Bewailing their own miseries and those of their lords, the people worked day and night very willingly to finish the task. Once this place was built, the Earl stationed a garrison there and left his son, Roger. Earl Simon besieged it and eventually captured it through starvation. The terms of surrender <note>original: "composition"</note> were that Roger should not bear arms against the Church for one whole year—a condition that greatly troubled this valiant lord. For that year, he withdrew to a house where he counted the months and days until the time expired when he could either die valiantly in battle or defeat his enemies. To this end, he often consulted with the son of the recently slain King of Aragon about how he might find a way to avenge his father's death.

In the meantime, the Legate Bonaventure used the same cunning with Earl Raymond <note>original: "Remond"</note> of Toulouse. He persuaded him to go to Rome to settle his affairs.

## The History, Book 2

The Pope was greatly moved by these outrages and would have willingly provided some justice, but he was told that if he forced the Earl of **Montfort** to return what had been taken for the service of the Church, he would not find anyone from that point forward who would fight for either the Pope or the Church. Furthermore, it was argued that even if he ordered the restitution, Earl **Simon** had good reason not to give up his territory until he was fully compensated for his labors and expenses.

The Pope referred these matters back to the Legate, commanding him in general terms to restore the lands to all those who proved themselves faithful to the Church. Regarding the son of Earl **Raymond** <note>original: "Remond"</note>, the Pope’s will was that the land Earl **Raymond** held in **Provence**—that is, the Earldom of **Venaissin** <note>original: "Venisse"</note>—should be reserved, in part or in full, for the support of his son. This was provided that he gave solid and guaranteed proof of his loyalty and good conduct <note>original: "conversation"</note>, showing himself worthy of divine mercy.

<margin>The Monk of the Vaux-de-Cernay <note>original: "Monke of the Valleis Sernay"</note>, Chapter 152.</margin>
Upon their return, they demanded that the Legate execute their papal bulls <note>formal edicts issued by the Pope</note>, requiring the restitution of their lands. The Legate answered that he faced certain restrictions, the resolution of which would require some time. He told them that, in the meantime, they should show "fruits worthy of their repentance" <note>original: "amendment"</note>, and only then would they receive what the Pope had decreed; otherwise, they would not.

When the Earls saw how they were being deceived <note>original: "deluded"</note>, they resolved to resort to force <note>original: "come to blowes"</note>.

The citizens knew only too well that as soon as the first reinforcements <note>original: "succours"</note> for the Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"</note> arrived, their city would be exposed to looting. When they were informed of the conditions for peace, the first article was this: that Earl Simon would agree to nothing until all the inhabitants had carried their weapons to the Town Hall. This point was obtained with great difficulty, but at last they yielded to it. Once this was done, Earl Simon ordered his people to make their approach. Having seized the Town Hall against a disarmed people and having moved their armor to the Castle of Narbonne, he imprisoned the leading men of the city. He then ordered them to be sent out of Toulouse to wherever he saw fit, treating them so rudely and with such inhuman cruelty that a great number died along the way. Thus was Toulouse emptied of its principal inhabitants, and the rest were forced to pay a ransom, by which Earl Simon greatly enriched himself. Shortly after, returning from the region of Bigorre where he had failed to take the Castle of Lourdes, he vented his anger <note>original: "discharged his choller"</note> upon this poor city. He permitted it to be plundered by his Crusaders and then ordered the remaining towers that still stood around the city to be torn down.

During this time, the poor Earl of Toulouse <note>Raymond VI</note> was at Montauban. Understanding the bad treatment of his miserable subjects, he could do nothing for certain months but bewail their lamentable state with sighs and tears.

He went on foot and without any companions so that he would not be recognized at the gate, and in this way, he escaped the great danger. Thus, in a single hour, he saw himself honored almost as a god—chosen and hailed as Prince and Monarch—only to then flee in disguise and hide himself like a lowly scoundrel <note>original: "scundrell"</note> for fear of the common people <note>original: "rascall people"</note>.

The Pope sent him a papal bull <note>original: "Bull"; a formal decree or charter issued by a Pope</note>, dated the fourth of the Nones of April <note>April 2, 1215</note>, by which he gave him authority to keep all those lands he had brought under his power. The Pope granted him the revenues, profits, and the power to administer justice, "considering," said the Pope, "that you neither can, nor ought to make war at your own expense." 

This papal generosity—given from another man's purse in a matter where the Pope had nothing to give—motivated Simon to go to the King of *France*. He went to be invested <note>to be formally granted a title and land by a monarch</note> with the Dukedom of *Narbonne* and the Earldom of *Toulouse*, together with all the lands which the Crusaders <note>original: "Souldiers of the Crosse"</note> had conquered and taken from those they called heretics or their protectors. He successfully obtained these from the King to hold in fee <note>a legal term meaning to hold land as a feudal tenant of the king</note>.

<margin>The Monk of Val-des-Cernay, Chapter 153. <note>original: "The Monke of the Valleis Sernay"; referring to the chronicler Pierre des Vaux-de-Cernay.</note></margin>

The monk says it was not possible for him to describe the honor shown to Simon on his journey to *France*. There was neither city nor town through which he passed where the clergy and people did not come out to see him, crying out, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" <note>original: "Blessed is hee that comes in the name of God"; a biblical greeting historically reserved for Christ or high holy figures</note>. For such and so great, says the monk, was the people's religious devotion toward him that there was no one who did not think himself happy just to touch the hem of his garments.

Count Raymond followed up on his victory, making himself master of the Castle of Narbonne <note>original: "Castle of Narbonnes"; this refers to the Château Narbonnais, the fortified palace of the Counts of Toulouse, not the city of Narbonne.</note> and fortifying it against the Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"; the author uses this term because those fighting in the Albigensian Crusade took religious vows similar to those of pilgrims.</note>, whom he knew very well would return the following year. In the meantime, he sent his son into the Agenais, who brought the towns of Condom, Marmande, Aiguillon, and other adjoining places under his father’s authority. On the other side, the Count of Foix besieged Mirepoix and summoned Roger de Lévis to restore it to him, telling him that he should no longer place any hope in Count Simon, for he was dead. He said that Roger should be satisfied with having kept what was not his for so long and so unjustly; if he pushed the Count’s patience into fury, he would lose both his life and Mirepoix together. It greatly troubled the "Marshal of the Faith" (for that was the empty title which the Legates had given him) to yield this place; but in the end, he delivered it into the hands of the Count of Foix.

The Count of Comminges also reclaimed his rights from a man named Joris, to whom the Legates had given everything the Crusaders <note>original: "Souldiers of the Crosse"</note> had taken in his territories; for the Count took it all back from him—including his life.

### Chapter 3: Of the Albigenses

[He feared he might] not be attacked along the way by the garrison of **Carcassonne**, and therefore he begged him for help. Young **Raymond** set out toward him and arrived at such a good time for the **Count of Foix** that, just as the Count was on the verge of losing his plunder while being pursued by the **Viscount of Lautrec** and the Captains **Faucant** and **Valas**, Raymond joined the battle.

<margin>Chassanion, Book 4, chapter 13</margin>
The said **Faucant** and **Valas** encouraged their Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"; participants in the Albigensian Crusade were called pilgrims because they received the same indulgences as those traveling to the Holy Land.</note> with a loud voice, saying that they fought for Heaven and for the Church. Young **Count Raymond**, hearing this, cried out to his men just as loudly: "Courage, my friends, for we fight for our religion and against thieves and robbers who use the name of the Church. They have stolen enough; let us make them vomit it up again and pay the back-taxes <note>original: "arrerages" (arrearages); meaning unpaid debts or items owed from the past.</note> for the thefts they have freely committed until now."

And hereupon they launched the attack. The **Viscount of Lautrec** fled, **Faucant** was taken prisoner, and all their troops were cut to pieces. **Seguret**, a captain and professional robber, was captured and hanged in the field from a tree. Thus victorious and laden with plunder, they came to **Toulouse** with their prisoners and cattle. 

The siege of **Marmande** continued, but fruitlessly and without any advantage. For **Amaury** <note>original: "Almaric"; referring to Amaury de Montfort, son of Simon de Montfort.</note> having ordered a general assault to be made, the inhabitants defended themselves with such valor and resolution that the ditches were full of the dead bodies of the Crusaders. This occurred at the time when the great expedition of **Prince Louis** <note>The future King Louis VIII of France.</note> arrived, who brought thirty Earls with him. This was an expedition for which the **Legate Bertrand** wrote to **King Philip** in these terms: 

> "Do not fail to be in the region of **Toulouse** for the entire month of May, in the year 1219, with all your forces and powers..."

"...powers, to revenge the death of the Earl of Montfort, and I will ensure that the Pope shall publish and preach the Crusade <note>original: "Croisade"</note>—an expedition of Christians throughout the world—for your better aid and support." Thus you see how the Legate commands the King of France. The King's son, Prince Louis, arrived at **Marmande** and summoned those within the city to surrender. They reached an agreement <note>original: "compound"</note> with him, and he promised to spare their lives. 

**Amaury** <note>original: "Almaric"; the son of Simon de Montfort</note> complained about this, saying that those who took his father's life were not worthy of living themselves. He assembled the Prelates <note>high-ranking clergy members</note> and declared to them the dissatisfaction he felt over this agreement, because mercy was granted to those who were the murderers of his father. The Prelates were all of the opinion that, despite the word already given, the people should all die. 

Prince **Louis’s** will was that the agreement should be honored. **Amaury**, nevertheless, caused his troops to slip into the city with orders to kill everyone: men, women, and children. They did so, which offended the Prince; he departed from the Legate and **Amaury**, and passing along, he summoned those of **Toulouse** to surrender. They defended themselves against him. He then received news of the death of his father <note>King Philip II of France, who died in July 1223.</note>, which caused him to retreat. Thus you see all the effects of this great expedition, which was intended to bury all the Albigensians alive, yet vanished without any final assault being made.

### CHAPTER 4.

*The Albigensian War changes its course because of the death of Pope Innocent III; the replacement of the Legate; the death of Earl Raymond of Toulouse; the illness of Raymond, Earl of Foix, and Lady Philippa de Moncada, mother of the Earl of Foix; and regarding the monk Dominic.*

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial T featuring floral and leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>The Legate <term>Legate: A personal representative of the Pope, often sent with high authority to oversee crusades or diplomatic missions.</term> Bertrand Bonaventure, being weary of the long labors of this war and perceiving that the danger was greater than either the pleasure or the profit, took the opportunity of his old age to retire to Rome. This occurred at the time when Pope Innocent III had passed away. His successor, Pope Honorius III, had not directed this war from its beginning and therefore understood neither its importance nor what direction to give. Consequently, he needed to be informed by his Legate regarding how to continue the conflict and the benefits that might arise for the Papal See <note>original: "his Seat"</note>. 

Bonaventure urged him to appoint another Legate and told him that the necessity of this war was such that it concerned not only the potential loss of all those Albigensian lands which had been conquered—since they might easily be recovered by the locals if no opposition were made—but also the ruin of the Church of Rome. He argued that the doctrine of the Waldensians and Albigensians directly shook the authority of the Popes and overthrew the statutes of the Church.

### CHAPTER IV.

*The war against the Albigensians <note>original: "Albingenses"</note> takes on a new character due to the death of Pope Innocent III; the replacement of the Legate; the death of Earl Raymond of Toulouse; the passing <note>original: "disease," here meaning death or fatal illness</note> of Raymond, Earl of Foix, and the Lady Philippe de Moncade, mother to the Earl of Foix; and the death of the monk Dominic.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

**T**he Legate Bertrand Bonaventure, being weary of the long struggles of this war and perceiving that the danger was greater than either the pleasure or the profit, took the opportunity—under the pretext of his advanced age—to retire to Rome. This occurred at the same time that Pope Innocent III had died. Pope Honorius, his successor, had not directed this war by his own authority from the beginning; therefore, he knew neither its importance nor what direction to give. He needed to be informed by his Legate regarding the means of continuing the conflict and the benefits that might come to the Papacy <note>original: "vnto his Seat"</note>. Bonaventure urged him to appoint another Legate and told him that the necessity of this war was such that it involved not only the loss of all those Albigensian lands that had been conquered—because they could easily be recovered by the inhabitants if no opposition was made—but also the ruin of the Church of Rome. This was because the doctrine of the Waldensians and Albigensians directly shook the authority of the Popes and overthrew the laws <note>original: "Statutes"</note> of the Church.

This war had been very costly <note>original: "chargeable"</note> and had cost them dearly. Within the space of fifteen years or less, more than three hundred thousand soldiers of the **Cross** <note>Crusaders</note> had died, having come at various times to end their lives in **Languedoc**. It was as if there were not enough room elsewhere to bury them, or as if there were a necessity in those times to be born in **France** only to die encountering the **Albigensians** <note>original: "Albingenfes"</note>. All of this effort would be lost if they did not continue to spend resources and weaken them until they were utterly destroyed. The Pope delegated a man named **Contat**, who went there.

<margin>1220.</margin>
Now, although **Almeric** was very valiant, he had not gained the authority his father <note>Simon de Montfort</note> had. His father had made himself a great captain at the expense of the Albigensians. He was loved by the soldiers, possessed admirable valor, was patient in affliction, invincible in his labors <note>original: "trauels"</note>, and diligent in his enterprises. He was foresighted in providing for the needs of an army and affable in person; yet he held an irreconcilable enmity against his enemies because he hated them only to seize their goods. Since he could not have their property until after their death, he procured and hastened their ends as much as he could, all under the mantle of a plausible pretense of religion. 

His son was a true heir to his father’s hatred, but he was slow and sluggish, loving his ease and in no way fit for actions of great importance. Besides, he was deprived of the monk **Dominic** <note>original: "Dominique"</note>, of whom his father had made very profitable use. By lodging Dominic in the conquered cities, Simon de Montfort gave him the task of finishing that destruction through his **Inquisition** which could not be accomplished through war. Dominic died in the year 1220, on the sixth of August. He was so rich that, despite being the founder of a mendicant order <note>original: "order mendicant," a religious order whose members originally relied on charity and avoided owning property</note>—that is to say, of the **Jacobins** <note>The Dominicans were known as Jacobins in France because their first house in Paris was near the church of Saint Jacques</note>—

Dominican <note>original: "Iacobin"</note> monks, yet he made it known before his death that a traveler's pouch <note>original: "scrip," a small bag carried by pilgrims or beggars</note> well-supplied was better than a rental income poorly assigned. For he left many houses and much property, showing thereby that he used his pouch only for show and the outward appearance of poverty; but in effect, he thought it good to have the means to live elsewhere. This is witnessed by the Protection which the Earl **Simon** gave him a little before his death, the wording <note>original: "tenure"</note> of which is as follows:

We will and command you to take special care to keep and defend the houses and goods of our most dear brother Dominic as if they were our own. Given at the siege of Toulouse, December 13.*

The death of this monk was a great comfort to the **Albigensians**, whom he had persecuted with such violence; but yet they were more weakened by the deaths of Earl **Raymond** of **Toulouse**, Earl **Raymond** of **Foix**, and Lady **Philippe de Moncade**, wife to Raymond, Earl of Foix.

Earl **Raymond** of **Toulouse** died of a sickness, as much lamented by his subjects as any man ever was. He was just, gentle, valiant, and courageous, but yet too quick to listen to those who gave him counsel that led to his ruin. At first, he was motivated only by a true love and charity toward those subjects of his who made profession of the religion of the **Albigensians**. But afterward, having been treated basely and dishonorably by the Pope’s legates, he recognized both the cruelty of the priests and the falsehood of their doctrine through those debates <note>original: "conferences"</note> that had been held in his presence.

The author who wrote the *History of Languedoc* says that he died a sudden death and that he was carried into the house of the Friars of the Hospital of **St. John**, but that he was not buried because he died as an excommunicated person. There was shown not long ago in **Toulouse** a head which some believed was the head of **Earl Raymond**, which was said to always remain without a tomb <note>original: "sepulture"</note>. However, there is no likelihood that he who died among his own people, and being their ruler, would not have enough respect after his death to be placed in a sepulcher. It is improbable that he who, by his valor, had restored all his subjects to their homes and their city to its former greatness—he whose death they mourned as for a father—should be cast out like a dog. It is neither true, nor does it have any resemblance to the truth, that they would deny him this last act of charity, which they did not refuse to bestow even upon their greatest enemies; for it was never heard that the **Albigensians** denied burial to anyone.

As for the **Earl of Foix**, **Raymond**, he was a prince of whom history gives this testimony: that he was a patron of justice, clemency, prudence, valor, magnanimity, patience, and self-restraint <note>original: "continency"</note>. He was a good warrior, a good husband, a good father, a good provider <note>original: "house-keeper"</note>, and a good judge <note>original: "justicer"</note>, worthy to have his name honored and his virtues remembered throughout all generations. When this good prince saw that he was to leave the earth for heaven, he faced death

<header>Chapter 5: Concerning the Albigensians.</header>

[The Earl of Foix displayed] a confident and steady demeanor and found comfort in leaving the world and its vanities. Calling his son **Roger** to him, he exhorted him to serve God, to live virtuously, and to govern his people like a father under the obedience of His laws; and so he breathed his last <note>original: "gave up the ghost"</note>. His wife, the **Lady Philippa of Moncada**, followed him shortly after, not without suspicion of poisoning by some enemy within her household <note>original: "domesticall enemy"</note> because she practiced the religion of the **Albigensians** with all devotion. 

She was a princess of great and admirable foresight <note>original: "providence"</note>, faith, constancy, and loyalty. Before her death, she uttered many excellent sayings <note>original: "sentences"</note> intended for spiritual instruction, spoken in both the **Castilian** <note>Spanish</note> tongue and in **French**, expressing a defiance of death. She received death with marvelous grace, strengthening her words with most Christian consolations to the great comfort and instruction of all who were present, and in this state, she departed this life.

All these deaths caused a great change in the wars of the **Albigensians**, affecting both sides.

## CHAPTER V.

*Amaury <note>original: "Almaric"</note> of Montfort restored the conquered countries of the Albigensians to King Louis VIII; the siege of Avignon; the King appoints a Governor in Languedoc. The war continues against the Albigensians; Toulouse is besieged; a treaty of peace is made with Earl Raymond and the people of Toulouse.*

**Amaury of Montfort** did not have the good fortune of his father in the wars of the **Albigensians**. For he had neither **King Philip Augustus**, who had permitted the recruitment <note>original: "levie"</note> of the Crusaders <note>original: "Pilgrims"; participants in the Albigensian Crusade were often called pilgrims because they received the same spiritual indulgences as those traveling to the Holy Land</note>, nor **Pope Innocent**...

...the third to appoint them. Moreover, there was neither city nor village in **France** where there were not widows and fatherless children because of the past wars of the **Albigensians**. And besides all this, the prelates <note>High-ranking clergy members like bishops</note> were often put into great fear by those cruel combats that were regularly fought; many of them left behind their miters <note>The ceremonial headdress of a bishop</note>, and some abbots left their crosses. Talk of the Crusades <note>original: "expeditions of the Cross"</note> was no longer as common. This was the reason why **Amaury** <note>original: "Almaric"</note> of Montfort did not long enjoy his conquered countries. Being much distressed by this, he went into **France** and surrendered to **Louis VIII**, King of **France**, all the rights he had to the said countries, which the Pope and the Councils of **Lavaur** <note>original: "Vaur"</note>, **Montpellier**, and the **Lateran** <note>original: "Lotran"</note> had granted to him. In return for this, King **Louis** appointed him Constable of **France** in the year 1224.

<margin>
Inventory of Jean de Serres, in the life of Louis VIII.

1224.
</margin>

To take possession of these lands, King **Louis VIII** came into **Languedoc**. Arriving at the gates of **Avignon**, he was denied entrance because, since the people there professed the religion of the **Albigensians**, they had been excommunicated and their city granted by the Pope to the first conqueror who could take it. At that time, **Avignon** was not the capital city of the County of **Venaissin** <note>original: "Venessin"</note>, as it is today, but belonged to the King of **Naples** and **Sicily**. The King, being greatly angered <note>original: "moved"</note> by this refusal, resolved to besiege it. The siege lasted for eight months, at the end of which they surrendered around Whitsuntide <note>A Christian festival celebrated seven weeks after Easter</note> in the year 1225.

<margin>

# CHAPTER VI.

## *The Articles of the treaty of Earl Raymond of Toulouse, with the Pope's Legate, Amelin, and the Queen Mother of Louis IX, King of France.*

<margin>
These articles are to be found in the Library <note>original: "Bibliothech"</note> of Pères, Volume 7.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'I' set within a square woodcut border featuring ornate floral and leaf scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
IT was an easy matter to finish this treaty, because the articles were proposed to Earl Raymond with the condition that they should be signed by himself without any reply or objection.

*Article 1.* That after Earl Raymond has asked for pardon according to the appointed order—that is to say, bareheaded, barefooted, in his shirt, and with a torch in his hand, for all that he had done against the Church—he shall promise to defend the faith and drive away all heretics out of his lands and territories.

*Article 2.* That he should pay three marks of silver to the Church every year for as long as he lives.

3. That he should give once and immediately <note>original: "incontinently"</note> the sum of six thousand marks of silver for the repairs of the cities, castles, and houses that had been destroyed and ruined either by himself or his father during the past wars.

4. That he should give two thousand marks of silver for the repair of the monastery <term>Moustier: an archaic term for a monastery or minster</term> and the maintenance and support of the monks of Cîteaux <note>A Cistercian monastery in France, the mother house of the order.</note>.

5. For the monks of Clairvaux <note>Another primary Cistercian monastery, famously associated with Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>, five hundred marks of silver.

6. For those of Grandselve and the repair of their monastery, a thousand marks of silver.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*Earl Raymond of Toulouse urges the Earl of Foix to align himself under the authority of the Pope: The tactics he uses to make him abandon the cause of the Albigenses, and how he allows himself to be influenced by the Pope’s Legate.*

The Earl of Foix, the Earl of Comminges, and the Prince of Béarn were still to be conquered or won over through strategic maneuvers <note>original: "practises"; in this context, it refers to diplomatic pressures or political schemes.</note>. The Legate Colmieu thought that Earl Raymond was a suitable tool to achieve the latter, and therefore he commanded Raymond to write to the Earl of Foix, telling him *that he should follow Raymond’s example, or resolve to perish miserably.* Raymond wrote to him in affectionate terms: *that the bond which had always existed between their houses obliged him to seek the Earl of Foix's well-being as his own; that if the Earl did not surrender himself into the bosom of the Church of Rome, Raymond saw such a storm ready to fall upon him that it must necessarily overwhelm him. Furthermore, having such a great enemy as a King of France, it was impossible for him to hold out.* Raymond therefore pleaded with him to accept his advice—and with it, a gift he offered as a further proof of his love: *if the Earl of Foix would comply with this submission to the Pope and the Church of Rome, Raymond would, from that day forward, release him from the oath of homage <term>homage</term> which he had traditionally performed for the Earldom of Foix.* He likewise urged him to secure similar submissions from the Earl of Comminges and the Prince of Béarn.

The Inquisitors entangled people of all types in such a way that there was almost no one they did not condemn—either as heretics, or as their supporters, or as relatives or allies of heretics. Not satisfied with proceeding against those who publicly professed the Albigensian <note>A group of Christian dualists in southern France targeted by the Catholic Church as heretics</note> faith, they committed strange acts of theft under the cloak of the Office of the Inquisition. This accusation against the Inquisitors was made before Earl Raymond <note>Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse</note> in the presence of five inquisitors and four officers of the Inquisition. These included William Arnaldi (a monk and inquisitor) and two other Jacobin <note>Members of the Dominican Order, who were the primary administrators of the Inquisition</note> monks; also Raymond de l’Escrivain (Archdeacon of the Church of Toulouse), the Prior of Avignonet de Cluze, Peter Arnaldi (the Notary of the Inquisition), and three others from Avignonet in the Diocese of Toulouse.

The inquisitor monks intended to reply and use the information gathered to frame indictments against those who had accused them of dishonorable conduct. They terrified the accusers with threats, which caused those who had provoked the monks' patience to realize that since they were destined to fall into the inquisitors' trap and be utterly ruined, it was better for them to liberate themselves once and for all and teach others to act more cautiously. Becoming increasingly aggressive and violent in their debate, they eventually came to blows. The inquisitor monks and their officers were overmatched; nine were killed (as the historian of Languedoc reports). These were the five monks specified above and the four officers. ### Chapter 11

***Alphonse, brother to King Saint Louis, takes possession of the goods of the last Earl Raymond of Toulouse: The persecution continues against the Albigenses until the time that the Gospel was received in France, and then the greatest part of those places where the Albigenses inhabited immediately <note>original: "presently"</note> received the Reformation.***

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter T at the beginning of the text, featuring intricate floral vines and foliage patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

The change of their Lord altered the condition of the Albigenses, for Earl Raymond having departed this life, Alphonse <note>Alphonse of Poitiers (1220–1271)</note>, brother to King Saint Louis <note>Louis IX of France</note>, took possession of all the lands, goods, and revenues of the said Earl. Consequently, all the ill will that the Pope and other ecclesiastical persons bore toward the house of the Earl of Toulouse ceased. And regarding the places which he was supposed to surrender as specified in the treaty, there was no further need to discuss that, because Alphonse, being free from all suspicion of dishonesty toward the Pope or the Church, peacefully enjoyed whatever belonged to him. But one hand washes the other; and therefore, just as Alphonse had become master of the goods of Earl Raymond through those wars that the Church undertook against the Earl of Toulouse, he was likewise bound to do his best to ensure that the Pope was honored in his territories. ->*The conclusion of this History of the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingenses"</note>.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut decorative initial I, featuring floral scrollwork and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>It is an easy matter to gather from the contents of this history of the Albigenses that the people inhabiting the country of Albi, Languedoc, and various other neighboring places have made profession of the very same religion as those who elsewhere were called Waldenses <note>A proto-Protestant group following the teachings of Peter Waldo</note>. This is further confirmed because their adversaries themselves have affirmed that they persecuted them as Waldenses. 

It is also clear that the greatest troubles that have fallen upon them were procured by the priests, whose corruptions they described and whose abuses they discovered. ## CHAP. XII.
### *The conclusion of this History of the Albingenfes.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' with floral and foliate patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc> It is an easy matter to conclude from the contents of this History of the Albigenses <note>original: "Albingenfes"</note> that the people inhabiting the region of Albi, Languedoc, and various other neighboring places have made profession of the very same religion as those who elsewhere were called Waldenses. These Inquisitors delivered as many people as they could capture to the secular magistrate <note>The civil authorities or local government, who carried out the physical punishments and executions decreed by the Church</note>. 

Since this method was somewhat too slow to eliminate them and see the end of them, the Popes drew their swords against them. They armed their Cardinals and Legates <note>original: "Legats"; high-ranking diplomatic representatives of the Pope</note> and drove the kings and princes of the earth into these bloody wars, offering Paradise as a reward to anyone who would take up arms against them and risk his life for their extermination for forty days. 

Many great lords desired to know the cause of the Pope’s irreconcilable enmity against their subjects. Having perceived that irrational passion drove those who were offended by the truth, these lords defended their subjects' cause, grounding their reason in this: that if they should ever be convinced of error by the word of God, they would give the glory to God. From this followed those cruel wars in which a million men lost their lives.

<header>The Doctrine of the Book, Book 1.</header>

Answer: For the purpose that I should know and serve him, and that I might be saved by his grace.

Question: *In what does your salvation consist?*

Answer: In three essential virtues, which necessarily belong to salvation.

Question: *Which are they?*

Answer: Faith, Hope, and Charity.

Question: *How do you prove it?*

Answer: The Apostle says in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, Chapter 13, verse 13: "These three things remain: Faith, Hope, and Charity."

Question: *What is Faith?*

Answer: According to the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1, it is "the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen."

Question: *How many kinds of faith are there?*

Answer: There are two sorts of faith: a living <note>original: "liuely"</note> faith and a dead faith.

Question: *What is a living faith?*

Answer: That which works through charity.

Question: *What is a dead faith?*

Answer: According to Saint James, that faith which is without works is dead. Furthermore, faith is nothing without works; or, a dead faith is to believe there is a God, and to believe those things concerning God, but not to believe *in* God.

Question: *What is your faith?*

Answer: The true Catholic <note>original: "Catholike"; here meaning "universal" or the traditional Christian faith, as the Waldenses claimed they held the true faith of the early church in opposition to the Roman Church</note> and Apostolic faith.

Question: *What is that?*

Answer: It is that which is divided into twelve articles in the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "Symbole"; from the Greek "symbolon," a common term for a creed or summary of faith</note>.

Question: *What is that Creed?*

Answer: I believe in God the Father Almighty, etc.

Question: *By what means can you know that you believe in God?*
Answer: By this: because I know that I have given myself to the observation of the commandments of God.
Question: *How many commandments of God are there?*
Answer: Ten, as it appears in *Exodus* and *Deuteronomy*.
Question: *Which are they?*
Answer: Hearken, O *Israel*: I am the Lord your God. You shall have no other gods but me. You shall not make for yourself any carved image <note>original: "grauen Image"</note>, nor the likeness of anything that is in Heaven, etc.
Question: *Upon what do all these commandments depend?*
Answer: Upon the two great commandments; that is to say: You shall love God above all things, and your neighbor as yourself.
Question: *What is the foundation of these commandments, by which everyone ought to enter into life, and without which foundation no man can worthily fulfill the commandments?*
Answer: Our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Apostle says in the first Epistle to the *Corinthians*: "No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ."
Question: *By what means may a person attain this foundation?*
Answer: By faith. As Saint *Peter* says in 1 Peter 2:6: "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, elect and precious, and he who believes in him shall not be put to shame <note>original: "confounded"</note>." And our Savior says: "He who believes in me shall have eternal life."

Answer: Because I know him to be true God and true man, who was born, and suffered, etc., for my redempti- <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "redemption."</note>

on, and Justification <note>original: "Iustification"; the process by which a person is made righteous before God</note>; and that I love him, and desire to fulfill his commandments.

*Question: By what means can a person attain the essential virtues, that is to say: Faith, Hope, and Charity <note>original: "Charity"; in this context, it refers to the theological virtue of divine love (Caritas).</note>?*

Answer: By the gifts of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "holy Ghost"</note>.

*Question: Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?*

Answer: I do believe. For the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and is a person of the Trinity; according to his divinity, he is equal with the Father and the Son.

*Question: Do you believe God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit to be three persons? Then there are three Gods.*

Answer: No, there are not three.

*Question: But yet you have named three?*

Answer: That was because of the difference of the persons, not of the essence <term>essence</term> <note>The underlying nature or substance of God that makes Him who He is.</note> of the divinity. For though there are three persons, yet there is but one essence.

*Question: In what way do you adore and serve that God in whom you believe?*

Answer: I adore him by an outward <note>original: "exterior"</note> and inward <note>original: "interior"</note> adoration. Outwardly, by the bowing of the knees, the lifting up of the hands, the bowing <note>original: "inclination"</note> of the body, with hymns and spiritual songs, fasting, and prayer <note>original: "inuocation"</note>; but inwardly by a holy affection and a will ready to do what he pleases. I serve him by Faith, Hope, and Charity, according to his commandments.

*Question: Do you adore and serve any other thing as God?*

Answer: No.

*Question: Why?* <note>original: "Wherefore?"</note>

Answer: Because of his commandment, by which he has strictly <note>original: "straightly"</note> commanded, saying: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve."

### The Doctrine of the Book, Part 1

...according to the truth <note>original: "veritie"</note> of the Ministry, these are the Ministers of Christ, along with the people subject to them or committed to their charge, using their Ministry through Faith, Hope, and Charity.

Question: *By what marks do you know the **Church of Christ**?*
Answer: By suitable <note>original: "conuenient"; here meaning fitting or appropriate for the office.</note> Ministers, and by the people who participate in the truth of that Ministry.

Question: *How do you know the **Ministers**?*
Answer: By a true understanding <note>original: "apprehension"</note> of faith, by sound doctrine, by a life of good example, by the preaching of the Gospel, and by the proper administration of the Sacraments.

Question: *By what marks do you know the **false Ministers**?*
Answer: By their fruits; by their blindness, by their wicked works, by their perverse doctrine, and by their unfit and disorderly administration of the Sacraments.

Question: *How may we know **their blindness**?*
Answer: When they—not knowing the truth that is necessary for salvation—observe human inventions as if they were the Commandments of God. Of such people, the prophecy that Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> spoke is proven true, which was also cited by our Savior Jesus Christ in Matthew 15: "*This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; but they serve me in vain, <note>original: "for nothing"</note> teaching the doctrine and commandments of men.*"

Question: *By what means or marks are **wicked works** made known?*
Answer: By those obvious sins of which the Apostle speaks in Romans 1, saying that those who do such things shall—

**Question:** *By what marks is false doctrine known?*

**Answer:** When men teach against Faith and Hope—such as various kinds of idolatry, worshiping rational, sensible, visible, or invisible creatures. **Question:** *By what marks is the disorderly administration of the Sacraments known?*

**Answer:** When the priests do not understand the intention of Christ in the Sacraments, and teach that all grace and truth are included in them by the outward ceremonies alone, leading people to participate in the Sacraments without the truth of Faith, Hope, and Charity. It is the will of the Lord that all his people should take heed of false prophets, saying, "*Beware of false prophets.*" And again, "*Beware of the Pharisees,*" that is to say, of their leaven and false doctrine. And again, "*Do not believe them; do not follow after them.*" David hates all such persons, and therefore he says, "*I hate the congregation of the wicked.*" And the Lord commands us to withdraw ourselves from among such people (Numbers 16:26): "*Depart from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be consumed in all their sins.*" And the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 6:14, "*Do not be unequally yoked together with unbelievers, for what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? And what communion has light with darkness? What concord has Christ with Belial, or what—*"

### Chapter 1: The Waldenses and Albigenses

*John says in Chapter 1, verse 17: "Grace came by Jesus Christ." And again: "We beheld his glory, full of grace and truth, and we have all received from his fullness."*

**Q. What is Grace?**
A. It is redemption, the remission of sins, justification, adoption, and sanctification.

**Q. By what means do we hope for this grace in Christ?**
A. By a lively <note>original: "liuely"; meaning a living, active, or vital faith.</note> faith and true repentance, as Jesus Christ says: "Repent, and believe the Gospel."

**Q. From where does hope proceed?**
A. From the gift of God and his promises. Therefore, the Apostle says: "He is able to accomplish whatever he promises." For he has promised himself that at whatever time a sinner knows him, repents of his sins, and hopes that he will have mercy, pardon, and justify him, etc.

**Q. What are the things that divert a person from this hope?**
A. A dead faith and the seductions of Antichrist <note>Historically, the Waldenses and other early reforming groups often identified the institutional Roman Church or the Papacy as the "Antichrist."</note> toward anyone other than Christ—that is to say, toward the Saints, and the power of that Antichrist in his authority, words, blessings <note>original: "benedictions"</note>, sacraments, and the relics of the dead. It also involves teaching people to have hope through means that directly oppose the truth and the commandments of God, such as various forms of idolatry and simoniacal <note>original: "Simoniacall"; referring to simony, the practice of buying or selling spiritual things or church offices.</note> wickedness, etc. This includes abandoning the fountain of living water given by grace to run after broken cisterns—adoring, honoring, and serving the creature <note>In this context, "the creature" refers to created things (like images, relics, or people) rather than the Creator.</note> through prayers, fastings, sacrifices, donations, offerings, pilgrimages, invocations, and so on. They trust to attain grace through these things, which no one can give except God alone in Jesus Christ. So that

# The Doctrine of the Book, Part 1

...they travel in vain, losing their silver and their lives—and undoubtedly not only this present life, but also that which is to come. For this reason, it is said that the hope of felons <note>original: "felons"; in this religious context, it refers to the ungodly or those who have committed spiritual crimes against God.</note> shall perish.

*Q. And what do you say of the blessed Virgin Mary? For she is full of grace, as the Angel testifies: "Hail Mary, full of grace," etc.*

A. The blessed Virgin has been, and is, full of grace in herself, but not to communicate <note>original: "communicate"; meaning to share or pass on to others.</note> it to others. For her Son alone is full of grace to bestow on others, as it is said of him: *And we all receive of his fullness, grace for grace.*

*Q. Do you not believe in the Communion of Saints?*

A. I believe there are two ways in which the faithful communicate <note>original: "communicate"; here meaning to participate in or share common ground.</note>: one is substantial, and the other is ministerial. They communicate in the substantial way through the Holy Spirit in God, by the merit of Jesus Christ. But they communicate in the ministerial or ecclesiastical <note>original: "Eccleſiafticall"; relating to the physical church organization.</note> way through the ministry duly exercised—that is to say, by the Word, by the Sacraments, and by prayer. I believe in both of these Communions of Saints: the first only in God by the Spirit, the other in the Church by Christ.

*Q. In what does eternal life consist?*

A. In a living, working faith, and in perseverance within it. Our Savior says in John 17:3: *This is eternal life: that they might know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.* And he who perseveres to the end shall be saved. Amen.

# An Exposition of the Waldenses and Albigenses on the Ten Commandments of the Law of GOD.

## CHAPTER III.

### An Exposition of the First Commandment.

->The first Commandment of the Law of God is this: You shall have no strange gods before me. Exodus 20, etc. <note>original Occitan: "Le premier Commandement de la Ley de Dio es aquest: Non aures Dio straing deuant mi. Exod. 20. &c."</note><-

->You shall have no other gods but me.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' depicting a figure looking upward toward a divine light or cloud.</image-desc>
<margin>Taken out of the Book of the Waldenses, titled *The Book of Virtues*, page 197.</margin>
All those who love the creature <note>referring to created things or people</note> more than the Creator do not observe this commandment. Whatever a person honors and serves more than God becomes a god to them. And therefore, Saint Chrysostom says in his commentary on Matthew: "The evil to which a person is a servant is to him a god." So, if any man should say, "I cannot tell whether I love God more or less than the thing God forbids me to love," let him know that in a case of necessity, the thing a person loves least is that which he is most willing to lose; and that which he truly loves is that which he keeps and preserves. 

Just as merchants do: if, when they are in danger of drowning, they willingly cast their merchandise into the sea to save their lives, they show they love their lives more than their merchandise. Likewise, consider this: if on any occasion you would rather lose your temporal <note>worldly or temporary</note> things, or suffer any loss or hindrance in them—such as in your money, your houses, or your

### Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven Image, etc.

<image-desc>Decorative initial T at the start of the paragraph.</image-desc>
You shall make for yourself no image carved out of stone or wood, or any other material that may be shaped into any figure or picture, or in any other manner whatsoever, *that is in heaven above*, such as the angels, the sun, the moon, or the stars; *nor in the earth beneath*, such as men and other creatures, as the Egyptians do; *nor in the waters, such as fish*. honor the image of God <note>This sentence continues from the previous page</note>. By doing good to men, we serve and honor the image of God. For the image of God is in every man, but the resemblance or likeness of God is not in everyone; it is only in those whose thoughts are pure and whose souls are humble.

But if we want to truly honor God, we must give place to the truth. That is to say, we do good to men who are made in the image of God. We show honor to God when we give food to those who are hungry, drink to those who are thirsty, and clothes to those who are naked. Therefore, what honor do we actually give to God when we serve Him through a block of wood <note>original: "stock"</note> or a stone? Why do we adore lifeless figures <note>original: "idle Figures"</note> without souls, as if there were some divinity in them, while we despise man, who is the true image of God? 

<margin>Chrysostom in Matthew, Homily 5.</margin> 
Saint *Chrysostom* says regarding the Gospel of *Matthew* that the image of God cannot be painted or pictured in gold, but is represented <note>original: "figured"</note> in man. The money of *Caesar* is gold, but the money of God is man. 

Therefore, the Jews were commanded under the Law to destroy all figures and images and devote <note>original: "addict"</note> themselves to the one and only God, as it is written in the first book of *Kings* <note>In older Bibles, 1 Samuel was often titled the First Book of Kings</note>. 

<margin>1 Samuel 7.</margin> 
*Samuel* said to the entire house of *Israel*: "*If you return to the Lord with all your heart, and remove all your foreign gods from among you, and commit your heart to the Lord and serve Him only, He will deliver you from the hands of the Philistines.*" 

Much less, then, should Christians depend on such signs and images, which even the Jews did not use. Instead, they ought to lift up their hearts <note>original: "affections"</note> toward Christ, who sits at the right hand of God.

<meta>catchword: An</meta>

<summary>The author argues that human beings are the true "image of God" and that serving others is the only valid way to honor that image, contrasting this with the "idle" worship of statues. It cites Saint Chrysostom and the Old Testament to argue that Christians should avoid physical icons and focus their devotion on Christ in heaven.</summary>

### An Exposition of the Third Commandment.

->*You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, etc.* <note>original French: "Tu ne prendras point le nom du Seigneur ton Dieu en vain, &c."</note><-

->You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, etc.<-

In this commandment, we are forbidden to swear falsely, vainly, and out of habit <note>original: "by custome"</note>, as it is written in Leviticus 19 <note>The author attributes the following quote to Leviticus 19:12, though the specific wording regarding the "plague" and "custom of swearing" is found in the deuterocanonical book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 23:11.</note>: *The man who is accustomed to swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall not depart from his house.* An oath acknowledges <note>original: "confesseth"</note> that God knows the truth, and its purpose is to confirm a doubtful matter; for an oath is an act of God’s service. Therefore, those who swear by the elements <note>referring to physical things like air, earth, or fire, rather than God</note> commit a sin. This is the reason why Jesus Christ forbids us to swear by anything—neither by heaven, nor by the earth, or anything else—but directs that our speech should be "Yes, yes" and "No, no," and whatever is more than this is sin. And Saint *James* says in the fifth chapter of his epistle: *Above all things, my brethren, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath, lest you fall into condemnation.*

[The servant of the] Lord must be careful of four things: The first is to cease from all earthly and worldly labors; the second, not to sin; the third, not to be idle regarding good works; and the fourth, to do those things that are for the good and benefit of the soul. Regarding the first duty, it is said: *In six days shall you labor and do all that you have to do, but the seventh is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; in it you shall do no manner of work.* And in Exodus it is said: *Keep my Sabbath, for it is holy; he who pollutes it shall die the death.* <note>original: "die the death," a biblical idiom meaning to be certainly put to death</note> In the Book of Numbers, we read that one of the children of Israel was seen gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. He was brought before Moses, who did not know what course to take in the matter; the Lord said to Moses: *This man shall certainly be put to death; all the people shall stone him with stones, and he shall die.* God desired that his Sabbath be kept with such reverence that the children of Israel did not even dare to gather Manna on that day, even when it was given to them from heaven.

The second thing which we are to observe is to preserve ourselves from sin, as it is said in Exodus: *Remember to sanctify the day of rest*—that is, to observe it by carefully keeping yourself from sin. Therefore, Saint Augustine says: "It is better to labor and to dig the earth on the Lord’s Day than to be drunk or to commit any other sins; for sin is a <term>servile work</term>, by which a man serves the devil." <note>term: servile work; traditionally refers to manual labor forbidden on the Sabbath, but here Augustine uses it metaphorically to describe sin as a form of slavery to Satan</note> Again, he says that it is better to labor productively <note>original: "with profit"</note> than to wander and roam about idly. For the Day of the Lord was not ordained so that a man should cease from worldly good works only to give himself over to sin, but rather so that he should devote himself to spiritual labors, which are better than worldly [labors...]

## An Exposition of the Fifth Commandment.

### These Commandments tell us how we are to behave toward our neighbors.

->*Not understanding only of outward reverence, etc.* <note>original: "Non sentend tant solament de la reverentia de fora, & c." The original is in the Waldensian/Occitan language.</note><-

->Honor your father and your mother, etc.<-

We are not to understand these words as if the requirement concerned only outward reverence; it also concerns the fulfillment of their needs and providing things necessary for them. Therefore, we are to do what is enjoined in this Commandment because of the honor that is due to fathers and mothers. We receive from them three excellent gifts: our existence, our nourishment, and our instruction—which we are never able to fully repay.

### An Exposition on the 6th Commandment.

*In this commandment, homicide is specifically forbidden, etc.* <note>original Occitan: "En aquest Commandament es desfen du ſpecialment l'homicidi, &c."</note>

->Thou shalt not kill.<-

Murder is especially forbidden in this commandment: but more generally, it forbids hurting our neighbor in any manner whatsoever, such as with words, detractions <note>speaking ill of someone to damage their reputation</note>, injuries, or deeds, such as striking our neighbor. Of the first sort it is said in *Matthew 5:22: Whoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of judgment.* And *Saint James* says in *Chapter 1:20: The wrath of man does not produce the righteousness of God.* And *Saint Paul* says in *Ephesians 3 <note>The text cites Chapter 3, but this verse is actually Ephesians 4:26.</note>: Let not the sun go down upon your anger.* He that is angry with his brother without cause is worthy of judgment; but not he that is angry upon a just occasion. For if a man should not be angry sometimes, the doctrine would not be profitable, neither would judgment be discerned, nor sin punished. And therefore, just anger is the mother of discipline; and those who in such a case are not angry, sin. For that patience that is without reason is the seed of vices; it

# An Exposition of the 8th Commandment.

->*In this Commandment is totally forbidden theft and fraud regarding the things of others, etc.* <note>original Occitan: "En aquest Commandament es deffendu totalment furt et fraud de cofas ftragnas, &c."</note><-

->Thou shalt not steal.<-

In this Commandment we are forbidden all manner of theft and all unlawful means to get for ourselves the goods of another by fraud, greed <note>original: "auarice"</note>, injury, or violence. For they are not only thieves who take the goods of another, but also those who command them to do so, those who receive thieves into their houses, and those who buy stolen goods and knowingly make a profit from them. All those who do such things, and those who consent to them, shall suffer equal punishment. Or, if you find anything and do not restore it, you have robbed your neighbor; for you are bound to make restitution of what you have found.

Those who deprive their subjects of their goods and commodities—as lords are accustomed to do by imposing unjust charges and taxations, overburdening the poor by their wicked schemes <term>inventions: contrivances or plots</term>, and imprisoning or many times even tormenting them to death if they refuse to do it, and so taking from them their goods unjustly—they are thieves. Of these the Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Eſay"</note> speaks in Chapter 1:23: *Your princes are rebellious and companions of thieves; everyone loves bribes and follows after rewards.* 

They are also thieves who withhold the wages of the laborer by fraud. Of such people it is said in the 19th chapter of Leviticus: *The wages of him who is hired shall not remain with you all night until the morning.* And as Saint James speaks in his fifth chapter: *You have heaped treasure together for the...* <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page provides an exposition of the Eighth Commandment, defining theft broadly to include receiving stolen goods, failing to return lost items, unjust taxation by rulers, and withholding laborers' wages.</summary>

They are also thieves who strive to profit through fraud, deceiving men in their wares and merchandise by selling the bad as good. Likewise, gamblers <note>original: "Gamesters"</note> are thieves, as they invite others to gamble out of greed <note>original: "auarice"</note>—the root of all evil—leading to robbery <note>original: "rapine"</note>, lying, vain and idle speech, oaths, blasphemies against God, bad examples, and the loss of time. Thus, by gambling, a man unjustly winds himself into the possession of another man’s goods.

The slanderer deserves to be hated by both God and man. The lash of a whip leaves marks in the flesh, but the stroke of the tongue breaks the bones.

## An Exposition of the 10th Commandment.

In this Commandment is forbidden the covetousness of the goods of others, etc. <note>original Occitan: "En aquest Commandement es defendua la Cubititia de cui li ben, &c."</note>

->**You shall not covet, etc.**<-

In this Commandment is forbidden the covetous desire for all goods—that is, for a wife, servants, fields, vineyards, houses, etc. It also forbids the lust <note>original: "concupiscence"</note> of the eyes and of the flesh. The lust of the flesh is like running water, but the lust of the eyes is like earth, by reason of our earthly affections. And just as physical mud is made from water and earth, so from lust is made the spiritual filth and "dunghill of the soul," which makes a person hateful to God. From this arises the pride of life, which like a violent

## The Conclusion of the Exposition of the Commandments.

->*These are the ten Commandments of the Law, etc.* <note>original Occitan: "Aquesti son li dies Commandament de la Ley, &c."</note><-

These are the ten Commandments of the Law, of which the first part concerns our duty to God, and the latter part concerns our duty toward our neighbor. And whoever wishes to be saved must keep these Commandments. Many excellent blessings are promised to those who keep these Commandments, and many grievous and horrible curses <note>original: "maledictions"</note> are promised to those who transgress them, as seen in *Deuteronomy 28*. 

If we truly acknowledge our sins, we know that we are far from God; for salvation is far from sinners, and the knowledge of sin brings us to repentance, for no one can repent who does not know their sin. The first step <note>original: "degree"</note> toward salvation is the knowledge of sin. Therefore, acknowledging our fault, we approach the throne of God's grace with confidence and confess our sins; for He is faithful and just to pardon our sins, to cleanse us from all iniquity, and to bring us to the life of grace. Amen.

### CHAPTER V.

## An Exposition of the Waldenses and Albigenses upon the Lord's Prayer.

<margin>Taken out of a book of the Waldenses, titled *The Treasure of Faith*.</margin>

<image-desc>An ornate decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a seated child or cherub holding a large vessel, set within a frame of foliage and fruit.</image-desc>

**Saint Augustine**, having been requested by a spiritual daughter of his to teach her how to pray, has said and written this: that a multitude of words is not necessary in prayer. Rather, to pray much is to be fervent in prayer. Therefore, to be "long" in prayer is to present necessary things with unnecessary <note>original: "superfluous"</note> words. To pray much is to earnestly seek <note>original: "solicit"</note> what we pray for with a proper decency and affection of heart, which is better done by tears than by words; because God, who sees the secrets of our heart, is more moved by a deep groan or sigh, and by the laments <note>original: "plaints"</note> and tears that come from the heart, than by a thousand words.

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, specifically addressing the quality of prayer over quantity and the idea that a virtuous life is itself a form of constant prayer.</meta>

But there are many today who resemble the Pagans, whom Christ did not want His disciples to be like; for they think and believe they will be heard more for using many words in their prayers. Because of this, they lose much time under the pretense of prayer. Job says (and experience also proves) that a person is never in the same state in this life, but is now inclined to do one thing and immediately after to do another. Therefore, no one can keep his mind and spirit focused and attentive to prayer for an entire day or an entire night together, unless God gives the special assistance of His grace. 

If a person does not have his heart fixed upon what he is saying, he loses his time because he prays in vain; his soul is troubled, and his mind wanders elsewhere. Consequently, God has appointed other exercises for His servants—virtuous, spiritual, and physical <note>original: "corporall"</note>—in which a person may normally occupy himself, sometimes in one and sometimes in another, either for themselves or for their neighbors. They should have their hearts lifted up to God with all their power, so that they may not be idle. Therefore, the person who lives well, according to the will of God and the doctrine of His saints, prays always. For every good work is a good prayer to God. 

And as for you who read this, know that all the prayers of the Old and New Testaments agree with this; no prayer can be pleasing to God if it does not refer to this <note>referring to the principles of the Lord's Prayer</note> in some way or another. Therefore, every Christian ought to apply himself to understand and learn this prayer, which Christ himself taught with His own mouth.

Therefore, those who live in the kingdom of grace—through which we must pass if we wish to enter the kingdom of glory—will undoubtedly reign in the kingdom of glory; and no one can reign there by any other means.

->**Thy will be done in Earth as it is in Heaven.**<-

A person cannot strive for <note>original: "affect," meaning to aim for or aspire to</note>, desire, or do any better thing in this life than to endeavor with all their wit and understanding, and with all their heart, to do the will of God, just as the angels do it in heaven. Now, to do the will of God is to renounce oneself—that is to say, one’s own personal will—and to arrange and employ everything that is within one's own soul and heart, or that is outside of oneself in worldly matters, according to the Law of God and the doctrine of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. It also means to be well satisfied with whatever it pleases God to do or permit, both in adversity and prosperity. 

There are many who think they should be excused because they say they do not know the will of God. But these people deceive themselves. For the will of God is written, plainly revealed, and proven by the Word of God, which they refuse to read or understand. Therefore, the Apostle says, *“Do not conform yourselves to those who love the world, but be reformed and renewed in the truth of your understanding, so that you may know what the will of God is.”* And again, *“This is the will of God: your sanctification.”* <note>original: "sanctification," the process of being made holy or set apart for God</note> There is no work that is small if it is done with a willing and fervent spirit. ->**Give us this day our daily bread.**<-

We may understand two kinds of bread here: physical <note>original: "Corporall"</note> and spiritual. By physical bread, we are to understand our food, drinks, clothing, and all things necessary for the body, without which we cannot live naturally. The spiritual bread is the Word of God and the body of Christ, without which the soul cannot live. And of this bread, Christ spoke to his disciples: 

> *Whoever shall eat of this bread shall live eternally.* 

And therefore, it is the duty of every person to ask for this bread at God's hands in all humility—for He is the one who can give it—saying: "O our Father, grant us the grace and favor that we may obtain through our honest <note>original: "iust"</note> labor the bread that is necessary for our bodies, and to use it with sobriety and moderation, always yielding you thanks and praise, and that we may charitably bestow some part of it upon the poor."

It should not seem, or be, grievous to any man to forgive his neighbor those offenses he has committed against him. ->*Lead us not into temptation, etc.*<-
<note>original: "Non nos amenar en tentation, &c." written in Occitan.</note>

->**And lead us not into temptation, etc.**<-

We are not to pray to God that He should never allow us to be tempted. For the Apostle Saint Paul says, *None shall be crowned unless he fights against the world, the flesh, and the devil.* And Saint James says *that he is blessed who endures temptation.* For when he has passed his trial, he shall receive a crown of life. 

No man can resist the power of the devil without the grace of God. We must therefore pray with all humility, devotion, and continual requests to our heavenly Father that we do not fall into temptations—or rather, that in battling them, we may gain the victory and the crown through His grace, which He has prepared to give us. We are not to believe that He hears the devil sooner, or more willingly, than the Christian; and according to what the Apostle Saint Paul says, *God is faithful, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond our power.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 10:13.</note>

# What the *Waldensians* and *Albigensians* have believed and taught concerning the Sacraments.

### CHAPTER VI.

->A Sacrament, according to the saying of Saint Augustine, etc.<-
<note>original: "Sacrament second le dire de Sanct Augustin, &c." written in Occitan.</note>

A Sacrament, according to the saying of Saint *Augustine* in his book *The City of God*, is an invisible grace represented by a visible thing. Or, a Sacrament is a sign of a holy thing. There is a great difference between the bare Sacrament and the cause of the Sacrament, even as much as between a sign and the thing signified. For the cause of the Sacrament is Divine grace, and the

For by his cruel Passion and the shedding <note>original: "effusion"</note> of his blood, he has obtained grace and righteousness for all the faithful. There are two Sacraments: one of water, and the other of nourishment—that is to say, of Bread and Wine.

The first is called Baptism, which means in our language the washing with water, either from a river or a spring <note>original: "fountaine"</note>. It must be administered *in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost*, so that first, by the grace of God the Father looking upon his Son, by the participation of Jesus Christ who has bought us, and by the renewal of the Holy Spirit who imprints a living <note>original: "lively"</note> faith in our hearts, the sins of those who are baptized are pardoned and they are received into grace; and afterwards, having persevered in that grace, they are saved in Jesus Christ.

[Christ was] baptized to fulfill all righteousness, just as it was his will to be circumcised, and just as he commanded his Apostles to baptize.

The things that are not necessary in baptism are exorcisms, ceremonial breathings, the signs of the cross made upon the infant (on either the breast or the forehead), salt put into the mouth, spit put into the ears and nostrils, the anointing of the breast, the monk’s hood <note>original: "Cowle"</note>, the anointing with holy oil <note>original: "Chreſme"</note> upon the head, and various similar things consecrated by the Bishop. Other unnecessary rituals include putting a candle <note>original: "Taper"</note> in the child’s hands, dressing them in a white garment <note>original: "vestment"</note>, the blessing of the water, and dipping the child three times in the water. All these things used in the administration of the Sacrament are not necessary; they are neither part of the essence of the sacrament nor required for it. In fact, many people use these rituals as an occasion for error and superstition rather than for spiritual growth <note>original: "edification"</note> toward salvation.

Now, this baptism is a visible and physical <note>original: "materiall"</note> act, which in itself makes the person neither good nor evil. This is shown in the Scriptures by the examples of *Simon Magus* <note>A man in the Book of Acts who was baptized but remained "full of bitterness and captive to sin"</note> and *Saint Paul*. When baptism is administered in a full congregation of the faithful, its purpose is so that the person received into the Church should be recognized and held by everyone as a Christian brother or sister. It also allows the entire congregation to pray for them, asking that they may be a Christian in their heart just as they are outwardly considered to be one. It is for this reason that we present our children for baptism. This duty belongs to those to whom the children are closest, such as their parents or those to whom God has given this charitable responsibility.
