The source <note>original: "cause"</note> of the Sacrament exists powerfully, essentially, and by authority in God, and meritoriously in Jesus Christ. For by his cruel Passion and the pouring out <note>original: "effusion"</note> of his blood, he has obtained grace and righteousness for all the faithful. But the substance <note>original: "thing it selfe"</note> of the Sacrament is in the soul of the faithful through participation, as Saint Paul says: *We have been made partakers of Christ.* It is present in the Word of the Gospel by proclamation <note>original: "annunciation"</note> or manifestation, and in the Sacraments, it is present sacramentally. For the Lord Jesus has lent or given these helps of the outward Sacraments so that ministers, when instructing in the faith, might adapt <note>original: "accommodate"</note> themselves to human weakness and thus better build up <note>original: "edifie"</note> the people through the Word of the Gospel.

There are two Sacraments: one of water, and the other of nourishment—that is to say, of Bread and Wine.

The first is called Baptism, which in our language means the washing with water, whether from a river or a spring <note>original: "fountaine"</note>. It must be administered *In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit*, so that—first, by the grace of God the Father looking upon his Son; and by participation in Jesus Christ, who has bought us; and by the renewal of the Holy Spirit, who imprints a living <note>original: "liuely"</note> faith in our hearts—the sins of those who are baptized are pardoned. They are received into grace, and afterwards, having persevered in it, they are saved in Jesus Christ.

<header>The Doctrine of the Book, Part 1.</header>

### *Of the Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ.*

Just as Baptism, which is received visibly, serves as an enrollment into the number of faithful Christians—carrying within itself a profession <note>original: "protestation"; in this context, a formal declaration of faith</note> and promise to follow Jesus Christ, to keep his holy ordinances, and to live according to his holy Gospel—so the holy Supper and Communion of our blessed Savior (the breaking of bread and the giving of thanks) is a visible communion made with the members of Jesus Christ. For those who take and break one and the same bread are one and the same body—that is to say, the Body of Jesus Christ—and they are members of one another, ingrafted and planted in him. To him they vow <note>original: "protest"</note> and promise to persevere in his service to their lives' end, never departing from the faith of the Gospel and the union which they have all promised through Jesus Christ. And therefore, just as all the members of a body are nourished with one and the same food <note>original: "viands"</note>, and all the faithful take one and the same spiritual bread of the Word of Life, the Gospel of Salvation, so they all live by one and the same Spirit and one and the same faith.

This Sacrament of the Communion of the Body and Blood of Christ is called in Greek *Eucharistia* <note>original: "Eucharistia"; literally "thanksgiving." The text translates it here as "Good Grace," likely connecting the Greek roots "eu" (good) and "charis" (grace)</note>, that is to say, "Good Grace." Saint Matthew testifies to this in his 26th chapter, saying, *Jesus took bread and blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body."* and Saint Luke, Chapter 22: *“This is my body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise, he took the cup and blessed it, saying, “This cup is the new Testament in my blood, which is shed for you.”*

<summary>This page defines the Lord's Supper (Communion) as a visible sign of unity among believers, comparing it to the enrollment of Baptism and emphasizing the spiritual nourishment of the Gospel.</summary>

This Sacrament was instituted by divine ordinance to signify perfectly to us the spiritual nourishment of mankind in God. By this means, the spiritual life is preserved, and without it, that life decays—the Truth itself saying: *If you do not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, there shall be no life in you.* Concerning this Sacrament, we must hold the following, according to the testimony of the Scriptures: we must confess simply and with a pure heart that the bread which Christ took at his Last Supper—which he blessed, broke, and gave to his disciples to eat—was left as a remembrance of his Passion <note>original: "Passion"; the suffering and death of Jesus</note> to be received through the ministry of his faithful pastors. In its own nature, it is true bread. By the pronoun "*This*," the following sacramental proposition is demonstrated: "*This is my Body*." These words are not to be understood identically (referring to a numerical identity <note>The author is arguing against the idea that the bread and Christ's physical body are the exact same physical object</note>), but sacramentally, really, and truly—though not in a measurable or physical way. It is the same body of Christ that sits in heaven at the right hand of his Father. Every faithful receiver must lift the eyes of their understanding to him, elevating their heart on high, and so eat him spiritually and sacramentally through an assured faith. The same is to be understood regarding the Sacrament of the Cup.

Saint Augustine says that the eating and drinking of this Sacrament must be understood spiritually. For Christ says, *The words that I speak are spirit and life.* And Saint Jerome says, *The flesh of Christ is to be understood in two ways: either spiritually*—of which Christ says in John 6:55, *My flesh is food <note>original: "meate"</note> indeed, and my blood is drink indeed*—*or it is to be understood as that flesh which was crucified and buried.* Regarding spiritual eating, Christ says: *He that shall eat my flesh, and drink*

There is also a twofold manner of eating: the one is sacramental, and in this way both the good and the bad eat; the other is spiritual, and in this way only the good eat. And therefore, Saint Augustine says, *What is it to eat Christ?* It is not only to receive his body in the Sacrament, for many eat him unworthily—those who will not dwell in him, nor have him dwell in them. Instead, he eats him spiritually who continues in the truth of Christ. And therefore, to eat the sacramental bread is to eat the Body of Christ in a figure <note>original: "in a figure"; symbolically or as a representation</note>. Jesus Christ himself said, *Nevertheless, as often as you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.* For if this eating were not figurative, Christ would be always bound to such a thing; for it is necessary that spiritual eating should be continual. As Saint Augustine speaks: *He who eats Christ in truth is he who believes in him.* <note>Augustine's famous principle: "Believe, and you have eaten."</note> For Christ says *that to eat him is to dwell in him.* In the celebration of this Sacrament, prayer is profitable, as is the preaching of the Word in the common tongue <note>original: "vulgar tongue"; the language spoken by the ordinary people rather than Latin</note>—such preaching as may edify and is agreeable to the Evangelical Law <note>The teachings of the Gospel</note>—to the end that peace and charity might increase among the people. But other things that are in use these days in the Church of Rome, and among those who are members of it, do not belong to the Sacrament at all.

# What the *Waldenses* and *Albigenses* have taught concerning *Marriage*.

## C H A P T E R  V I I.

<margin>In the book titled *The Spiritual Almanac*, folio 50.</margin>
Marriage is holy, having been instituted by *God* in the beginning of the *world*. Therefore, it is an honorable thing when it is kept as it should be in all purity: when the *husband*, who is the head of the *wife*, loves her, protects her <note>original: "keeps her"</note>, and conducts himself honestly toward her, being faithful and loyal to her; and that the woman, for her part—who was made to be a helper to man—be subject to her *husband*, obeying him in whatever is good and honoring him as *God* has commanded her. She should take care of his household affairs, keeping herself not only from wrongdoing, but from all appearance of evil, continuing faithful and loyal to him. Both of them should persevere in what is good according to the will of *God*, working together to earn their living by honest and lawful means, wronging no one, and instructing those children whom *God* has given them in the fear and teaching <note>original: "doctrine"</note> of the *Lord*, so that they may live as our *Lord* has commanded them.

Prayer and fasting are profitable when there is a question of the celebration of matrimony, as are the reasons, instructions, and advice <note>original: "advertisements"</note> concerning it. But the imposition of hands, the ritual bindings <note>original: "ligatures"</note> made with the priest's stole <note>original: "stoole"; a liturgical vestment. This refers to the practice of wrapping the priest's stole around the couple's joined hands</note>, and other things commonly observed therein by custom—without the express word [of God]...

## CHAPTER 9.
### The Conclusion of this Book.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'B' within a square frame, decorated with a figure and floral patterns.</image-desc>

Based on what is contained in this book, and what has been faithfully gathered out of the books the *Waldenses* <note>original: "Waldenfes"</note> have left to us, it appears that the *doctrine* which they maintain in these days—those who make a profession of reformation—has been maintained by them for many ages before those who are enemies of it would even acknowledge it. There is nothing in all that is delivered here that either contradicts <note>original: "repugne"</note> the Word of *God* or is not altogether conformable to that which is taught in the reformed churches. For the *Waldenses* and *Albigenses* <note>original: "Albingenfes"</note> have known the necessity of instructing their children by making use of such familiar catechisms as have been practiced in the early church <note>original: "Primatiue Church"</note>. They have confessed their sins to the one and only *God* with terms of true humility, proofs of great zeal, and a holy confidence in the mercy of *God* through His Son and our Savior, *Jesus Christ*. They have acknowledged the Law of *God* as the only rule for their obedience. Confessing themselves to be far distant from that perfection which ought to be in us to appear blameless before the face of *God*, they have used their own imperfection as an occasion to seek the only righteousness of the Son of *God*, our Redeemer. The Law serves them as a looking glass <note>A mirror.</note> to make them aware of their stains and blemishes, and to send them to *Jesus Christ*, the true basin <note>original: "lauor"; a washing bowl or laver.</note> or washing pool.

<summary>This concluding chapter asserts that the doctrines of the Waldenses and Albigenses are ancient, biblical, and fully consistent with the teachings of the Protestant Reformation. It highlights their use of catechisms, confession to God alone, and reliance on Christ's righteousness rather than their own perfection.</summary>

## CHAPTER III.

### On the Instruction of Children
<note>original: "Del' Enseignament de li filli"</note>

*Children who are born to carnal parents must be returned to God, etc.*
<note>original: "Li filli liqual naisson a li pairons carnals deuon esser rendu, &c."</note>

### Of the Instruction of Children.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure, possibly a child or angel, surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>Children born of their carnal parents must be made spiritual unto God by discipline and by instruction, as it is said in the 30th chapter of Ecclesiasticus, verse 1 <note>Ecclesiasticus (also known as Sirach) is a book of wisdom from the Apocrypha, frequently quoted in medieval and early modern moral treatises</note>: *“He who loves his son causes him to feel the rod often, so that he may have joy in him in the end, and so that he does not knock at the door of his neighbor <note>original: "knocke not at the doore of his Neighbour"—meaning to beg for bread or help due to a lack of upbringing</note>. He who chastises his son shall have joy in him and shall rejoice because of him among his acquaintances. He who teaches his son grieves his enemy, and he shall rejoice in him before his enemies. Though his father dies, yet he is as if he were not dead, for he has left behind him one who is like himself; while he lived, he saw and rejoiced in him, and when he died, he was not sorrowful. For he left behind him an avenger against his enemies and one who shall repay kindness to his friends.”* Do not despair of your child when he is unwilling to receive correction, or if he does not quickly prove to be good; for the laborer does not gather the fruits of the earth as soon as it is sown, but he waits for a fitting time.

A man must also keep a careful eye over his daughters. Do you have daughters? Keep them within, and see that they do not wander. For Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, was corrupted <note>referring to the biblical account in Genesis 34</note> by being seen by strangers.

### CHAPTER V.

### Concerning Ecclesiastical Correction.
<note>original: "De la Correction Ecclesiastica"</note>
->*Likewise, corrections should be made by the introduction of fear, etc.*<-
<note>original: "Semblablement deuon eſtre faict, corrections per induction de temors, &c."</note>

## Of Ecclesiastical Correction.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'S' set within a square woodcut border featuring stylized leafy vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>
In the same way, corrections are to be used to keep people in fear [of sinning], so that those who are unfaithful may be punished and separated <note>This refers to excommunication or temporary removal from the community</note>—whether because of their wicked lives, their erroneous beliefs, their lack of charity, or any combination of these evils found in a person. Now, our Savior tells us that it is necessary to use such corrections, saying:
> *If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone; and if he repents, forgive him.* <note>Luke 17:3</note>
The Apostle [Paul] confirms the same, saying to the Galatians:
> *If a man is caught in any sin, you who are spiritual should instruct him in a spirit of gentleness.* <note>Galatians 6:1</note>

But because not everyone receives these corrections with a charitable heart, our Lord teaches our spiritual guides what course they should take, saying:
> *If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.* <note>Matthew 18:16. The original text uses the word "justified" here</note>
Our Lord’s meaning is that this applies if the fault is not public or known by many people. However, it is not so if the sin is manifest <term>manifest: clearly apparent or public</term> and known to everyone. In such a case, the punishment must be made public as well. The Apostle tells us as much in the first epistle to Timothy, chapter 5, verse 20:
> *Those who are sinning, rebuke in the presence of all, so that the rest also may fear.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'B' featuring floral scrollwork and two bird-like figures within a square frame.</image-desc>

That is to say, tell the Guides <note>In this context, "Guides" refers to the elders or pastors who oversee the congregation's spiritual life.</note> by whom the Church is ruled and preserved, so that the person may be punished, especially for contumacy <note>term: contumacy — stubborn refusal to obey authority, particularly a legal or ecclesiastical summons.</note>.

In modern English bibles, this is usually translated as "a Gentile and a tax collector"—people who were traditionally excluded from the religious community.</note>; that is to say, let him be deprived of all aid from the Church, from the Ministry, from the company of the Church, and from union with it.

### CHAPTER VII.

->Of Marriage.<-
->*Marriage should be performed according to the degrees that God has permitted, etc.*<-
<note>original Occitan: "Le Mariage se deo far second li gra liqual Dio a permes, &c."</note>

->Of Marriage.<-

Marriages are to be performed according to the degrees <note>In this context, "degrees" refers to the degrees of kinship or consanguinity—how closely related two people are by blood.</note> permitted by God, but not according to those he has forbidden. However, we should have no worries of conscience regarding those rules made by the Pope, even if a man has paid him no money for a dispensation <note>term: dispensation — a formal exemption from a church law or a vow, which in the medieval and early modern period could often be purchased from the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. For whatever God has not forbidden can be done without the Pope’s permission. The bond of holy Matrimony must not be formed without the consent of the parents of both parties, for children belong to their parents.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*The tavern is the fountain of sin, the school of the Devil, etc.*<-

A tavern is the fountain of sin and the school of the Devil; it performs "wonders" that suit such a place. It is God's custom to show His power in His Church and to work miracles—that is to say, to give sight to the blind, to make the lame walk, and to make the mute

...makes them go to hell. A man sins in dancing in various ways: in his pace (for all his steps are numbered), in his touch, in his ornaments, in his hearing, sight, speech, and other vanities. Therefore, we will prove first by the Scripture, and afterwards by various other reasons, how wicked a thing it is to dance. 

The first testimony that we will produce is that which we read in the Gospel of Mark, chapter 6. <note>original: "Marke 6" — This refers to the story of Salome dancing before King Herod, which resulted in the beheading of John the Baptist.</note> It pleased Herod so well that it cost John the Baptist his life. The second is in Exodus 32. When Moses, coming near to the congregation, saw the [golden] calf, he threw the stone tablets from him and broke them at the foot of the mountain; afterward, it cost twenty-three thousand people their lives. 

Furthermore, the ornaments which women wear in their dances are like crowns for the many victories which the devil has won against the children of God. For the devil has not only one sword in the dance, but as many as there are beautiful and well-adorned persons in the dance. For the words of a woman are a glittering sword. Therefore, that place is much to be feared where the enemy has so many swords, since even one of his swords alone is to be feared. 

Again, the devil in this place strikes with a sharpened sword, for women do not come willingly to the dance if they are not painted and adorned; this painting and decoration is like a grindstone upon which the devil sharpens his sword. Those who deck out and adorn their daughters are like those who put dry wood on a fire so that it may burn better. For such women kindle the fire of lust <note>original: "luxury" — In Early Modern English, "luxury" (from the Latin *luxuria*) specifically meant lechery or sexual lust rather than material wealth.</note> in the hearts of men. Just as Samson’s foxes set fire to the Philistines' grain, <note>A reference to Judges 15, where Samson ties torches to foxes' tails to destroy his enemies' crops.</note> so these women have fire in their faces, and in their gestures and actions, their glances and wanton words, by which

--- Page 474 ---
<meta>This page continues the Waldensian critique of dancing, specifically how it serves as a tool for the devil to tempt men through women and leads to the breaking of the Ten Commandments.</meta>

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>Chapter 9. Waldenses & Albingenses.</header>

They consume the wealth of men. Furthermore, in the dance, the devil uses the strongest armor he has, for his most powerful weapons are women. This is made clear to us by the fact that the devil chose a woman to deceive the first man [Adam]. So did Balaam, so that the children of Israel might be rejected. Through a woman, he caused Samson, David, and Absalom to sin. The devil tempts men through women in three ways: that is to say, by touch, by the eye, and by the ear. By these three means, he tempts foolish men into dancing: by touching their hands, by their beholding of beauty, and by their hearing of songs and music. 

Furthermore, those who dance break the promise and agreement which they made with God in baptism, when their godfathers promised on their behalf that they should renounce the devil and all his pomp. For dancing is the pomp of the devil, and he who dances maintains his pomp and sings his Mass. For the woman who sings in the dance is the devil’s prioress, those who respond are the clerks, the spectators are the parishioners, the music represents the bells, and the fiddlers are the ministers of the devil. For just as when hogs have strayed, if the hog-herd calls one, they all assemble together; so the devil causes one woman to sing in the dance or to play an instrument, and immediately all the dancers gather together. 

Furthermore, in a dance, a person breaks the Ten Commandments of God. As for the first: *“You shall have no other gods but me,”* etc. <note>Exodus 20:3</note> For in dancing, a person serves that individual whom he most desires to serve; and therefore Saint Jerome <note>original: "Sant Ierom"</note> says, "Every man's God is that which he serves and loves best." He sins against the second commandment when he makes an idol of the one he loves.

<meta>This page continues the Waldensian critique of dancing, specifically mapping how the practice leads to the breaking of each of the Ten Commandments, following the discussion of the first and second commandments from the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>66</page-num>

<header>The Doctrine of the Book 2.</header>

Against the third commandment: oaths <note>original: "oathes," referring to swearing or taking God's name in vain</note> are frequent among dancers. Against the fourth: for by dancing, the Sabbath day is profaned. Against the fifth: for in the dance, parents are many times dishonored when many bargains <note>This likely refers to secret marriage engagements or social contracts made without parental consent</note> are made without their counsel. Against the sixth: a man kills in dancing, for everyone who stands to please another kills the soul as often as he persuades them toward lust. Against the seventh: for the person who dances, whether male or female, commits adultery with the person they lust after. *For he who looks on a woman and lusts after her has already committed adultery in his heart.* <note>Matthew 5:28</note> Against the eighth commandment: a man sins in dancing when he withdraws the heart of another from God. Against the ninth: when in dancing he speaks falsely against the truth. Against the tenth: when women strive for the ornaments of others, and men covet the wives, daughters, and servants of their neighbors.

Again, a man may prove how great an evil dancing is by the multitude of sins that accompany those who dance; for they dance without measure or number. And therefore says Saint Augustine, "The miserable dancer does not know that for as many paces as he makes in dancing, he makes just as many leaps to hell."

They sin in their ornaments <note>Clothing, jewelry, and physical decorations</note> in a five-fold manner. First, by being proud of them. Secondly, by inflaming the hearts of those who behold them. Thirdly, when they make those ashamed who do not have similar ornaments, giving them occasion to covet the same. Fourthly, by making women demanding <note>original: "importunate"</note> in requesting similar ornaments from their husbands. # THE THIRD BOOK OF THE THIRD PART OF THE HISTORY
## of the Waldenses and Albigenses; containing a refutation of various doctrines of the Church of Rome.

### CHAPTER I.
### A Treatise by the Waldenses and Albigenses regarding Antichrist.

<margin>
This book on Antichrist is found in an old manuscript which contains many sermons by pastors dated to the year 1120. Therefore, it was written before Waldo <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1205) was the leader of the Waldensian movement; the author notes this text is older than Waldo himself.</note> and around the time of Peter Bruis <note>Peter of Bruys (died c. 1131) was a popular French reformer and preacher.</note>, who taught in Languedoc. He was burned at Saint-Gilles before Waldo departed from Lyon. This treatise was afterward preserved by the Waldenses of the Alps, from whom we received it, along with several others.
</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'A' depicting two scholars or clerics seated and reading books.</image-desc>

**A**ntichrist is the falsehood or untruth of eternal damnation, covered with an outward appearance of the truth and the righteousness of Christ and his Spouse <note>The "Spouse" of Christ refers to the Church.</note>. It is opposite to the way of truth, righteousness, faith, hope, and charity, and to a moral life and the ministerial <note>original: "ministeriall verity," referring to the truth practiced by the clergy or the ministry of the church.</note> truth of...

...the Church, administered by false apostles and obstinately defended by both ecclesiastical and secular powers. Or, Antichrist is a delusion which hides the truth of salvation in matters of substance; or it is a fraudulent contradiction against Christ and his Spouse <note>The "Spouse" of Christ refers to the Church.</note>, and every faithful member. It is not any specific person ordained to a certain rank, office, or ministry, but it is that falsehood itself which opposes the truth—which covers and adorns itself with beauty and piety outside the Church of Christ, using names, offices, Scriptures, Sacraments, and various other things. That iniquity which operates in this manner, along with all its ministers, great and small, and all those who follow them with a wicked heart and hoodwinked eyes—this congregation, I say, taken as a whole, is called Antichrist, or Babylon, or the fourth Beast <note>A reference to the vision in Daniel 7.</note>, or the Whore, or the man of sin, or the son of perdition.

The ministers are called false prophets, lying teachers, the ministers of darkness, the spirit of error, the apocalyptic whore, the mother of fornication, clouds without water, trees without leaves—dead and twice uprooted—waves of a troubled sea, wandering stars, Balaamites <note>Followers of the biblical figure Balaam, often used to signify those who lead others into idolatry for profit.</note>, and Egyptians.

It is called Antichrist because, while being covered and adorned under the pretense <note>original: "colour"</note> of Christ, his Church, and its faithful members, it opposes <note>original: "oppugneth"</note> the salvation purchased by Christ and truly administered in the Church of Christ, of which the faithful are partakers through faith, hope, and charity. Thus it contradicts the truth by the wisdom of the world, by false religion, by counterfeit holiness, by spiritual power, secular tyranny, riches,

Therefore, because it is obvious to everyone that Antichrist cannot appear in any form or fashion whatsoever except when all these things mentioned above are joined together to create a perfect hypocrisy and falsehood—that is to say, involving the worldly-wise, the clergy <note>original: "the Religious"</note>, Pharisees, ministers, and scholars <note>original: "Doctors"</note>, together with secular power and the people of the world. Therefore, it was more easily recognized, destroyed, and kept under control; being unrefined <note>original: "rude"</note> and rustic, it was as yet silent <note>original: "dumb"</note>. 

It lacked the wisdom and the logic to excuse itself or to define and pronounce legal sentences. It did not yet have untruthful ministers, it lacked human laws and statutes, and outwardly it had no religious followers. And therefore, even though it had fallen into error and sin, it had nothing to cover its villainy and the shame of its sin. Because it had neither wealth nor endowments <term>dotations: gifts of land or money given to a church or institution</term>, it could not recruit ministers for its service, nor could it multiply, preserve, or defend its own interests. It lacked secular power and assistance, and could not force or constrain anyone to turn from the truth to falsehood. 

Because so many things were lacking, it could not pollute or scandalize anyone with its deceptions <note>original: "trumperies"</note>; thus, being still young and weak, it could find no place in the Church. ## What the works of Antichrist are.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
The first work of Antichrist is to take away the truth and change it into falsehood, error, and heresy. The second is to cover falsehood with the truth and to confirm an untruth through an appearance of faith and virtue. He also mingles falsehood with spiritual things among those people who are subject to him, whether it is by means of his ministers or the ministry itself. Now, this twofold way of proceeding contains a perfect and most complete malice, which could not be found in any ordinary tyrant.

**Objection.** But what other works proceed from these first?
**Answer.** Those that follow.

## CHAP. II.
### Of invented Purgatory.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring scrolling foliate and floral motifs.</image-desc>

The Purgatory which various priests and monks seek to promote and teach as an Article of our Faith—using many lies and fables—is this: they affirm that after this life, and after the Ascension of Christ into heaven, the souls (especially of those who shall be saved) who have not satisfied the debt for their sins in this life, must endure physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> pains and are cleansed in Purgatory. They claim that after they are cleansed, they leave Purgatory—some sooner, some later, and some not until the Day of Judgment. They teach that all the faithful can and should help these souls after they have departed this life through the bond of charity, using prayers, fasting, charitable works <note>original: "alms-deeds"</note>, and Masses.

Regarding this Purgatory, to satisfy their greed <note>original: "avarice"</note>, many have invented various uncertain things which they have taught and preached. They say that such souls are tormented in this Purgatory, some submerged up to the neck and some to the waist. They even say that sometimes these souls sit and eat at a table and hold banquets, especially during the Feast of All Souls <note>A Christian holy day (November 2) dedicated to prayer for the souls of the deceased who are believed to be in purgatory</note>, when the people are giving generous offerings upon their graves <note>original: "sepulchres"</note>. They also say that sometimes the souls gather the crumbs under the rich men's tables. By these means, and various other similar fantasies <note>original: "dreams"</note>, greed and simony <note>The buying or selling of religious offices or spiritual benefits</note> are increased and multiplied. Their cloisters <note>monasteries or convents</note> are advanced, their lavish temples are built and enlarged, and their altars are multiplied beyond

### CHAPTER III.
### Of the Invocation of Saints.

We are now to speak of prayer to Saints, which certain "great masters" and their followers preach to the people. They extol and publish this with great diligence as an Article of their Faith, affirming that the Saints who are in their celestial home <note>original: "country"</note> are to be prayed to by us in the very same manner that the priests were accustomed to do, and as others among the people do by their instruction, commanding them many other things as aids to their invocation. Through this invocation, authorization, and glorification <note>original: "magnification"</note>, the people believe it in a carnal and erroneous way. They imagine that, just as it is the custom and practice before earthly kings—that when they are angry, those who are not in a temper <note>original: "choller," meaning bitter anger or bile</note> should intercede for others and pacify the king's anger—so the people think it is with God. That is, they believe the Saints appease the wrath of God when he is angry with sinners.

But we are not to believe any such thing; for if it were so, there could be no true conformity between the will of the Saints and the will of God. It would seem that the Saints are not angry with those against whom God is moved to anger. Secondly, by this glorification and invocation of Saints, the people fall into

idolatry, putting their trust more in Saints than in God, and serving them with greater affection than the only God. Secondly, we know and believe that the man Christ Jesus is the Mediator between God and man, and the Advocate to God the Father. He has paid for the sins of those who come to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them (*Hebrews 7:25*). No man comes to the Father except through him. *And whatever you shall ask in my name, that I will do, says he (John 14:13).* He gives to all abundantly and reproaches no man (*James 1:5*). He is our Advocate to God the Father, and he forgives our sins. He offers himself to us by all means before we offer ourselves to him. He is at the door, and he knocks so that we may open to him.

### Chapter 4.

## On Baptism and the Other Sacraments of the Roman Church.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter T featuring intricate scrollwork and floral foliage patterns.</image-desc>

The things that are not necessary in the administration of baptism are the exorcisms, breathings <note>original: "breathings"; refers to the ritual of exsufflation, where the priest blows on the candidate to symbolize the expelling of evil spirits.</note>, the sign of the cross upon the forehead and breast of the infant, the salt put into his mouth, spittle into his ears and nostrils, the anointing of the breast, the monk's cowl <note>original: "Monkes Cowle"; likely referring to the *chrismale*, a white linen cloth or hood placed on the head of the newly baptized.</note>, the anointing with the chrism <term>chrism: a consecrated mixture of oil and balsam used in church rituals</term> upon the crown of his head, and all other things consecrated by the bishop, such as putting the wax candle into his hands, clothing him with a white garment, the blessing of the water, and so forth. All these things used in the administration of this sacrament are unnecessary; they are neither part of the essential substance nor required in the sacrament of baptism. Many people take these rituals as an occasion for error and superstition rather than edification toward salvation, and according to the opinion of some doctors <note>original: "Doctours"; referring to established theologians or "Doctors of the Church."</note>, there is neither power nor profit in them.

->*Of the Chrism or Confirmation.*<-

We are now to speak of the Chrism <term>Chrism: consecrated oil used in rituals like baptism and confirmation</term>, which at this time is called a Sacrament, despite having no basis for it in the Scriptures. First, it is claimed that it must be consecrated by a Bishop and made with olive oil and balsam, applied to the forehead of the baptized person in the shape of a cross, and with these words:

> "I sign you with the sign of the Cross, and confirm you by the sign of salvation, In the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost"; 

This is performed with the laying on <term>imposition: the ritual act of placing hands on a person to confer a blessing or office</term> of hands and with white garments <note>original: "vestments"</note> bound to the head. This is what they call the Sacrament of Confirmation, which was never ordained by Christ or his Apostles. For Christ, the pattern and presiding example of the whole Church, was not confirmed in his own person; neither did he require a chrism at his Baptism, but water only. And therefore this "sacrament" cannot be necessary for salvation. By practicing it, a person blasphemes the Name of God. It was introduced by the prompting <note>original: "motion"</note> of the devil so that the people might be deceived and deprived of the true faith of the Church, and so that they would instead place their trust and confidence in these outward ceremonies <note>original: "solemnities"</note>.

The author contends that since Christ was baptized only with water, the addition of oils and specific priestly formulas is unnecessary and deceptive.</summary>
<keywords>Baptism, Chrism, Confirmation, Holy Orders, Sacraments, Liturgy, Church Reform, Roman Catholic Ritual</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Roman Catholic sacraments, moving from the discussion of Confirmation on the previous page to "Extreme Unction" (the anointing of the sick) and the practice of fasting.</meta>

<page-num>102</page-num>
<header>Of Baptism. Book 3.</header>

### *Of Extreme Unction.*

The seventh Sacrament of the Roman <note>original: "Romish"</note> Church is the extreme unction <term>extreme unction: the ritual of anointing a sick or dying person with oil for spiritual or physical healing</term> of the sick, which they attempt to prove by that saying of Saint James <note>See James 5:14-15</note>. But we do not find that it has been ordained by Christ or his Apostles. For if this physical <note>original: "corporall"</note> anointing were a Sacrament, as they would have people believe, Christ or his Apostles would not have been silent in demonstrating how it should be performed. When this is well considered, we should not dare to hold and confess, as an article of our faith, that this Sacrament was instituted by Christ and his Apostles.

### *Of Fasts.*

There is a two-fold fast: spiritual and physical <note>original: "corporall"</note>. The spiritual fast is to abstain from sin; the physical is to abstain from food and drink. However, a Christian has the liberty to eat at all times and to fast every day, provided that he does not fast superstitiously, as if it were a merit of self-control <note>original: "vertue of continency"</note>.

Note also that there are certain fasts which are not to be observed or commended by the faithful, but rather to be abhorred. These include: the fasts of the Scribes and Pharisees, which are ordained by Antichrist and reek <note>original: "smell"</note> of idolatry; the fasts of heretics and superstitious persons, which are observed by enchanters, sorcerers, and necromancers <note>original: "negromancers"</note>; and fasts dedicated to created things <note>original: "creatures"</note> rather than to the Creator, which are not grounded upon the Law of God. There are also disorderly fasts, observed with delicate foods <note>original: "viands"</note> of the highest price—such as fish, figs, raisins, and almonds—

<meta>The text breaks off here; the catchword is "which," indicating the list of luxurious fasting foods continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>The author argues that Extreme Unction lacks biblical authority and distinguishes between true spiritual fasting and the hypocritical or superstitious fasting practices of the Roman Church and occultists.</summary>
<keywords>Extreme Unction, Sacraments, Saint James, Fasting, Idolatry, Superstition, Necromancy, Asceticism</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the author's critique of superstitious and hypocritical fasts, specifically those involving expensive "fasting" foods that the rich enjoy while the poor suffer. It finishes the section on fasts and concludes the third book.</meta>

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>Chap. 4. *Of Baptism.*</header>

...which the poor are deprived of, and the rich gorge <note>original: "glut"</note> themselves with, whereby alms <term>alms: money, food, or other donations given to the poor</term> are withdrawn from the poor. Whereas, if they fasted in such a way that they afterwards ate a common diet of lower price, they might be better able to provide for their families and the poor.

<margin>1 Timothy 4:4</margin>
Moreover, fasts do not consist in abstaining from physical <note>original: "corporall"</note> foods <note>original: "viands"</note>, as if they were unclean; for all things are clean to those that are clean, and we are to refuse nothing that is taken with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the Word of God and by prayer. All these fasts mentioned above are rejected and detested by the faithful, and no man is to be blamed for not observing them.

## FINIS.

---

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on fasting, arguing that true fasting should facilitate charity for the poor rather than the consumption of expensive "fasting" delicacies by the rich. It asserts that no food is inherently unclean and that believers are not bound by superstitious religious dietary laws.</summary>
<keywords>fasting, charity, alms, 1 Timothy 4:4, dietary laws, religious hypocrisy, viands</keywords>
